I'm pretty sure ATC notified Company if only just the local ops folks. The checklist was handled correctly but as ALTN system failed and we were directed to go to manual. The cabin pressure spiked and dropped several times and then failed. That was certainly an enormous distraction and it took us a minute to get masks on and fully reengaged with the checklist. Feel like I could've done a better job leading in those moments. Will say that I was very happily surprised by how much our training kicked in; when the event got bad. Kudos to the training folks!

A routine flight changed as we began our initial descent. Aircraft pressurization began to fail which led to the loss of cabin pressurization. Between FL380 and FL360 the Auto Fail light illuminated; along with corresponding dashes in the FLT ALT window and LAND ALT window on the landing altitude selector panel. I was the PM for this leg; and as such I completed the QRH 2.4 Auto Fail Checklist. This drove the pressurization mode selector to be placed in the ALT mode. This did extinguish the Auto Fail light and temporarily allowed for control of the outflow valve. At this point the CPT and I felt pressure changes in our heads and noticed somewhat erratic oscillations in both the cabin differential and cabin altitude. The Captain made the decision to don the O2 masks at this point. I referred back to the QRH 2.4 Checklist as the cabin altitude was now not controllable. The checklist drove us to selecting the manual mode on the Pressurization Mode Selector. The Captain communicated with the cabin crew to; as to their status and the status of the passengers. We were approaching FL300 at this point and communicated with ATC that we needed lower; due to a cabin pressurization problem.Very shortly after donning our O2 masks the CAB ALT light illuminated along with the corresponding warning horn. Captain called for QRC Cabin Altitude Warning Checklist. We were granted lower by ATC as well as handoff to APP Control. Thanks to both ATC and Approach and Tower; we were able to basically keep our descent going all the way down from cruise to 6000'; and subsequent visual approach. The passenger O2 masks deployed automatically as we worked through the QRC Checklist. The Captain; again; checked in with the Cabin Crew to verify O2 masks had been deployed as well as their wellbeing. We learned here that a female passenger had fallen unconscious temporarily. She regained consciousness as we descended. As I continued to monitor the cabin altitude and manipulate the outflow valve the CPT let APP know we needed EMS standing by for her. At the completion of the QRC we continued on with 2.1 of the QRH and stayed with this checklist for the duration of the flight. The cabin altitude depressurized; as necessary; as we descended below 10;000 feet. The approach and landing were uneventful. I contacted Operations taxiing in to the gate and verified with them our request for EMS to meet us. They had not received word about the Passenger needing assistance. I fully thought I had contacted them airborne. This must have been missed on my part in all the commotion. Nonetheless; EMS showed up within a few minutes of setting the parking brake. The Captain proceeded to contact the Chief Pilot; Maintenance; and Dispatch to proceed with the necessary paperwork and communications. The things that I see could have been improved upon are communications and understanding task loading. Verifying each of our required tasks were accomplished could have been better. As these events unfolded rapidly; it definitely emphasized the importance of keeping a good pace; usually a slower pace; as tasks have the potential to be compounded.

Instructor and student pilot reported a planned engine out exercise resulted in a runway excursion.

During the initial take-off of a multi-engine training flight; the instructor retarded the mixture of the left engine to simulate an engine failure on takeoff. As the flying pilot; I executed the first two steps of the published emergency procedure (1. Throttles to IDLE; 2. Apply maximum braking) upon aural recognition of the loss of power along with a significant (45-60 degree) yaw to the left. To counteract the left yaw; full right rudder and differential braking was applied. The aircraft responded to the control input and swerved back to approximate alignment with the runway; but by then had deviated far enough left that the left main tire was off the hard surface and into the grass. The aircraft again yawed slightly to the left and the nose tire left the hard surface. Once the main and nose tires left the runway; additional control inputs to correct to the right were ineffective and the aircraft came to a stop in approximately 75 feet. Attempts to return to the pavement from the resting position were ineffective and the aircraft was shut down. Upon exiting the aircraft; the nose wheel was determined to be buried nearly to the top of the tire in a muddy rut which was 30-40 feet long. With the assistance of airport personnel and maintenance personnel from the flight school the aircraft was tipped back toward the tail far enough to raise the nose wheel out of the mud and put a 3X5 foot board under it to support its weight. The aircraft was pulled back onto the runway and towed to the flight school using a standard tow bar.As for a root cause analysis of the events leading up to the incident; I think there are several:1. Relative inexperience of flying pilot: I had 5.9 hours in the aircraft and this was my third flight with this instructor. Two previous flights occurred with a different instructor at a different school; the most recent being 35 days prior to this incident. I had to switch schools as the aircraft at the original training site became unavailable due to long-term maintenance issues. This was my second-ever engine failure on takeoff practice. The maneuver was not briefed by the instructor; though I assumed it was likely to occur.2. Slow reaction time: I noticed the change in engine noise just prior to the onset of adverse yaw. I believe I hesitated for a second or less prior to pulling the throttles to idle. This exacerbated the yaw which ultimately led to the runway departure.3. Misunderstanding of the written emergency procedure: I applied significant braking as I attempted to control the aircraft and prevent it from exiting the runway; to include differentially applying heavier braking to the right main. During a debrief with the instructor and flight school owner; they explained that the heavy braking may have reduced directional control of the aircraft. I saw no evidence of locked brakes; but I am not an expert in such matters. As a low time multi-engine pilot; I suppose I have to defer to the instructors' experience. Given the discussion surrounding the potential negative impact of applying maximum braking during this procedure it seems that the phrase 'Braking-As Required' or similar might be better than 'Braking-Maximum' as written in the flight school's current checklist.4. Failure of the instructor to back me up on the controls on only my second exposure to this maneuver. As mentioned; I may have hesitated briefly before retarding the throttles to idle. It was suggested that this may have allowed the situation to develop into and unrecoverable maneuver; but at no point did the instructor physically touch either throttle or verbally indicate I needed to take different actions.

While doing a multi engine training flight there was a loss of directional control on the runway. When performing a takeoff; the engine failure on takeoff maneuver was being performed. The mixture to the left engine was closed to simulate an engine failure shortly after applying power for takeoff. There was a momentary pause by the student ~ 2 seconds before the throttles were closed. As the throttles were closed the nose of the aircraft was pointed roughly 45' to the left side of the runway. While trying to regain control of the aircraft; the student at the controls applied max brakes to get the aircraft to stop. With the aircraft pointed towards the side of the runway; and max force being applied to the brakes; little usable rudder force was left for the instructor's rudder pedals. The nose was slowly pulled to the right; but the momentum of the aircraft caused the plane to come off the runway. The left main gear and nose gear were off the side of the runway in the grass with the right main still on the runway. Within the past 24 hours there had been substantial rainfall at the airport. The turf next the runway was wet and waterlogged. When the nose gear of the aircraft left the pavement; it caused the nose to sink into the grass ~ 12-14 inches. With the reduced clearance of the nose gear; and the right engine still over the runway; the blade of the right engine struck the pavement. After coming to a complete stop both engines were shut down and the aircraft wasn't moved until maintenance inspected the aircraft. After reflecting on the events that lead to this occurrence there a few lessons I have learned. First is having a more open communication with the student about what is expected of them during the recovery of a maneuver such as a single engine failure on takeoff. A more thorough brief should be discussed on what the corrective action looks like during this maneuver and what does directional control mean on the runway. A demonstration of the correct recovery done by the instructor might also be performed so a clear standard is set.

Air carrier Captain reported experiencing mechanical problems after pushback resulting in a return to gate.

We were scheduled for a ferry flight from ZZZ - ZZZ1 at XA00 local. Due to our current situation; I have not flown a lot lately; and as a new Captain; have not done a ferry flight. I showed up early; as there are extra things to do on a ferry; and my FO was DH and not scheduled to land until 40 minutes prior to our scheduled departure. I had contacted him the day before to say we would meet at the aircraft.I called Dispatch to check whether this was a repositioning ferry or a maintenance ferry; because the release just said ferry and there was a log entry saying it required a maintenance action. Dispatcher told me that it was just a repositioning flight. I went to the aircraft and cleaned; performed the initial preflight and checked all the switches (finding several things out of place) and circuit breakers. I initialized the ACARS and started my preflight flow. When I checked the last maintenance release form it was dated [date]. While I was loading the FMC the printer started sending a quite lengthy maintenance ferry document; and at some point after that a mechanic came in. He talked about the lengthy maintenance ferry document and I asked to verify it was a maintenance ferry and he said yes because the aircraft had 2 checks that were overdue. He discussed with me that there were no maintenance items that would affect the operation of the aircraft. He also let me know the aircraft had been in storage since the last flight. I called Dispatch back to let her know we were a maintenance ferry; and asked if it needed to be on the release as such. Dispatcher thanked me for keeping her in the loop and said no it didn't; and we were good with the release as is.As I started through the maintenance ferry document my FO showed up. I told him to get settled and I would catch him up on where we were. I said I had just started to go through the maintenance ferry document and it was going to take some time; it was 1X pages; out of sequence; and interspersed with things I had printed. I thought the ACARS copy had to be in the book also. There were a lot of major systems that had been disabled and circuit breakers pulled and reset; and I didn't want to rush through; needed to make sure everything had been signed off.He expressed concern that we were not going to get out on time and that his DH ZZZ1-ZZZ2 was the last flight that day. He was a little upset that they had called him to fly all the way from ZZZ2 to fly a 1 hour flight on his last day of reserve. I said we would try our best; but the aircraft had just come out of storage and we needed to be thorough; this and the flight being a ferry flight were operational threats. He went back to check the cabin for ferry items. The agent closed us up and the FO armed the doors; and I went to check them as well. We got all our tasks completed and did push late. Pushback and start were normal; we did the after start and I asked for taxi clearance. Then the R Gen Off EICAS message came on. I asked him to tell Ground Control that we had a maintenance item and needed to run a checklist; and to run the Gen Off checklist. He talked to Ground as he got the checklist; and just then we lost all electrics. I tried to start the APU but it would not start.Both engines were running; both generator switches were on; but we had only battery power. We decided to return to the gate; and the FO told Ground. He asked Ground if we were ok there for a few minutes; they said yes. Then he called operations to tell them we were returning to the gate. We also noticed the aircraft shaking; but only had backup engine instruments and could not check the vibration indications as all screens had gone blank. I had thought it was wind but looking outside; there really wasn't much. Standby instruments looked good. There was a delay while operations said they were deciding where to put us; and I heard him say we wanted to go back. After that he told Operations something along the lines of; 'well then; weare a priority handling aircraft.' I did not ask to get priority; nor was I asked if that was what we should do. I didn't feel we were ever in danger; and the FO subsequently told me that he said that he did it; so we could get our gate back because our screens had failed. I believe part of the issue was time pressure to get home.Not being sure what was going on with the aircraft; we chose to shut down the engines to be on the safe side. It may not have been necessary at the time; but we were right by the gate and there was no traffic that we were blocking. I thought about running the checklist and getting a gen back; but with the aircraft shaking also; decided against it. I told ground what we were doing; and called operations for a tow in. Ground asked if we needed anything and we declined. No equipment was requested; no assistance received. Maintenance subsequently replaced the right GCU but could not find a reason why the left gen dropped off also. They said the APU had a fault; which they cleared. They said the shaking was simply due to the aircraft being so light; no cargo; passengers; galleys; and not a lot of fuel; with the engines running. It was unlike anything I had felt before; but we were only 153;000 lbs; and I have never been that light; but they said that is what happens when they run engines with empty aircraft. They started both engines to see everything was normal and test the electrics and power transferring. APU started normally; engines were fine; and electrics fine except that the right gen needed to be cycled to get it to come online. As I was asking one mechanic about that; as it was not normal; they were shutting down. They restarted the right engine to check it again; and this time the gen came online normally. They said sitting for a while may have been the cause of the some of these issues; but all was operating normally now.We got the aircraft ready to go; waited a while for a new release form; and flew to ZZZ1 uneventfully.I'm concerned about the priority handling; and to Operations; not ATC. It was busy but I feel I should have rescinded that.

B767 flight crew reported Flight Director malfunction on approach.

Vectored to join the Rwy XX ILS inside ZZZZZ; called the field and cleared for the visual. Disconnected to autopilot to descend and join the glide slope (which was below us). Continued to hand fly since the Aircraft wouldn't lock the glide slope outside the localizer. As localizer came in; the flight directors remained on the horizon and unusable. I asked the FO (First Officer) to turn off and turn on both flight directors to regain their use. At that point (just outside ZZZZZ1) the flight directors were giving us good glide slope and localizer information. We put the gear down and commenced to slow to approach speed inside ZZZZZ1 (still hand flying) and I disconnected the autothrottles somewhere around 1000 ft. AGL. Approximately 600 ft. (inside 3 miles) we received an aural 'Glide Slope; Glide Slope' warning. At that time I noticed that while my flight director in the HUD and on the PFD was centered; the glide slope information was deflected all the way to the top of my display. A quick scan of the FO's PFD showed centered flight director as well. Checking the PAPIs for Rwy XX showed 4 red. I leveled off and added power to fly to the glide slope again; readjusted power; and landed uneventfully. No warnings or cautions were displayed.When we reconnected the Flight Directors inside ZZZZZ; descending on the glide slope; they came back directly where I wanted them showing me on glide slope and on course. I did not check LOC and glideslope annunciations on the PFD. Is it possible they did not capture the glideslope? I would doubt that since I got a Glideslope aural warning. I have no idea why the flight directors both sides had us descending below glide slope inside 3 miles on the approach. Wrote [a maintenance] entry; called [maintenance control] and conferenced in the Avionics tech for a verbal debrief on the gripe.I guess I could have caught the error had I been cross checking the glide slope on the right hand side of the HUD display; but I sit back far enough that I have to make an effort to see it; and it's not in my habit pattern on a visual. I'm normally working lineup; glide slope; airspeed; and any crosswind correction looking outside and through the HUD. It was my error for not scanning the PAPI to detect the gradual settle - which I'll put down to fatigue - but the flight director was centered! Long day. Error captured and uneventful landing - but very troubling to see the flight directors do that.

On visual approach to ZZZ Rwy XX; we were GS/LOC captured; on speed with the AP off. I was looking outside when the PF (Pilot Flying) asked me to cycle the FD's (Flight Directors). This was at approximately 1000 ft.; to my recollection; and I complied; ensuring the correct switches (FD's). After cycling them off then on; all appeared normal and the PF verbalized this. A few moments later; however; we were below GS which I noticed when I looked back outside and saw the PAPI. I remember hearing the aural 'Glideslope' warning once; but I do not remember exactly when this occurred. We did not receive any other alerts. The FD had been centered on my side; but I don't recall the GS indicator position. I did not notice the FMAs (Flight Mode Annunciators); which were likely no longer in approach mode: V/S (Vertical Speed) and HDG (Heading Hold) Hold; as I believe we never re-selected the Approach tile. I was looking outside at the PAPI which was red; and was starting to say this when the PF leveled off. He made airspeed corrections as well. We were red over white and stable at 500 ft. I did note then the GS indicated we were slightly low; consistent with a non-coincident PAPI. Landing was uneventful and we were VMC the entire approach with a visual clearance.The approach appeared normal to me until the PF asked me to cycle the FD's. Even immediately after; the aircraft appeared to be in the correct altitude/attitude. As I was focusing on making sure I had selected the correct switches (FD's); it took that small amount of time for the actual aircraft position to become apparent to me. I viewed my centered FD; which appeared normal; and visually crosschecked the PAPI's; which were abnormal - red over red; at approximately 800-700 ft. This led to a moment of confusion and I was not focused on the FMA's; which were likely in basic mode after cycling the FD's. As far as I remember; we never re-selected the Approach tile. With the delayed recognition of being low; receiving an aural GS alert; leveling off; throttle movement and airspeed monitoring; and thinking about a possible go around; a lot was occurring in quick succession. I failed to recognize the situation early and this could have led to an undesired state if left unchecked.My focus was outside until becoming distracted by the call to cycle FD's. My focus then shifted inside. While doing so; I failed to effectively monitor the aircraft position; PAPI; and FMA status. Focus must be on 'flying the aircraft' first and being a good pilot monitoring. I should have been more proactive in verbalizing the aircraft state; once noticed; and my attention should always be on active monitoring. I should have gathered more information about what the CA (Captain) saw when we cycled the FD's. Finally; my failure to notice the start of deviation from red over white to red over pink would have allowed more of a buffer to correct other failures; such as reselecting Approach tile or verifying the GS indicator against the PAPI as well as cross checking CA/FO indications.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
A320 flight crew reported a fumes event during initial climbout resulting in a return to the departure airport. The flight crew reported health issues and decided not to take the following flight.

During boarding a musty dry odor was discovered with the APU Bleed on and the issue was written up in the maintenance logbook and the cabin odor sheet was completed. Parties were then notified (dispatch and the Captain spoke with the ZZZ Chief Pilot); maintenance troubleshooted the issue and ended up deferred PACK 1 with the appropriate MEL. After departure and on initial climb out; the same musty odor returned intermittently. The Captain made contact with the cabin crew to check on if any unusual odors were present in the cabin- which they did not detect but were also wearing masks for coronavirus. As the climb continued; the Captain began to experience physical symptoms consistent with a fume event. The Captain asked the First Officer if he was experiencing any symptoms and he replied he was. At that time both crewmembers donned their oxygen masks using the 100 percent setting and decided that a return to ZZZ was the safest course of action. ATC was advised of an issue with the air conditioning system and request to return to ZZZ. No emergency was declared (aircraft was controllable; requested altitudes were granted and a pretty much straight course was given on return). The supplementary procedures for elimination of odor/fumes was run however since PACK 1 was deferred PACK 2 could not be turned off. Descending through 10;000 PACK 2 was turned off and the aircraft began depressurizing. The AIR PACK 1 and 2 procedure was followed and the RAM Air Valve began to ventilate the aircraft. Because this event happened on initial climb out and the extra fuel (FLT Plan had an alternate of ORD due to WX in DTW) the overweight landing procedure was followed. The Captain landed the aircraft at roughly 153;000 lbs. During taxi in; cockpit windows were opened to help ventilate. After the parking checklist was completed; the fume event and overweight landing were written up in the logbook and the associated cabin odor sheet. After all passengers were deplaned; the flight crew and cabin crew discussed the events that had just happened. The Captain notified the chief pilot and then both the Captain and First Officer contacted Medical and followed their directives.

I have had multiple recent events and am worried about continued exposure to possible dangerous chemicals. It seems maintenance only investigates/correct these issues after they have occurred. Sometimes; maintenance discovers the problem quickly which means they know exactly where to look to find the issue. These common areas that cause fume events (APU; engines; packs) should be inspected at least once a week to prevent a dangerous fume event.Objective cabin and cockpit sensors should be installed fleet wide to test for any dangerous chemicals in the air. The sensors should be able to warn Cabin and Flight Crews of the condition so it can be rectified. It should be set to warn us at levels that are much lower than what is dangerous so any negative effects of an exposure are mitigated.What is the status of the newer/upgraded cabin air filter installation that is supposed to remove these chemicals from the air?Flight crews should be able to proactively turn PACK 1 to OFF on descents to prevent exposure. We can only first be exposed and then run a procedure to hopefully remove the fumes.During boarding with the APU BLEED ON; I noticed an abnormal musty dry odor in the cockpit normally associated with a fume event/air quality event.Flight Attendants (FAs) were asked if they smelled anything unusual and they replied that they didn't.PACK 1 was selected OFF because the odor was present in the cockpit.The odor dissipated.The issue was written up in the maintenance logbook and the cabin odor sheet was filled out.Dispatch and the Dispatch Shift Coordinator (DSC) were notified as well as the ZZZ Chief Pilot.Maintenance secured PACK 1 closed and the item was deferred with the appropriate MEL.The flight left delayed due to the maintenance action.After departure and during initial climb out; the same musty dry odor returned with intermittent frequency and what seemed like reduced intensity.I was trying to determine if this was another fume event related to PACK 2.I called back to the Lead FA to see if they could smell any abnormal odors. The Lead FA reported that she did not smell anything abnormal.I texted Dispatch and notified them that we were having a possible fume event and we could return to ZZZ.As the aircraft continued to climb; I began to experience physical symptoms consistent with a fume event to include: numbness/tingling in the arms; fingers and top of head; lightheadedness; headache; nausea and fogginess. I asked if the First Officer (FO) was experiencing any symptoms and he replied that he was.I decided it was a fume event and we both donned our oxygen masks and used the 100% setting. A quick return to ZZZ was decided as the safest course of action.I took control of the aircraft from the FO; stopped the climb and notified ATC that there was an issue with the air conditioning system and we desired to return to ZZZ.ATC began giving prompt lateral and vertical instructions for a return to ZZZ.No emergency was declared because in my judgement; the situation was under control; the pilots were not compromised while using oxygen masks; the airplane had no control deficiencies. and the crew was already receiving expeditious handling by ATC.I pulled up the 'Supplementary Procedure for Elimination of Odor/Fumes in the Cockpit/Cabin' and began running it with the FO.Cross-cockpit and ATC communication was very difficult while using the oxygen masks.The goal was to eliminate the source of the fumes. PACK 2 would eventually have to be set to OFF; but since PACK 1 was already deactivated and deferred; it would result in the depressurization of the airplane. An emergency high-rate descent was decided against due to the proximity of mountainous terrain; the fact that the Lead FA did not report smelling any abnormal fumes and because it would further lead to an increase in workload while having to run various abnormal procedures while communicating with ATC.After running the relevant itemsin the fume event procedure; it leads you to consider the AIR PACK 1 + 2 FAULT to have a structured way to depressurize and ventilate the aircraft.During all this; the Lead FA noticed that the aircraft was descending and called the cockpit. I notified her that we were having a fume event; we were turning around and descending to ZZZ and to prepare the cabin for landing.I made an announcement to the passengers and notified them of an air conditioning problem and that we were returning to land.The FO assisted with the procedures and got the ATIS and ran a Landing Distance Assessment.At approximately 10;000 feet MSL; PACK 2 was selected OFF and the aircraft began depressurizing.The AIR PACK 1 + 2 procedure was followed and the RAM AIR valve was opened to ventilate the aircraft.We removed our oxygen masks following the aircraft ventilation. The abnormal odor subsided and now communication was much less difficult.The Overweight Landing procedure was followed and the aircraft was around 153;000 lbs upon landing.During taxi-in; the cockpit windows were opened for further ventilation.The fume event and overweight landing were written up in the maintenance logbook. The cabin odor sheet was filled out.After all passengers deplaned; both myself and the FO notified all FAs as to what happened and what actions we took. We notified them that we did not feel well and we were going to call Medical and seek medical attention. I advised them that if they were experiencing any adverse physical symptoms to call Medical and seek treatment. All FAs reported that they were fine.I notified the Chief Pilot about the event.I answered a call from the DSC asking about the event.We were both still experiencing negative physical symptoms and could not continue to operate another flight. Medical was called and we were seen at the Emergency Room for an inhalation injury.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Q400 flight crew reported an uneventful air return due to a flap malfunction during final approach at destination.

We had been cleared for the RNAV RNP Z Runway XX into ZZZ. We were on speed and profile and I began configuring for landing at ZZZZZ which is also where I called 'Runway Landing' as conditions near the field were VFR and we both had the runway in sight. 1 mile prior to ZZZZZ1 at approximately 4500 MSL with the gear down and flaps at 15 degrees; I called for FLAPS 35. The PM selected FLAPS 35 which resulted in no response from the flaps and a FLAP POWER CAUTION. I disconnected the autopilot and executed a missed approach at this point.As ZZZ Tower was closed; we switched back to Center. We advised them we were on the missed approach out of ZZZ and we were [requesting priority handling] and requested vectors and a climb to start heading back towards ZZZ1. We were given a northwest heading and cleared to 14000 MSL. Once we reached 14000 MSL I called for the FLAP POWER CAUTION checklist. The checklist drove us to reset the FLAPS CONT CB L7 Essential as it was NOT tripped. After the prescribed 20 seconds following the CB reset; the FLAP POWER CAUTION was no longer present and per the checklist we could select flaps as desired and that was the END of the FLAP POWER CAUTION checklist.I called for FLAPS 0 to configure for normal cruise. I then called the flight attendants and told them the situation that we were returning to ZZZ1 due to a flap malfunction; that we would be landing in 10 to 15 minutes; and to anticipate a normal landing. There were no special instructions for them and since they were seated there was no need to report back to me. Next; I made a PA to the passengers in which I told them we had an indication that there was an issue with our flaps and we were returning to ZZZ1 as a safety precaution due to it having more resources. I told them to anticipate a normal landing and apologized for the inconvenience and told them to follow the direction of the flight attendants. Next; I called Dispatch and informed them of the problem; our actions so far; and that we were currently headed back to ZZZ1. They conferred with Maintenance who wanted us to go back to ZZZ1 as they said Maintenance could handle it there. I conferred with my FO (First Officer) and we quickly decided that due to this being the last leg of a long day; it being night; [there being] terrain; smoke and GA activity in [the] vicinity of ZZZ; [a] closed Tower and that we were already over halfway back to ZZZ1; neither of us were comfortable with going back to ZZZ1. I advised Dispatch as such and our destination was changed to ZZZ1.We advised ATC that we would like vectors for the RNAV X Runway XYR; [the] longest runway available as XYL was closed. We were given direct ZZZZZ2 and a descent to 4000. I briefed a visual; backed up by the RNAV X XYR. I also briefed the missed approach procedure with FLAP POWER CAUTION in the event we encountered the same problem we did on approach in ZZZ. We ran the descent and approach checklists. We were told [to] cross ZZZZZ2 at or above 2000 and cleared for the RNAV X XYR. Our plan was to configure early in case of another issue with the flaps. Gear down and flaps extension in sequence to 15 degrees went normally and approximately 1 mile outside of ZZZZZ2; I called for flaps 35. Again there was no response from the flaps and we received a FLAP POWER CAUTION. As we had briefed; I called missed approach and upon positive rate we retracted the gear but did not attempt to move the flaps. ZZZ1 Tower gave us vectors to the northwest and a climb to 3000. We again [requested priority handing] and asked for emergency equipment to be deployed as a precaution in case there was any unknown damage to the aircraft that was causing this problem that could result in a fire or aircraft controllability upon landing. We then ran the FLAP POWER CAUTION checklist again.Due to the checklist stating that we were limited to ONE FLAPS CONT CB reset; we followed the flow chart to YES after 'Is the FLAP POWER CAUTON still illuminated' which drove us to leave the flaps in the last position and land with available flaps. Since we had flaps 15 degrees per the checklist; we pushed the GPWS Flap Override button and planned a flaps 15 landing. At this time we were on a wide right down wind for XYR heading east at 3000 ft. We asked ATC to inform company of the new situation that we went missed again and were currently planning a normal landing. Our EFB's had not given us performance for the entire flight so we amended IBugs to retrieve numbers for a flaps 15 landing in ZZZ1. We were given vectors for a visual backed up by the RNAV X XYR. We ran the descent and approach checklists. When all this was accomplished we were approaching a right base for XYR.I felt that fatigue was becoming an issue and moreover we didn't know if there were any deeper issues with the airplane that was causing the repeated flap power cautions. Taking this into consideration I felt that getting the airplane safely on the ground as soon as possible was of paramount importance. Because of this; we decided not to make any additional calls to the flight attendants or the passengers as their instructions and information we would pass had not changed from the first call. We made a normal approach and flaps 15 landing. We exited at Taxiway XX and requested the fire department to inspect the flap area of the aircraft visually and with thermal sensors for any abnormalities. They said there were none and we were give taxi clearance back to the gate.Normal taxi-in and shutdown with the exception of leaving the flaps in the 15 degree position. We were both present in the cabin for passenger deplaning and all passengers were very positive and grateful for a safe return to terra firma. I received a text from the Duty Officer whom I called back after making the Maintenance logbook entry and briefing Maintenance. Crew Scheduling immediately called to inform us we would be taking another aircraft to ZZZ to which the entire crew was not comfortable with so we were given a hotel in ZZZ1.

As we approached ZZZ on the RNAV Z XX; we began configuring for landing around ZZZZZ. As we selected flaps 35; the flap indicator froze at 15 degrees. A master caution FLAP POWER immediately appeared on the annunciator panel. Seeing this; we executed a missed approach and [requested priority handling]. We mistakenly brought the flap lever to zero; one notch at a time; as we were executing the missed approach procedure - but it did not move the flaps. We agreed to climb to a safe altitude before proceeding further. Once we were at 14000; we began to run the flap power caution checklist. We reset the L7 circuit breaker per the checklist; and the caution disappeared. We then put the flaps up one notch at a time to get back to a cruise setting per the checklist. Once we determined we may have a zero flap situation; we decided to return to ZZZ1 where we would have a longer runway; ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting); Maintenance; and more options for passengers. We then contacted Dispatch; told ATC our intentions; informed the flight attendants; and updated the passengers on the situation. The airplane was 'normal' at that point; but we suspected the flaps may not work again. As such; we decided to configure early; and execute a missed approach on the first indication of any abnormality. With that in mind; we used normal flaps 35 bugs from iBugs; EFB's were not receiving data for some reason. When we were cleared for the RNAV X XY R; we discovered the flaps once again would not extend past 15 degrees. This time we executed a missed approach and left the flaps at 15 degrees where they stayed for the remainder of the flight. We then ran the E&A checklist again. It concluded with us pushing the GPWS FLAP OVERRIDE and landing with available flaps. We then asked ATC for fire rescue trucks just in case; and set up to land on XYR. We landed without incident; and the trucks didn't see anything abnormal such as oil or other substances when they inspected the airplane prior to taxiing into the gate.

B767-200 flight crew reported malfunctioning flap sensor after flap retraction.

Departed runway XX in ZZZ with no issues. During our climb out everything was normal and we retracted flaps on schedule. After bringing the flaps to the UP position and indicating UP we received a takeoff config warning for flaps. This was confusing and alarming seeing how we were receiving a takeoff configuration warning while in flight: CONFIGURATION discrete light; FLAPS EICAS; and aural warning horn. I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) so I ran the QRH for the issue. The QRH gave no guidance for this alarm while in flight. I directed my FO (First Officer) to stay below 240 knots and we leveled off at 14;000 ft. while with ZZZ center. I advised ATC of our situation and decided to remain on our flight plan route but would be staying low and at 230 knots while working our issue. We eventually climbed to FL200 and stayed at 230 knots to protect the flap max altitude and flap speeds in case we had flaps out that were not indicating properly. Attempting to silence the takeoff configuration warning horn we brought the flaps to 1 and the alarm turned off. When we brought the flaps back to zero eventually the takeoff configuration warning came back on and could not be silenced. At this time I had my FO fly the airplane and talk to ATC while I contacted the company. Being on a 767-200 with no satcom or ACARS I used ARINC (Aeronautical Radio; Inc.) to get a phone patch to dispatch. Once I was communicating with Dispatch I advised them of our situation and got patched in with maintenance control. I explained the situation to maintenance control and then it took a few minutes for them to get back to me. They had us troubleshoot the alarm by reducing the thrust lever position. With the thrust lever reduced the alarm turned off. With this information maintenance control confirmed that there was a sensor issue causing the takeoff configuration warning to activate in flight. Communicating with maintenance control was difficult due to the horn and a weak and almost unreadable phone patch. After we determined this was a sensor issue; I was trying to ask if there was any way we could silence the alarm and got no response from maintenance. This whole process took until we were around the ZZZ2 area; about halfway to ZZZ1. At this time I heard a phone ringing sound over the radio and radio advised us that our phone patch had dropped. I advised them we needed to switch [frequencies] to stay in their radio coverage. Next; I requested to be patched back to Dispatch but after multiple attempts we were never able to be patched back to company. I tried two or three more times and never got the phone patch back. During the flight I was monitoring fuel. We were planned to land with 15;000lbs of fuel. Halfway in to the flight with us re-cruised to FL200 and 230 kts we were showing landing fuel of 17.8. I made the decision to continue to ZZZ1. At this point with our issue being confirmed as a sensor issue and plenty of fuel to make it to ZZZ1 and the takeoff configuration warning light; EICAS and horn were still on. The warning horn is very loud and very distracting. After talking with my FO we decided for the safety of the flight and our ability to communicate effectively to pull the aural warning circuit breakers to silence the aural warning horn. After doing this the horn stopped. I briefed my FO that we would not have altitude call outs on our approach. My FO had the idea and briefed me that once we had flaps deployed and the CONFIGURATION warning extinguished to reset the left aural warning circuit breaker so we would get normal aural alerts on approach and landing. This breaker is directly above the Captain's seat so it was easy to push back in. We landed uneventfully and with 17;000 some pounds of fuel in ZZZ1. Upon parking and talking with maintenance; they advised me that right nose wheel was showing cord down the middle of the tire. Their theory was that the tire was wearing too much on the scrubber after gear retraction and it was possible part ofthe tire destroyed the nosewheel air-ground sensor. Having this odd takeoff warning issue in flight was quite confusing and distracting with the warning horn blaring for 30 minutes while we were trying to fly; communicate and troubleshoot. This was an odd maintenance issue. Our plane was airworthy when we left ZZZ and the nosewheel tire was fine my FO and maintenance did exterior walk arounds and no defects were found. This weird situation took a lot of communication and troubleshooting. I think my FO and myself worked well and had good CRM during this event. I kept my FO in the loop with maintenance control and my FO kept me up with ATC. I think we made a good decision to stay low and slow to protect the flaps just in case there was some issue with a flap or slat hanging out that shouldn't have been. Being on a 767-200 with no SATCOM or ACARS makes communicating with the company difficult. Our VHF phone patch to the company was hard to understand and communicate. Multiple times I had to repeat myself; speaking slowly and deliberately. I had to tell maintenance control multiple times to speak up and slow down. When on with maintenance control I could hear multiple people in the background while we were talking. It seemed like they were using their phone on speaker phone; making it hard to understand them. Also I don't know why we lost the connection with them when I heard a phone ringing sound. ZZZ radio advised me that they hung up on us. This obviously was not good because I was unable to reestablish communication with the company and I don't understand why they would hang up on an airplane in flight. I would advise maintenance control to use their hand set or a head set while communicating with an aircraft in flight to help with communication clarity. SATCOM would have made communicating much easier than a VHF phone patch. I considered [requesting priority handling] but decided against it after troubleshooting with the company and determining this was just a sensor problem. Our flaps worked properly; we had plenty of fuel but we were distracted by the takeoff configuration horn blaring at us. In hindsight; [requesting priority handling] might have helped us get better communication with the company using ATC to help us communicate with them.

While climbing out from ZZZ we started to get a takeoff configuration warning. We consulted the QRH then contacted MX and determined it was a sensor issue. However; we were unable to silence the alarm while the flaps were up; so in the interest of safety and reducing distractions; we pulled the aural warning circuit breakers while we were in cruise. As we configuration for the approach we pushed a circuit breaker back in to get the RA callouts for our approach and landing phase of flight. We also monitored fuel quality while flying at a different altitude and airspeed than planned.

B737-800 flight crew reported an uneventful diversion due to unreliable airspeed and altitude indications during cruise.

Due to weather and a supposed power outage at the airport; we were delayed approximately 1 hour from our scheduled departure time. This was the start of leg 2 for the day as we already operated out of ZZZ. There was another issue I will discuss after the conclusion of our [priority handling] event. [The] FO (First Officer) was pilot flying at the time. We took off out of ZZZ1 in very light rain throughout our departure. My FO stated it was barely enough rain to notice on the windshield. Light chop may have been experienced temporarily at most; but it was mostly smooth on climb out. We were cleared to flight level 31;000 where we stopped our descent. Shortly thereafter; while autopilot B was engaged; the autopilot started a significant descent all by itself. Unbeknownst to me and after speaking with my FO on the ground; the FO noticed his altimeter jumped from 31;000 ft. to 31;800 approximately. As soon as the autopilot started its descent; I took controls from the FO; disconnected the autopilot and leveled the airplane at 31;000 using my altimeter. I don't think we lost much altitude because I almost immediately disconnected the autopilot to arrest the pitch down moment. ATC shortly queried our altitude and we read back 31;000. ATC stated he saw us at approximately 31;700. About that time I looked over at the FO side and saw his altitude was the same as ATC verified 31700 ft. and looked at my display; which showed 31;000ft. ALT disagree was showing. At the same time; I noticed the FO airspeed was significantly slower than my airspeed and cross-checked the standby indicator - FO airspeed approximately 80 kt. slow. Airspeed disagree showed.At some point; I issued a pan pan pan. Standby airspeed and CA airspeed was the same and based on our thrust setting and altitude there was no doubt my FO's airspeed indicator was incorrect; 70-80 kt. too slow for our thrust and pitch setting. At that point; I determined; maybe incorrectly as I analyzed things on the ground; that since ATC had his altitude readout; I was basing our actual altitude on my FO's display and airspeed on my display. My reasoning is that 700-800 ft. high was safer than 700-800 ft. low; close to the ground; during approach and landing. Since I was now flying airspeed on my side and altitude on my FO's side; my altitude fluctuated up and down due to a gigantic 4 ft. scan instead of a normal 10 in. scan. Once I determined I could not hold altitude as expected; I asked for a block of altitude for airspace protection and was granted that clearance. The QRH for airspeed disagree was started; which led us to unreliable airspeed. We completed the checklist for unreliable airspeed and turned back towards ZZZ1. At some point after this realization I changed our pan pan to [requesting priority handling]. ATC apparently missed our [priority handling request] as he [provided priority handling] for us several minutes after I made the call myself. Upon realizing our altitude and airspeed unreliable; and ATC confirming ZZZ2 was VFR; I decided to turn back around another time to divert to ZZZ2 as it was a safer airport. Eventually; several altitude step downs were given to us for our descent into ZZZ2. QRH was completed and calls to Dispatch were then attempted.FO tried numerous times to contact company to relay our status and was unsuccessful. We attempted several calls on ZZZ3 Radio with no response. We asked ATC to call company and to contact us via ZZZ3 Radio; with no response from Dispatch. We then called on Guard to ask them to contact our Dispatch and let them know to contact us on ZZZ3 Radio; communication with Dispatch was never successful. With everything going on; I did not feel comfortable having my FO heads down sending an ACARS message...we were too busy.Descent checklist was soon completed and approach checklist was completed below 18;000. Holds were also accomplished to allow us time for checklists and getting weather info and setting up for the approach into ZZZ2 which were indicating 1100 ft. ceilings and better than required visibility. At some point in the descent; below 10;000 ft.; my FO realized the EEC were both in alternate mode and a discussion commenced. We discussed the thrust lever position and thrust changes that occurred in ALT mode but due to our [priority handling situation] and attempting to get the airplane on the ground safely; I forgot to have the FO run the QRH for the EEC alternate mode. Due to having no weather forecast and knowing weather was in the vicinity of ZZZ2 due to the hurricane remnants; my main concern was getting the aircraft on the ground safely in as close to VFR conditions as I could get.After landing; while discussing the events with my FO; we realized we probably should have made time to run this QRH procedure. I just didn't have the weather info in flight to make a call to continue holding to accomplish this checklist instead of landing. Landing VFR in my mind was a safer option than running this checklist and possibly losing VFR conditions due to hurricane remnants. The approach was set up and briefed and we commenced our approach. Checklists completed. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) standing by for us. The approach and landing was uneventful.After landing we were given instructions to taxi down a taxiway; XX or XY; [which] I did not feel was safe for us to turn down [to] as it was too narrow for my comfort. I also had concern that the taxiway could support our weight and relayed to Ground Control that I would not be accepting that taxiway. We did a 180 on a closed runway as Ground gave us permission to do so and frankly; that was our only option due to where the aircraft was stopped on the taxiway.We then returned to [the FBO] and parked. [The] incident was written in [the] logbook with my initial impression on what happed; the caution messages we received and that I thought airspeed was good on my side only and altitude was good on the FO side only. Airplane was chocked and secured; no door seals were on the aircraft. We shut down; secured the airplane; and then did the supplementary procedure for powering the aircraft down. We then exited the aircraft and closed the door. We called for the FBO to remove the stairs from the airplane for security purposes. The stairs were then pulled back from the aircraft and we exited the Ramp into the FBO. [The] Chief Pilot; DOO; Dispatch and Maintenance Control [were] all notified via my personal phone. The earlier situation I referenced was a runway change at clearance for pushback. Since we had not started the engines or changed configuration; I had the FO change our assigned runway and then consulted the TLR (Thrust Lever Resolver) for new numbers. I showed the FO the TLR data and he verified correct data for runway change. I then read him the new data to input since we were pushing back. What I did not realize is that RTO1 had not been selected at that time; but all other number were entered. At some point during the takeoff; prior to 60 kt.; thrust was set; I noticed we had TO (Takeoff) selected instead of RTO1 based on the N1 setting. When I referenced our airspeed at this realization; we had already exceeded 80 kt. I think I made the 80 kt. call at 82 kt. I determined the safest outcome was to continue the takeoff based on our rejected takeoff parameters. I had in the back of my mind a 5 kt. difference in V1 between RTO1 and TO as I had looked earlier due to the weather in ZZZ1 at the time. This situation has led me to realize it is most likely a better habit to have the FO read off the TLR data and I enter the numbers myself in the FMC. This was something I just didn't catch as I was starting to get tired from sitting there for an extended time.[The cause was] airspeed and altitude [being] unreliable due to an unknown problem. After reflecting on what occurred; I believe none of the altitude or airspeed information on my FO's outboard display unit was correct. I erroneously believed that ATC's readout of our altitude confirmed my FO's altimeter was correct without realizing his entire system had likely failed; providing erroneous information to ATC. The weather from the hurricane was certainly a contributing factor as my main concern was getting the airplane on the ground safely and landing in VFR conditions.

Unreliable airspeed was the first issue. While flying level at FL310 it was my leg; and autopilot B was engaged. Suddenly; my altimeter shot up to FL317 and the autopilot initiated a descent. The Captain immediately took controls and disconnected the autopilot. As we were cross-checking and trying to gain an understanding of the state of the airplane; ATC queried our altitude because they showed us at FL317 instead of 310. Cross-checking revealed that the FO (First Officer) side was indeed showing FL317 while the CA (Captain) side showed FL310. Simultaneously; the FO-side airspeed showed an enormous slowing trend. Lastly; IAS and ALT disagree messages popped up on both the FO- and CA-sides.The Captain declared a pan pan pan at first then a bit later; [priority handling was requested]; but ATC apparently missed the call as he [requested priority handling] for us at a later time. The [priority handling] was reported [due to] unreliable airspeed and altimeter disagreement. I ran the checklist for IAS DISAGREE; which referred me to the UNRELIABLE AIRSPEED Checklist. In communicating with ATC; we determined that the standby and CA-side altitude did not agree with ATC; and the CA-side airspeed made the most sense when compared to the ATC reports. The difference was about 80 kt. between CA- and FO-side IAS. Also; the displayed GS was always within about 10 kt. of ATC's speed reports. At this point; the Captain was flying with reference to his airspeed and the FO's altitude.The Captain initially asked for a return to ZZZ1 and a block of altitude as he struggled fly with reference to both sides. Because there was still about a 700 ft. discrepancy between FO- and CA-side altimeters; it was decided to pick a field that had VFR landing conditions. The nearest such airfield was ZZZ2. As I continued with the checklist; we selected 'all on 1' on the ALT SOURCE switch. At that time; the 'disagree' messages went away; and the airspeed matched; but altimeters still did not agree. Upon reflection; I realize that the Captain had transitioned to the local altimeter setting below 18000; but I was still in the standard 29.92. Once I updated my altimeter setting; both altimeters matched. Now the only error message was 'source 2' because we had de-selected it. The checklist also directed to disable transponder altitude reporting. It occurred to us later that the transponder may have been providing ATC an erroneous altitude because it was coupled to the FO-side. At some point; unclear exactly when; we noticed the EEC switches were both showing ALTN with the corresponding ENG master caution. Once the UNRELIABLE AIRSPEED checklist was completed; we spent the rest of the flight trying to contact Dispatch about our [situation] and diversion; but at this point; we were unsuccessful as we were probably too low to communicate over ARINC frequencies. We were also busy setting up the approach into ZZZ2. We landed without incident.The second issue was departure with wrong takeoff thrust programmed. When we were finally ready to push and start engines; Ground Metering advised us on an updated ATIS and were told to expect Runway XXR departure. I reloaded the SID in the FMS with the updated runway and got a message that V speeds were erased. I went to the page to re-load the V speeds while the Captain referenced the TLR (Thrust Lever Resolver) for the new speeds for the new runway. As he referenced the TLR; he read aloud that we still had an R-TO-1 takeoff; same flaps; same weight; same N1 values; and same CG. He then read me the new V speeds which I loaded in the FMS. Since the engines hadn't started yet; we considered these items as part of the preflight brief and declined to do a runway change checklist. At some point; the Captain noticed that we were at full TO (Takeoff) thrust instead of R-TO-1 thrust. My low time on the aircraft prevented me from having the experience necessary to know that changing the runway not only deleted the V speeds; but also deleted the takeoff thrust settings. I should have verified all of the information was still correct as the Captain read it out.The cause of TO data error was task saturation. Weather conditions at ZZZ1: IFR / rain / 500 ft. CIG / winds gusting around 15 from the east. Outside factors [include] delay to cargo loading. Pushed an hour late. Updated ATIS 3 times while waiting to depart. All 3 said departing on Runway XY. Realizing the transponder was transmitting erroneous altitude information earlier would have greatly simplified matters. All performance data should have been reviewed in the FMC for the runway change.

CRJ-200 flight Captain reported an uneventful landing at destination after experiencing ADC1 failure during flight and successfully overcame failure.

I was called out on a reserve callout to deadhead to ZZZ to pickup an airplane that needed to be repositioned to ZZZ1. I noticed in the Maintenance log that Maintenance had been working on the standby Airspeed Indicator/Altimeter. I assume that this is why the airplane was stranded in ZZZ. First Officer and I completed our preflight checks and briefings to include the Non Routine Flight Operations task cards per normal; with nothing unusual occurring. We taxied out to ZZZ Runway XX; and departed normally via the ODP. The winds on takeoff were a strong gusty crosswind to about 30 knots from the right. The takeoff roll was normal with no abnormalities. We called positive rate; and then I called for 'Gear Up'. Shortly after selecting the landing gear up; all of my air data instruments went blank; and displayed Red IAS; ALT; & V/S flags. The autopilot was not engaged; and my flight director did not indicate with the loss of air data indications. I told my First Officer that I lost my airspeed and air data; and left the power set for takeoff and pitched for 10 degrees nose up. My First Officer read out the speeds on his speed tape and the standby gauges. While I had a hunch that his indications were correct; due to the Maintenance write-ups and recent work; and the unusual and immediate failure; we elected to initially diagnose this as an unreliable airspeed emergency; at least until we could verify that both the First Officer's ADC and the standby gauges were correctly indicating. I suspected an ADC 1 failure of some sorts. After reaching a safe altitude and completing the After Takeoff Checklist; I transferred the flight controls over to my First Officer; and told him to climb on course initially while we could work to verify that the airspeed indicators on his side were correctly indicating. ATC was notified of the instrument failure and of our request to climb on course for the time being. We were in VMC conditions and felt it was safe and prudent to continue to climb away from the terrain around ZZZ. As the airplane was empty; it's climb performance was exceptional. After verifying our speed; power settings; and pitch attitudes using the charts from the Unreliable Airspeed procedure we were able to affirmatively establish that both the First Officer's indications along with our standby instruments were indicating correctly. We at this point elected to abandon the unreliable airspeed procedure; as we still had two functioning airspeed indicators and instead address this as an ADC 1 abnormal procedure and failure. I felt that the unreliable airspeed procedure; while providing us with good situational information to verify that our other two indicators were functioning correctly; was irrelevant because we didn't have varying unreliable airspeed indications; but rather a complete loss of air data information. Although I suspected it was simply an ADC failure initially; due to our low altitude and critical phase of flight; we elected to initially treat the failure as an unreliable airspeed situation to assure that we were flying a safe pitch and power setting regardless of airspeed to reach a safe altitude clear of the terrain. ATC was updated that we suspected an ADC 1 failure. An emergency was never declared with ATC. We spoke to Dispatch and agreed that with the ADC 1 failure a diversion to the nearest suitable airport was not necessarily required; which is an important difference from the unreliable airspeed procedure; although we did discuss as a crew and with Dispatch the possibility of a diversion to ZZZ2 or another nearby airport along our route. We agreed that with the situation stable and well diagnosed; we felt it was pertinent; legal; and safest to continue on to ZZZ1. We landed in ZZZ1 where the ADC failure was written up in the Maintenance log as a discrepancy; and Maintenance was briefed on the phone. I called the Flight Dispatcher and debriefed with him as well; and he assured me that he was in agreement with our decision making and the [Dispatcher] was aware of the situation; and no further calls or reports were required. Maintenance later removed; and replaced ADC 1; prior to dispatching the aircraft on it's next flight. The cause of this event was a failure of ADC 1. I am curios as to whether or not the Maintenance work done on the standby airspeed/altimeter could have contributed to the failure of ADC 1. In terms of recurrence; and preventing this; from a flight ops standpoint I'm not sure what to recommend. However; I will say that this is the 2nd time in a month I have dealt with an unreliable airspeed issue; pitot/static issue; or ADC issue on the CRJ. Maybe I'm snakebit; but I have taken notice to the increase in frequency with these events. We train for this; and just a week ago I went through [training]. In our training we ran through the unreliable airspeed procedure. Because of this; I was familiar that if an initial climb is required; or just after takeoff; in the CRJ200 the checklist tells you to pitch to 10 degrees nose up at takeoff power. Fortunately; the recent familiarity with that procedure 100% helped; and was highly effective through the initial diagnosis and trouble shooting of our abnormality. There isn't a great checklist for 'loss of airspeed' in the QRH; you have to pick between unreliable airspeed; and an ADC failure. We used the Immediate Action Items from the unreliable airspeed checklist; along with the pitch/thrust reference tables; to help assure that we were climbing in a safe flight path state; and that our remaining operational airspeed indicators were properly functioning; however; then rediagnosed the issue as a full ADC 1 failure; and felt it was more prudent to treat this as an ADC failure as opposed to an unreliable airspeed emergency. I realize today though that in real life...It could be difficult to truly distinguish between the two. As a crew; we elected to start with the ultra safe option; and then once we gathered more information about the problem; were able to move into a different; and more accurate checklist; that more appropriately addressed the problem. If I could make a recommendation; I think that we need to add both memory items; and a QRC checklist for a suspected Unreliable airspeed or loss of airspeed immediate response. The immediate action items in the QRH; should absolutely be committed to memory; and probably be backed up by a QRC. While I was fortunately familiar with these; should we have a new Captain/ First Officer pairing on the aircraft in the future; that maybe isn't familiar with the aircrafts normal performance; this could potentially be an unforgivable consequence. Just a recommendation after taking some time to look back at the events of today.

B737 flight crew reported inflight shut down and diversion due to hydraulic system failure.

Captain and I [deadheaded] to ZZZ to pick up a 737-800 to ferry back to ZZZ1 due to a loss of system A hydraulic fluid. Preflight showed no leaks and everything ok with the aircraft. I was PM and upon takeoff the Master Caution light came on for engine driven hydraulic pump for system A. The light went out and continued. Abeam ZZZ2 the master caution came back on for engine driven hydraulic pump number 1 system A. I pulled out the QRH and ran the Hydraulic Pump Low Pressure checklist which had us turn the pump switch off. With quantity and pressure still good using the electric pump we decided to continue to ZZZ1. Maintenance techs on the aircraft agreed with the decision. Soon after passing ZZZZZ intersection the number 1 Engine Oil Filter Bypass indication on the upper engine MFD illuminated. I pulled out the QRH and we decided to request a lower altitude since we knew we could not maintain level flight with one engine at idle. We asked for a descent to FL 200 and told them we were working on a problem with our left engine. Since the OIL FILTER BYPASS indication remained illuminated the next step per the QRH was to shut the engine down. As a result we had to land at the nearest suitable airport. We decided that ZZZ3 was the best choice since it was close the weather was good and we were both familiar with the airport. I continued with the checklist as [the Captain] flew the aircraft; [requested priority handling]; and requested the diversion. We were cleared direct to the airport and a descent to FL 70. Shutdown and descent proceeded normally with me accomplishing the shutdown and [the Captain] continuing to fly and maintain communication with ATC. We then moved to the one engine inoperative and landing checklist which included calculating single engine landing distance. Hydraulic system A at this point had gone down to 25 percent. We prepared for the possibility of losing total system A pressure and a manual gear extension but was not a factor as the gear operated normally; [the Captain] performed a visual approach and landing with a safe landing in ZZZ3. We then sent a message to dispatch via ACARS that we were safe on the ground.

First Officer and I deadheaded to ZZZ to pick up a 737-800; which had been down for maintenance due to failure of the number 1 engine driven hydraulic pump failure and loss of system A fluid. Upon arrival we did our normal preflight and found no problems with the aircraft. The 3 Tech OPS employees who fixed the aircraft were embarked and we prepared to fly.Start up; taxi; and takeoff were normal. I was flying pilot and [First Officer] was monitoring. Early in the climb master caution light for the hydraulics came on and [First Officer] noted that the low pressure light for the engine driven hydraulic pump on engine 1 was on then quickly went out. Thinking it was anomaly with sensor and hydraulic quantity and pressure normal we continued. We were abeam ZZZ2 and the master caution for Hydraulics once again illuminated and [First Officer] noted the Low Pressure light for engine driven hydraulic pump on the left (number 1) engine was illuminated and stayed on. [First Officer] pulled out the QRH and proceeded to run the Hydraulic Pump Low Pressure checklist which lead to the pump being turned off. With quantity and pressure still good using the electric pump we decided to continue. We did get one of the Maintenance Techs to come to the flight deck and we showed and conversed with him about the issue. Nothing changed our thought process so we continued.Soon after passing ZZZZZ intersection and headed directly to ZZZZZ1 intersection; the number 1 Engine Oil Filter Bypass indication on the upper engine MFD illuminated. [First Officer] once again pulled out the QRH and we decided I would continue to fly and talk and he would run the checklist. We were at FL300 and decided to request a lower altitude as we knew we could not maintain level flight for long with one engine at idle. We asked for and received a descent to FL200 and told him we were working on a problem with our left engine. [First Officer] worked our way through the checklist resulting with the OIL FILTER BYPASS indication remaining illuminated. Per the checklist the next step was to shut down the engine and as a result of that we would need to land. We chose ZZZ3.[First Officer] continued the checklist as I [requested priority handling] and requested to divert. We were cleared direct the airport and a descent to 7;000. Shutdown and descent proceeded normally with [First Officer] completing the shutdown checklist. With the engine secured we moved on to the one engine inoperative and landing checklist to include the non-normal single engine landing distance. As we got closer to ZZZ3 the hydraulic issue took another turn. The quantity began to change first climbing to 106 percent and then slowly starting to decrease to mid-70 percent and then working its way down slowly till as we were coming down final it was in mid-20's. [First Officer] brought up the possibility of losing the 'A' system; so both of us were both prepared should that happen. Fortunately we did not have to run that checklist. Visual approach and landing was uneventful and normal. Landed and taxied to parking spot.We sent a message to Dispatch using ACARS that we were safe on the ground. The call I got after we had been on ground for 15 min. or so from the FODM gave me the feeling that it didn't go through but it was sent. It was confirmed by maintenance that in fact the 'A' system was depleted to about 25 percent and still leaking.

Flight Crew reported recurring ECAM messages after a rejected takeoff and subsequent maintenance action on the next flight.

The aircraft had preexisting maintenance issues when we received it for dispatch. There was a Class II Flight/Control maintenance message that was defferred. The number 3 IRU was differed from an inbound write up that stated the 'Capt Mach/Airspeed Inop and Nav/Alt discrepancy repeat writeup went to Air Data Capt3 position.' The MEL required that IRU 3 be maintained in the off position. Finally; the First Officer noted a skid mark on the number 1 tire that was subsequently found to be within limits by maintenance. Our Flight was cleared for take off with the Captain flying and Tower indicating that there was a 5 knot tailwind. The 100 knots call out had not yet been made and the thrust levers had been set to FLX/MCT when we received a Level II ECAM. The Captain glanced at the ECAM and noted an Auto Flight Auto Thrust Off ECAM. The Captain elected to continue the take off and to set TOGO thrust. The Captain's thinking at this point was that an Auto Thrust Failure would not affect the ability of the aircraft to fly and that setting TOGO would help with the tailwind. The First Officer then stated that there was another ECAM which indicated an Auto Flight Rudder Travel Limit System Failure. At this point; the V1 call out had not yet been made so the Captain elected to abort the take off. The Captain's thinking at this point was that there was a question now as to the ability of the aircraft to fly since the additional ECAM was potentially a flight control issue and the fact that both ECAMs were received after thrust power had been set. The Captain performed a rejected take off procedure. The aircraft appeared to be under normal control with no other apparent issues so just prior to bringing the airplane to a stop; the Captain instructed the First Officer to make a PA announcement for the passengers to remain seated. The Captain wanted to clear the runway at Taxiway X which is approximately halfway down the 10;187 foot runway but noted to the First Officer that it appeared that the aircraft was not moving forward easily after coming to a stop. At this point the First Officer and Captain discussed the possibility of a tire failure as a potential reason for the difficulty in moving the aircraft but it had not felt like a tire failed. We decided to tell the tower we were going to maintain our position on the runway until we could figure out what the issue was. At this point; we received a call from the flight attendants concerning a faint rubbery/acrid odor that was perceptible in the cabin. The Captain noted that the brake temperatures were still between approximately 450 and 550 degrees Celsius; although increasing; with no other abnormal system indications. The Captain and First Officer discussed that the smell was most likely from the aircraft tires as a result of the rejected takeoff and informed the flight attendants and passengers. The Captain was subsequently able to move the aircraft forward surmising that the aircraft may have been in a low spot on the runway that may have caused the difficulty in moving forward. As the Captain moved the aircraft slowly forward he noted that the aircraft was now moving freely and that there did not appear to be any issues with the tires. The First Officer requested from tower to clear the runway at Taxiway D; we completed our checklists; briefed our passengers and coordinated clearance to hardstand parking Spot 20 so that maintenance could look at the aircraft's condition. Upon arriving at parking Spot 20; the Captain talked with maintenance over the intercom and asked them to inspect the tires and the rest of the aircraft as a result of the rejected take off. Maintenance indicated that there were no visible issues except for the fact that the original skid mark on the number one tire was now larger. After maintenance inspected the aircraft exterior they brought the air-stairs up to door 1L and boarded the aircraft to run maintenance system checks. The wheelswere chocked and the parking brake was released to help cool the brakes. The Captain and Station Manager discussed deplaning the passengers and returning them to the terminal to await the results of the maintenance procedures. The Station Manager did an outstanding job of taking care of our passengers during the deplaning process and also provided our passengers with a complementary meal voucher. The Captain subsequently communicated with Maintenance Control; dispatch and the Duty Manager concerning the rejected take off. The Flight and Cabin crew also debriefed each other concerning the rejected take off. The Captain and First Officer discussed with Maintenance Control what the maintenance plan would be for the aircraft since we were still scheduled to take the aircraft to ZZZ1 and there appeared to be multiple maintenance issues. Maintenance Control indicated that they would perform various checklists and resets. The First Officer advocated that if time permitted that we should attempt to bring in a 320 Systems specialist if possible to answer some of our concerns including why we received the ECAMS after what we thought should have been an inhibited time period after take-off power was set. ALPA Safety reached out to the Captain during this time period so the Captain asked if ALPA Safety could connect the flight crew with an A320 systems specialist to talk about these issues which they did. Maintenance Control subsequently cleared all the maintenance issues with the exceptions of deferring the Auto Thrust system and Class II maintenance messages for Flight/Control and Air Bleed. Maintenance also changed out the number 1 tire due to the skid mark being worse after the rejected take off. We were subsequently dispatched again from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on the same aircraft. Just after take-off roll and beginning the climb out; with the Captain flying; the Captain lost his airspeed and mach indications. The Captain transferred control of the aircraft to the First Officer and the First Officer continued the climb out. The Flight then received a Nav/Alt Discrepancy ECAM. We performed the checklist. In order for us to restore the Captain's Airspeed/Mach indication we had to select Air Data Capt3 for the Captain just like the previous write up. We also had to select the First Officers Auto Pilot 2 since the Captains Auto pilot 1 would level off 500 feet off altitude. We Contacted Dispatch to get a phone patch to Maintenance Control and told Maintenance Control we were still having Air Speed; Mach and altimeter issues for the Captains side and wrote up the issues. We then proceeded to ZZZ1 with no further issues.

Rejected takeoff due to multiple ECAMs which were triggered and addressed as we transitioned from low speed to high speed regime. The reject actions were as per SOP and the flight attendants thanked us for a prompt Remain Seated; Remain Seated notification. Taxi back to ramp and a multi-hour maintenance delay ensued.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
CRJ200 flight crew reported a #1 IDG light illuminated on takeoff and elected to continue; subsequently turning off the #2 IDG; causing the deployment of the Emergency Air Driven Generator and resulting in an air turnback.

The first 3 flights were uneventful and on arrival in ZZZ we were swapped into Aircraft Y - a broken airplane for ZZZ - ZZZ1. We were then swapped into Aircraft X - an airplane coming from the hangar that was a first flight and had a deferred APU. There was no ground air available at the gate and we were now an hour late. We boarded 30 passengers and had a Company Dispatcher Jumpseater. We started one engine at the gate and taxied out and performed a cross bleed engine start for #1. ATIS was reporting wind shear and we used wind shear numbers for takeoff on XXR; [Taxiway] XX; with ignition ON.On the takeoff roll I noticed an intermittent IDG 1 caution message; followed by an intermittent CONFIG SPOILERS warning message; a BTMS 3 that was dashes and two probe/window heat messages. I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. I believed the message to be associated with a MEL on a previous flight; and I said; 'Associated; continue;' and continued the takeoff. The winds were very gusty. After takeoff we had a GEN 1 caution message and I ran the QRH for GEN 1; and in the process I accidentally switched off GEN 2; resulting in the ADG deploying. We [requested priority handling] and returned to ZZZ; landing on XYR. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) was there and escorted us to Gate XXX. No injuries or complaints were reported. We were met by Maintenance and then had a 5-way call with Company; Maintenance; [another person]; and one or two other people. I explained what had happened and told them of my mistake. I and the First Officer said that we were done flying and we were taken off our schedules. We then had a call with Maintenance and wrote up the airplane; including the #1 IDG; ADG deployment; and spoiler warning message.I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. Once airborne; and running the QRH; I should have confirmed that the GEN1 switch was selected and confirmed with the flying pilot prior to actuating the switch.

The day began early with an XA45 wake up to accommodate an XB45 van and [an] XC15 show. We completed the first three flights of the day without issue.
