Upon landing in ZZZ and swapping our good airplane for the plane we were taking to ZZZ1; we found out that that aircraft had maintenance issues and would require us to swap aircraft again. We were informed that there would be a delay in getting a new aircraft from the hangar. After waiting for about an hour the aircraft was finally coming from the hanger and we found out that it had an inoperative APU and it was its first flight of the day. Additionally; we would be having a Company Dispatcher in the jump seat. We were able to complete our first flight of the day items; acceptance checklist to include the first flight of the day items; complete an air start; push back; single-engine taxi out; and complete the cross bleed start without incident. We were set up for a wind shear takeoff with continuous ignition on.We were given a lineup and clearance and taxied onto the Runway of XXR at [Taxiway] XX. After a momentary wait; we were then given the takeoff clearance with a turn to the north. I was the flying pilot at the time; so I was given controls upon completion of the takeoff checklist. I pushed the thrust levers up and commanded for thrust to be set; the CA (Captain) confirmed thrust set and guarded the thrust levers. Shortly after this; a caution message appeared and the CA called out 'IDG 1' and called for the abort initially; but then said; 'Wait; that's associated.' The CA did not perform the abort; so I continued to fly the plane to ensure the positive control of the aircraft. Shortly after this; a warning message appeared momentarily; and the CA called out; 'Config Spoilers;' and the message disappeared. We continued the takeoff normally and began our turn to the north per ATC instructions.I was initially hand flying but shortly after reaching acceleration altitude; I called for the autopilot to be engaged. I called for the after takeoff checklist and noticed the caution messages that were present and called for the QRH. The Captain began to run the GEN 1 caution message QRH for the caution messages that were present. We noted the associated probe and window/windshield heat messages. While he was running the QRH he called out; 'GEN 1 off/reset; then on;' and reached up to perform this action. It appeared that he accidentally reset GEN 2 and the aircraft went dark momentarily; our EICAS and instrumentation screens went dark momentarily; and we heard the ADG automatically deploy. The CA immediately acknowledged his mistake and I continued flying by hand to maintain positive control of the aircraft while we sorted out the generator issue. The CA turned GEN 2 back on and communicated with me that we should return to ZZZ; I agreed.The CA then communicated to ATC that we needed to return to ZZZ and [requested priority handling]. The CA then communicated to Dispatch; the FA (Flight Attendant); and passengers that we were returning to ZZZ and to expect a normal landing. He did mention that there would be emergency vehicles near the aircraft; but that they were just a precaution and not to worry. We were then given vectors for the approach to Runway XYR; giving us time to brief our approach and landing; complete our in-range; approach; and landing checklists. We completed a normal landing; taxied back to our departure gate of XXX with an emergency escort; and arrived at the gate without issue.It would have been wise to perform the takeoff abort procedure at the earliest possible indication of an abnormal situation while the airspeed was still low and safe to do so. This would have prevented handling the aircraft issued in the air. Additionally; it is important to always confirm guarded switches with our fellow crew members to avoid making a stressful and abnormal situation worse.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
CRJ-200 Flight Crew reported overboard valve failure resulted in pressurization failure.

Our preflight; deice; and taxi all went normal. We took Runway XX as cleared and took off. We made our initial climb and made our left turn towards ZZZZZ as directed by ATC. Sometime after that while in the climb we received an OVBD COOL caution message and INBD COOL FAIL status message. We ran the QRH and it advised to simply monitor pressure. All indications were in the green so we continued to climb. I noticed and brought cabin alt. to the Captain's attention when it was around 5;200 [ft.] and the cabin rate showing an increase. I were at about FL180 at that point. When the cabin got to around 6;000 [ft.] I brought it to his attention again. All indications were green at this time but the cabin alt. was slowly continuing to increase. When the cabin alt. turned yellow we immediately called ATC for lower and to return to ZZZ. They gave us 13;000 [ft.] and direct to ZZZ and we began our decent and turn back. We descended around 2;500 ft. per minute initially but then I increased it to 3;500 ft. per minute. We received a cabin alt. warning message while in the descent and we promptly put on masks [received priority handling] and ran the QRC then QRH. The cabin pressure started decreasing in the decent. I was still flying and talking to ATC. Captain was running the QRH; talked to the passengers dispatch and the flight attendant. The pressure stabilized around 13;000 [ft.] while in the descent but because of the terrain and altitude we had to level off at 13;000 [ft.] and not knowing when ATC could get us lower the Captain made [an] announcement to the pax (passengers) that masks were going to be dropped and then we dropped the passenger oxygen masks as directed by the QRC. At some point ATC asked if we wanted to divert to another airport and we declined due to the increased workload that would have presented to figure out new airport Information. We I ran for new landing numbers to make sure we wouldn't land over weight and we plugged in landing numbers from our speed cards. We used weather from when we took off from ZZZ and we ran the descent check when able. We knew winds favored Runway XX so we asked for the RNAV Runway XX received vectors and then landed. We then taxied to the gate and began calling the company to inform them we were ok and what happened. The cause of the event was the OVBD COOL and INBD COOL FAIL status message. We could have asked for lower or to divert sooner but we saw a slowing increase rate in cabin pressure and thought that it may have been a plane that kept higher cabin pressure. We monitored the pressure the whole climb out while everything was showing green indications and acted as soon as green indications went away.

After takeoff in the initial climb we received an OVBD COOL caution message and an INBD COOL FAIL status message and I ran the QRH for the OVBD COOL message and the QRH stated that if cabin pressure was normal that 'no further action required.' All indications at that time and continuing into the climb appeared normal. At approximately 18;000 feet I took a photo with my phone of ED 1 & 2 so I could remember what to write up when we got to ZZZ1. Indications at that time were normal showing a 100FPM rate up with a cabin altitude of 5;500 feet all indications were green. The First Officer and I were observant of the pressurization system as we discussed the training I had received in the hypobaric chamber. As we continued our climb at approximately 27;000 feet my First Officer pointed out that the cabin altitude readings felt a little high to him and this prompted me to open and begin reading the section on pressurization in PRM. At this time the cabin rate and cabin altitude began to increase at a quick pace and it became obvious that something was incorrect. I notified ATC that we were having a pressurization issue and that we needed to level off then begin a decent to 10;000 feet or the lowest he could give me with regards to the mountainous terrain in the area and that we would like a turn back. ATC gave us a decent clearance to 13;000 [ft.] and a left turn direct ZZZ. I entered ZZZ in the FMS and confirmed that 13;000 feet hand been entered into the altitude preselect. I had the First Officer continue flying and I started the CABIN ALT caution QRH after beginning the decent we got a CABIN ALT warning I then [received priority handling] with ATC and I began the QRC and QRH after donning my O2 mask and ensuring that the FO (First Officer) had donned his as well. I called the flight attendant and informed her that we were having a pressurization emergency that we were returning to ZZZ; that the O2 masks might drop and that we would be on the ground in approximately 18 minutes. I was hesitant to drop the masks if it was not 100% necessary so I again called the FA to [assess] the cabin and she didn't want to make the call so with the cabin altitude at approximately 13;000 [ft.] and no estimate of when we would be able to descend further I made a passenger announcement that we had had a problem with our pressurization system and that the oxygen mask above their heads would be dropping down momentarily I then selected the PASS OXYGEN switch light as directed by the QRC. I continued to run the QRH and communicate with ATC the workload was extremely high. After [descending] to a safe altitude I removed my mask and made a passenger announcement that it was now safe for them to remove their mask. We then attempted to get landing data for ZZZ but the FMS did not send back good data so I inputted the speeds manually off the 43;000 lbs. card. We ran the decent check and prepared the aircraft for landing. We landed in ZZZ without incident a smooth underweight touchdown well below 100FPM. We taxied to the terminal and I shut down the engines because we had received an ACARS message that ZZZ Operations had gone to lunch and there would be no one there to accept us. After a short while ZZZ ground staff arrived and I started up #2 and taxied to the gate. We were met by the fire crew and I answered his questions we then deplaned. All passengers appeared to be ok a few appeared slightly shook up from the experience. Failed OVBD COOL valve.

text:
C150 pilot reported multiple issues with the passenger door opening in flight on a rental plane.

The planned flight was VFR from ZZZ to ZZZ1 via ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 at XA:00 on November [date] 2020 in Aircraft X (Cessna 150) rented from Company. I was PIC; Person Y was the only passenger. We had previously flown Aircraft X on July [date] 2020 from ZZZ; ZZZ4; ZZZ3 and had noted that the passenger door was not closing properly -- a small gap in the upper-left corner of the window frame allowed wind to enter the cabin. The owner of the plane investigated the issue then and found that the upper window frame was bent. I assumed that the issue was fixed by an A&P mechanic after the investigation. The plane has been regularly flown by other pilots since July.On November [date] 2020; I noticed no irregularities during pre-flight. During run-up; I noticed that the gap in the passenger door was still present and was a bit bigger than I remembered it from July. I thought that the slight wind in the cabin would be unpleasant but not otherwise an issue and continued with the flight. During the take-off roll just after rotation; the passenger door swung open. Once we were stabilized on the downwind; I shut the door and reassured my passenger. However the passenger door swung open again -- the wind through the upper-left gap torqued the entire door outward and that overpowered the door latch. So I requested landing clearance from ZZZ Tower and executed a precautionary landing without any incident. I taxied back to parking; shut off the engine and investigated the passenger door. The upper window frame was flexing slightly and could be bent to snap into the correct position. I pushed the frame into the correct position; verified that the frame was now snug against all the door frame inserts and that no wind was leaking into the cabin.I took off from ZZZ around XB:00 and noted no issues this time. As we were transitioning ZZZ3 Class D airspace; my passenger noted that she heard some sound from her door. I verified that the gap in the window frame was not present and that the door was shut properly. Shortly after we flew through the Class D; my passenger also reported that she could feel cold air from near the lower-right part of her door. As we flew past the marina; the door again swung open. This time the door shook violently which caused the window also to be flung open. I requested landing clearance from ZZZ3 was given priority and then I clarified my situation. I noted that reducing the throttle helped remove the violent door shaking. I reached over to shut the door; then pulled the upper window frame back into the door inserts and then closed the window. The ATC alerted me with a low altitude warning; so I decided to ignore the door and climb 300 ft. to intercept the glide slope and fly the plane first. As I increased RPM; the door again flung open. The door was twisting and wobbling around the hinge like a sheet of paper with the hinge as a paper-clip; and either wind or resonant frequency was increasing the severity of the wobbles. My passenger held the door to dampen its shaking. The landing at ZZZ3 was without any incident; and I taxied to a maintenance shop on the field. An A&P mechanic diagnosed that the passenger door needs to be replaced entirely and that the plane was not airworthy. We drove back to ZZZ after ensuring that the owner of Aircraft X knew what had happened and where to find the plane's key.In follow-up communication with the owner; I do not believe that the plane door was inspected and fixed by an A&P mechanic in July. The owner mentioned that he adjusted the door latches and attempted to bend the window frame back into place. This 'fix' ensured that the 'door shut properly 90% of the time'. He mentioned that he drove up to ZZZ3 with a spare C150 door and replaced it -- I do not know that he is qualified to make such repairs. His name does not show up in the airmen registry as holding an A&P license. The owner also mentioned that he was checking the door occasionally and that it had clearly worsened in the lastcouple of weeks and that there is no strength left in the window frame.Based on our conversations; I believe that the owner fixed the discrepancies that pilots reported using methods that are not by the book.(1) Normalization of deviance. I should have canceled the flight after landing at ZZZ after the initial trouble with the door.(2) Normalization of deviance. Owner should have replaced the door in July; rather than waiting for the door condition to get worse and create an [issue].(3) Crew management. I should have briefed my passenger during/after the [event]. She thankfully did all the right things (e.g. dampen the door vibrations) purely on instinct.(4) Aviate & Declare. I did not use 'emergency' or 'mayday' in my communications; despite that; the ATC at ZZZ and ZZZ3 both realized that something was up and gave me priority. Kudos to them. When diverting to ZZZ3; I flew very close to the prohibited airspace near marina to minimize my flight path to the runway.(5) Pre-flight Airworthiness Check. I should have insisted on viewing the maintenance records of the airplane to verify that my previous squawks were satisfactorily addressed.

Air Carrier flight crew reported an uneventful divert due to a fume event during cruise.

During cruise flight at 40;000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously the master caution came on for ELEC and the TRU (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. I as Captain was Pilot Flying and initially transferred control to the First Officer for me to chase down the TRU checklist. I accomplished the checklist; noting that approach mode with the flight directors would be unavailable... At this point the smoke was getting thicker; and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established we notified ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude; and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that the First Officer made me aware that all his flight and NAV displays had failed. He thus transferred control back to me as the Pilot Flying and he took over the smoke/fire/fumes checklist in the QRH.ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1; but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport so that was closest. We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach; and used our emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in order to expedite landing. At this point the First Officer discontinued the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20; having noted at step 16 that we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. I asked the First Officer to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch but at that point the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the master caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TRU and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit.With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. I disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS XXL. I quickly realized that electric trim was inoperative and proceeded to trim manually. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so I asked the First Officer to back me up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident where CFR was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR (crash fire rescue) to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside; we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our passengers stop breathing fumes.After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. Then we took a breath and asked each other (at the same time) 'well; how'd that go'. Of course sitting on the ground I feel like I can armchair quarterback the situation and nitpick some of the decisions; but overall I feel like we handled the situation well. We had good crew coordination given the circumstances (on O2) and the First Officer did a great job of running the checklists as well as keeping an eye on my flying once we had to transfer controls back to me. It did feel weird turning away from ZZZ2 since it was practically right below us; but I still feel like it was the correct decision given the circumstances and the amount of time it would take to descend; and how much of a distraction an orbiting descent into mountainous terrain would be while trying to deal with smoke.One thing I would do differently has to do with after the situation was over on the ground. I ended up talking with the Chief Pilot; then the firefighters; then the mechanic outside the aircraft on the ramp. By the time I got back inside I couldn't find the flight attendants to debrief and see how they were doing. Upon opening the flight deck door the A had told me that they were all fine; but I would have liked to make sure and check in with them individually. I called scheduling to try and get them to transfer me in order to at least talk with them on the phone; who then transferred me to the scheduling desk where I waited on hold until it disconnected. I still hope to talk with them at some point to learn how things went in the back and find out what we could have done better for them.

During cruise flight at 40;000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously; the Master Caution came on for ELEC and the TR (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. The Captain was Pilot Flying; and initially transferred control to me; in order to run the TR checklist. He accomplished the checklist; and it was around this same point the smoke was getting thicker; and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established the Captain told me to notify ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude; and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that I noticed all my flight/nav displays and radios had failed as well as ACARS No Comm" being displayed on the FMS. I immediately notified the Captain and said that it might be better if he flew. He agreed and took control back as the Pilot Flying and I took over the smoke/fire/ fumes checklist in the QRH. ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1; but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport. We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach; and the Captain used his emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in the descent order to expedite landing. A short time later I advised the Captain that I'd like to discontinue the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20 since I had reached a decision point in the QRH; and it appeared I would most likely be heads down for almost all of the rest of the flight into ZZZ1 with this exhaustive checklist; and not be able to properly; and safely perform my duties as a PM. I came to this decision based on the fact that step 16 states we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. He agreed. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. The Captain asked me to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch; but I reminded him that the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the Master Caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TR and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit. With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. The Captain disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS 17L. I noticed during the approach that the Captain had to trim manually; which led me to believe that we had obviously lost electrical control. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so the Captain asked me to back him up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident; where CFR (crash fire rescue) was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside; we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our pax stop breathing fumes. After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. A short time later; CFR and a maintenance person were able to find the cause of the TR failure and pulled one of the TR boxes out of the E&E bay (electronics & engineering); which showed significant electrical fire damage. Lesson learned: maintain awareness of the type of emergency and aircraft state; compared to how long QRH steps could take you out of the critical Pilot Monitoring role. This checklist taught me to bring my head back up and get a grasp on the fact that we were in a rapid descent; over mountains; with half of our displays and comms out and I was only half aware of some of the radio calls and aircraft state. This was more concerning to me."
