text:
Flight Crew reported compressor stalls on the Number 1 Engine and inadvertently shut down the Number 3 Engine.

Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls; we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back; while starting #1 Engine; we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert; we referred to the QRH; it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start; the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that; I replied if he was okay; I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN; then selected it again to the normal function; the alert went away. Later as we taxied out; I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance; but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up; so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway; the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly; I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL; with the gear up and flaps extended; we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane; there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1; EGT; and N2 indications were identical). Around 1;000 ft. AGL; the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down; I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD; also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle; Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim; and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time; Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine); the Captain said 'left side; I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1;000 ft. AGL; the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2;000 ft. MSL was okay to level off; Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left; I adjusted the altitude to 2;000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power; the banging went away; I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field; I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX; adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected); and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight; I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land; I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page; I called for the approach check and turned base to final; on dogleg; I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete; I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency; he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful. We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire); we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution.

Alerted that Aircraft X might be returning to ZZZ due to problem with #1 Engine. I immediately contacted ZZZ Tower. I was told; right after flight was wheels up controllers in tower saw sparks/flames coming from left engine and also heard 3 to 4 loud booms. Flight returned to airport and landed without issue on Runway XX. I talked to the Captain. He said that right after takeoff; there was compressor stall #1 Engine. They advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. The aircraft was met by the Fire Department. The Captain said he did not know what caused the loss of the #1 Engine. He also said the maintenance told him there was damage to the engine.

Flight attendants reported smelling a burning odor during boarding and experiencing health issues.

Upon stepping aboard Aircraft X; I immediately detected an odor that had a burnt wire smell. The other FA's also made comments such as; 'What is that smell? It smells like something is burning' as they stepped onboard. I was the D FA and began checking my safety equipment. I looked in the galley to see if any circuit breakers had popped and also looked in the oven to determine if the odor was from a forgotten burnt meal. All circuits were in proper place and there was no food in oven. I then walked down the aisle to determine if the burnt-wire smell was coming from the aft galley. I stopped at Row 21; aircraft right and stepped up on Seat 21 D as the odor was very strong above the OH bin. I could not visibly see any sign of smoke but the odor was quite strong. I then walked back up to fwd galley as I saw that the Captain was beginning a briefing. Captain stated that this aircraft had just come out of 'mothballs' and had just cleared a major inspection in State X. He stated that it had just arrived to ZZZ and the Captain of that flight informed him that a smoke alarm for the aft cabin activated upon landing. Captain stated that this happens from time to time and poses no threat of fire. All of us 4 FAs told him that we smelled a burnt wire odor in the cabin. A male individual; name unknown; representing Maintenance stated that we 'probably were smelling new carpet glue'. Captain waited for the Maintenance personnel member to step off of the aircraft and then told us FA's that if we were not comfortable with the odor that he backed us and would insist that we fly a different aircraft to ZZZ1 or return to hotel if aircraft was not available. All 4 of us FA's unanimously and instantly stated that we did not feel comfortable on this aircraft and we wanted to change aircraft in the interest of Safety First. I then told the Captain that I noticed the odor was particularly strong by OH compartment of 21D. We then walked to that row and Captain also noticed that it had a strong odor of either 'heated dust' or 'hot wire' on the lighting ballast. He then asked me if I personally felt safe taking this aircraft. I told him that I am very safety minded and the odor was not normal or usual to me. We all stayed in the first class seating area and continued personal conversations among us. The Captain was not present as he was talking to Operations. After approximately 15 minutes of remaining in the first class seating area; the other FAs noticed that my voice was getting hoarse and that I was beginning to lose my voice. To the best of my recollection; I believe that C FA; and B FA; both stated that their throats felt scratchy.After approximately another 15 minutes of staying and waiting for a decision onboard; in the first class seating area; we were told by [the] Captain that we were changing into different aircraft for our flight back to ZZZ1. We then deplaned the aircraft and walked to the other waiting aircraft. My voice remained coarse for an additional 30 minutes and I developed a migraine during the boarding process. I had the migraine the entire flight to ZZZ1; and it continued until early afternoon of date. Additionally; I awoke on the morning of date with a sore and scratchy throat. Both my migraine and scratchy throat subsided around 1400 hours on date. I have had a continuous low-grade headache since date through present date. I did not seek any medical attention as I 'normally' suffer from low grade sinus headaches regularly and use an OTC nasal spray along with Tylenol.I commend our Captain; for valuing and backing our decision to prioritize safety first.I would hope that Aircraft X was ferried back to ZZZ without full crew and guests in the pursuit of safety.

Upon crew boarding aircraft for return ZZZ-ZZZ1; [flight attendants] smelled what seemed like an electrical burning smell. It was not possible to find a fresh place of air on the plane; but the smell did seem worse as we walked further back. Our Pilots were met by that aircraft's ferrying pilots who also explained an aft lav smoke alarm went off while they were flying/descending after couple hours flight.The aircraft had just completed its mechanical run through after being 'unparked' from its holding location where it had been for 5 months. Unsure what that smell was; and given the circumstances of the aft lav smoke detector going off just previous to our boarding; our crew was offered another aircraft to take back to ZZZ1 which we accepted.At that point we had sat on the plane for likely about 30-45 minutes waiting for the phone calls and approvals and aircraft delay or swap or grounding decisions to be made. The flight attendants were in the cabin the whole time. Pilots came and left to discuss in jetway. Agents boarded for a couple of minutes and concurred on the smell immediately.Crew spoke of headaches; sore throat; and itchy/stuffy nose afterwards. Just concerned for aircraft returning to operation after long time [of being] parked.

Learjet 35 flight crew reported engine fire indication in flight; resulting in an inflight shutdown followed by a precautionary landing.

We departed ZZZ part 91 to relocate Aircraft X to ZZZ1. Few minutes after crossing ZZZZZ intersection at FL370 in contact with ZZZ Center; I notice a red fire light blinking on left engine accompanied with both red master working lights. No indication of engine stall; no vibration felt; no lost of power notice.Within 5 seconds I retarded to idle the left throttle; 3 seconds later the 'ENG FIRE PULL' Handle light extinguish making me believe that was only bleed air leak in the sensing loop; but 7 seconds later; the 'T' handle again starting flashing indicating fire.I pulled the thrust lever in cutoff position; I pulled the 'T' handle and once the two arm lights where illuminated; I pressed left one first; seconds later when I realized that the fire light was continued flashing; I pressed the second fire extinguishers light to the same engine.Unfortunately; the 'ENG FIRE PULL' handle was still flashing; taking the decision to turn left to the closest airport.We were flying the [airway] eastbound at 85 nm from ZZZ; only 3 airports where closest before ZZZ; but no rescue services most likely or not enough runway available for our landing configuration (gear down; max flaps 20 deg).Since the checklist says 'land as soon as possible' and bad weather was in front of us; while my copilot was advising ATC I started my left turn while descending; circumnavigating the weather (during my 90 deg turn; I looked behind my left shoulder to see if a white or black smoke trail was left behind; but I couldn't see nothing); and after clear of mountains I continued descending to 5;000 feet where I preferred to maintain a low altitude and close to the shoreline if a ditching was necessary.During our diversion we had time to talk to the Controller where we answered every question he asked.Every question was answered at the moment and once we were established on the localizer about 20 nm out; the fire light extinguish. While on my final descent I asked the tower that the ground equipment if possible; to be waiting on the left side of the runway since I was requesting a visual confirmation if actual fire was still on the left side or not.After landing I stopped the airplane and I requested again a visual confirmation and the answer was 'they are on the way.' At that moment with the right engine running; I asked my copilot to open the upper main door since I never felt or saw fire and to have his visual confirmation from him.My intentions were to taxi the airplane out of the runway if no danger or fire existed.As soon as my First Officer opened the door; he gave me the visual that NO FIRE WAS ON LEFT ENGINE and I talked to the Tower that my intentions was to move the airplane out of there to the ramp. The Tower responded to not move since the fire truck was already in my left side. When I saw to my left; I saw a fireman with his hose in position so; I turned off the right engine shutting down everything and jumping out of the airplane. By the time I was stepping out; the fireman started to spray the left engine and I thought that finally a real fire was there.Few seconds later all the fireman started to spray with soapy water the hole airplane; from the cockpit; fuselage; wings and the two engines from the front side and from behind (right engine was only from behind).As soon as I see all that I started to ask the fireman if they saw actually fire; but no fireman spoke Spanish or English. I tried to speak with 5 of them but was a loss of time.By the time they finish spraying the airplane; people from different departments approached the airplane and as soon as I found one who could speak English I asked him to translate the only question I've been asking.'Did anybody see fire?''Can someone say if actually a fire was on either engine?'And the answer was 'No fire was detected by anyone.'After that; we proceeded to tow the airplane out of the runway.

While following our route of flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we leveled at 37;000 feet before entering ZZZ [Center] airspace just before the fix ZZZZZ. As we passed that fix; ZZZ Center switched us to ZZZ2 Center and before first contact was made; we had an indication of fire on the left engine.The Captain proceeded with the memory items procedure. He put the left power to idle and we were waiting for that light to extinguish; it did; but in about 8-10 seconds it started flashing again; giving the indication that fire might still be present. Then the Captain continued with the procedure of cutting out the engine to secure it and pull the T-Handle of the left engine; continued by pressing the ARM button of one of the fire extinguishers.The flashing light indicating the possibility of fire in the left engine continued; so the Captain pressed the second ARM button. In both intents to extinguish the light with the fire extinguishers the flashing light of the T-Handle never shut off. So the PIC decided to call on the requested checklist out of the planes QRH and initiated [expedited] descent. I; as the First Office went through the procedures on tab 5 'Engine Fire Shutdown' section of the QRH. I went through all the checklist out loud and twice to confirm everything requested was performed. Then followed the checklist to the single engine landing procedure on tab 14 abnormal checklist; and went through it twice and out loud.While the descent was performed; I advised ATC and asked for vectors to the closest airport; which in this case the only appropriate airport and closest was ZZZ1. The Controller first indicated to fly to a fix which I could not understand and when I asked about 2 times to spell it or give us vectors; he then instructed to fly to the ZZZ VOR. I immediately set the FMS and GPS to the VOR and ZZZ1 airport. The Captain continued VFR descent and decided to cross the mountains as soon as possible so that we can continue descending and get closer to the ground and shore and make a straight in into ZZZ1.While the descent was being performed the left fire; light continued to flash. The Captain took communications while I was setting the procedures into ZZZ1 on the GPS and FMS. In about 3 miles short of the airport. We noticed the light stopped flashing. The Captain requested the Tower to let the rescue and firefighters know that they were needed in our left side once we landed; they confirmed that they were ready and waiting for us. Once we landed and the airplane came to a complete stop I got out if my seat and opened the left exit door to verify if there was any fire present at the moment; I communicated to the Captain that NO fire was visible from the front of the engine and then he instructed for me to get out. As soon as I got out; he was still in communication with the Tower; he shut the right engine as instructed by the Controller and exited the airplane.Once we stepped away from the airplane the firefighters started spraying the left engine immediately through the front and back of the nacelle; and seconds after; another group of firefighters started spraying the right engine. I personally told the captain that if they were spraying is because probably; they saw fire but when I noticed them spraying the right engine too then we thought it was their protocol to follow.Once they stopped spraying the captain asked if they saw fire to several of the Firefighters but they could not understand what we were asking; it was not until a ground handler or someone that understood English approached the airplane and we asked him to ask them if someone saw fire; they answered that No fire was visible. We then proceeded to tow the aircraft out of the runway.Personally; I believe this could be a glitch on the system of the aircraft. I am not a mechanic so it's hard for me to say what might have caused the aircraft to give that indication of fire on the engine. We treated the indication as a real fire so the airplane couldbe secure and everyone on board too. I don't know if this could be a maintenance issue or if it has happened before. My suggestion is just to continue to give the progressive and preventive maintenance to the aircraft as they are required and for the pilots to continue to communicate with maintenance any issues given big or small as no matter how small it may seem it could lead to other problems in the long run. Definitely the airplanes have their years so the more they are used for the missions they are going to require more and more maintenance.

Flight Crew reported multiple EICAS and STATUS messages caused a diversion and precautionary emergency landing.

Aircraft X; ZZZZ-ZZZ1; Captain; First Officer; International Relief Officer; and 3 747 qualified ACMs. FO (First Officer) was Pilot Flying shortly after reaching cruise altitude the EICAS message 'Yaw Damper LWR' appeared. In a very brief time after; approximately 5 seconds; more messages began appearing; accompanied by numerous status messages. Ultimately; over the period of about 10 minutes 6 EICAS messages and 20 status messages appeared. They included faults on numerous unrelated systems--environmental; fuel; flight controls; hydraulic; navigation. I called the IRO (International Relief Officer) into the flight deck; ensured the FO focused on flying the aircraft; and began discussing the issues with the IRO. The IRO called one of the ACMs to the cockpit; who is a simulator instructor on the aircraft; and initiated a satellite call with Flight Control; who; in turn; connected us to countless resources on the ground. While the IRO and ACM were working on the situation with Maintenance Control; the FO and I began working on selecting places to land in case we couldn't resolve the issues. Options included ZZZZ2 (>500 miles in front of us); ZZZZ3 (288 miles ahead); and ZZZZ (>300 miles behind). While discussing these options; the remaining two ACMs requested to go down to the main cargo deck to check for any further evidence; which I allowed. They shortly came back and reported the odor of electrical smoke; but no visible signs of smoke. We decided to divert to ZZZZ2; declared 'Pan' with ZZZZ1 Control and proceeded direct. Many options for the arrival were discussed; including what checklists to run; what systems may or may not be available upon landing (Ground spoilers? Thrust reverse? Autobrakes? Anti-skid? Etc.). We discussed dumping fuel; but were unsure if that would even work; or from which tanks the fuel would come if it did work. We chose not to dump but to land overweight. As ACARS Flight Deck Performance was unavailable; Flight Control did a live calculation and provided us with landing distances for landing at 720;000 lbs. without thrust reverse or autobrakes. (The number; 5;800 feet; proved to be very accurate.) Now primarily focused on arrival and landing; we configured the aircraft slowly and very early; turning the autopilot off after each configuration change to ensure that we had control of the aircraft. This all led to an otherwise uneventful visual approach and landing on Runway XX in ZZZZ2. I manually deployed the spoilers on touchdown; the FO extended the thrust reverse levers (the levers fully extended; but the reversers did not deploy) and applied maximum manual braking. We stopped on the runway to allow the fire department to analyze the aircraft and brakes for fire indications; which were reported as negative. We opted to then taxi off of the runway and into a large taxiway intersection (XX and YY Taxiways) to allow access to the aircraft from all angles. We calculated brake energy and cooling requirements; and monitored the brake temperatures on the synoptic page. Because our calculations put us on the edge of the warning zone for fuse plug melting; we sat and did not set the parking brake and called for towing. Normal after landing and shutdown procedures were accomplished. The tow took approximately an hour to complete; during which the brakes cooled back to normal temperatures without any damage. There were many people and agencies involved; the aircrew; Flight Control; Maintenance Control; SME's; ZZZZ2 Gateway; and others; all of whom were ready on a moment's notice; helped tremendously; and performed their roles flawlessly. Thank you to all.

After a normal climb to Flight Level 350 I began to exit my flight station when I heard the Captain call attention to the EICAS which at the time showed; I believe; two amber advisory messages; >YAW DAMPER LWR and RUD RATIO SNGL. Almost immediately thereafter several other EICAS advisory messages appeared on the primary EICAS screen along with a full page of status messages on the secondary EICAS screen. I immediately took my place back at the FO (First Officer) station and was advised by the Captain to resume Pilot Flying duties along with communication with ATC. Our IRO (International Relief Officer) was advised by the Captain to begin a patch with dispatch and begin troubleshooting measures with maintenance control. Among the three jump seating crew members was an instructor pilot who was also summoned to the flight deck for assistance. During this trouble shooting period it was determined that multiple systems including flight controls; hydraulics; pneumatic's and navigation equipment were all seriously degraded from normal. Also; it was decided that the two remaining jump seaters should go and inspect the main deck. Those crew members reported that no smoke was visible however a distinct electrical burning odor was present towards the front of the main deck. A diversion to ZZZZ2; including an overweight landing was agreed upon following all operating crew members vote. Clearance to ZZZZ2 was obtained with ZZZZ1 Radar and thus we began our diversion. I requested with ZZZZ1 a descent to FL250 so as to reduce the total time required to descend from altitude yet still provide for adequate differential pressure in case the need for equipment cooling override mode was required. After each initial flap configuration change we agreed upon disconnecting the autopilot momentarily to check flight control effectiveness. I found the aircraft to exhibit normal flying characteristics though slight porpoising occurred while on final approach as it was also discovered that the aircraft's right side glide slope was inoperable. I then disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the remainder of the approach to landing. During this landing it was pre briefed that the Captain would manually deploy the speed brakes and I would manually apply brakes as the auto deploy functions for both were disabled. I found the aircraft to have very effective stopping power as we stopped prior to the [Taxiway] XX high speed turn off. We remained on the runway with the parking break off while emergency vehicles inspected the fuselage and brakes for possible fire. Once it was determined that no visible fire was present we taxied clear of the runway onto a very large intersection at XX so that fire vehicles could more easily access the landing gear area if needed. We again held manual brakes only and did not set the parking brake during this wait for ground tow as our brake temperatures slowly climbed to a 6 on several indicators. After about an hour after landing we were towed to our parking gate. Incidentally; it was pointed out later on by the Captain that he was very quickly able to determine a possible diversionary landing site by his use of the 'Surface Conditions' line select item in the Weather Layers feature of our Jeppesen Flight Deck Pro app. Its simple and very intuitive red vs. green color gradation made the direction to turn from altitude a quick one; much quicker than having to dial up various ATIS frequencies. Perhaps this method could be stressed somewhat more during training? It was a great way to get a big weather picture of our surrounding area during an intense information overload situation.

Lead Technician reported refusing to sign an Engineering Order due to compliance issues.

My Recommendation: Because there is what I believe to be a low but uncertain chance that the primary pressure vessel of the Aircraft X has a current active failure; the aircraft should be immediately grounded; and an investigation be initiated into whether this issue is just a classification and engineering oversight; or indeed a failure to the aircraft's primary structure. Aircraft X (Boeing-767-300) is potentially operating on an inapplicable airworthiness sign off and may fly (already has flown) with a possible serious defect to the aircraft's primary structure (pressure vessel). Aircraft X arrived at ZZZ station December 2020. Upon arrival the following defect was found and recorded into the maintenance log book:Discrepancy: Undocumented Speed tape found concealing stripped & unsecured mounting screw to extruded Main Cargo Door (MCD) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel.I notified Maintenance Control of the defect and submitted via email a proposal for a temp repair utilizing non-standard substitution parts available on-hand at our station that I hoped would allow for a timely repair keeping the aircraft on scheduled revenue flights despite the need for an Engineering Order (EO) and additional authorizations. After an appropriate time; an outline of maintenance action to be completed was submitted to our station for a yet unapproved EO numbered: XXXXXXXX; that was a substantial deviation from my own earlier proposed temp repair. This EO after performing a Detailed Visual Inspection (DVI) merely called for reattaching the panel in place with RTV-106 sealant; no hardware; and a covering of multiple layers of aluminum speed tape. Knowing that an external application of tape over a hole in the primary pressure vessel of an aircraft did not meet the basic criteria for acceptable maintenance standards; I contacted maintenance Control to inform them that we (aircraft technicians under my purview) at ZZZ would not be able to comply with the EO maintenance instructions as they were currently written because of the safety implications.After expressing my unwillingness to press forward with the draft EO I began receiving pressuring communications from various maintenance controllers; maintenance duty managers; and Company management; saying everything from 'just do it;' to 'it'll be fine.' Additionally; it was overheard in background talk on more than one phone call with maintenance controllers that they did not believe the panel in question was actually a primary pressure vessel fitting as I had asserted in multiple emails and phone conversations; and was merely a weather seal. Worried that I had somehow made an egregious mistake about the panel in-fact being a pressure hull seal; I enlisted both additional night shift mechanics to assist with a cabin pressurization leak check (referencing AMM 05-51-24-782-001) with the damaged MCD Manual Drive cover panel removed. As I operated the cabin pressure manually; utilizing APU bleed source; the two assisting technicians reported a strong; unrestricted flow of air emanating from the uncovered hole; while I was observing only 1 PSI indicated differential cabin pressure. Believing that this observation adequately supported my previous assertation; I terminated the test; returned the aircraft to its previous configuration; and felt confident that my continued refusal to repair the aircraft as outlined in the draft EO to be a safe and correct judgment call.The scheduled departure of the aircraft was altered from XA:15z to XE:00z. At XB:16z I received an email asking me to 'please call In to Maintenance Control to advise on current status of approved EO compliance;' (no approved EO had been received or transmitted to anyone at ZZZ station). Given the ongoing pressure from phone calls and condescending emails to comply with an EO I had yet to see; I advised [the] maintenance controllers that I would not be complying with the EO and to direct all future communications to be in writing. I then suggested at that point that they 'just AOG (aircraft on ground) ship the required parts necessary to return this defect to its original condition;' with the observation 'that the original undocumented speed tape repair has already been proven to fail;' as my own justification for non-compliance with an EO that called for doing the same thing; only with more tape.At XD:50z we received the first approved copy of the EO XXXXXXXX via email from the Maintenance Manager; which upon review was consistent with the advised sealant and tape repair already rejected. The scheduled aircraft departure was once again pushed back to XG:00z; well after the scheduled arrival of the oncoming maintenance day shift. At XE:15z I received a phone call from my Company Regional Manager asking me why I was not complying with the EO and then; regarding taping over a hole in the pressure vessel; to 'explain how this is a safety concern?' After briefly elaborating to him about how the loss of cabin pressure makes flight crews go to sleep and planes to become lawn-darts; he said that I would 'have coverage in terms of liability because the engineer signed off on three layers of speed tape.' After mutually disagreeing; he proceeded to switch the subject to asking me which maintenance technicians were coming in on day shift; then; seeming unsatisfied; continued to ask me about the status of other technicians not scheduled for shift. Several minutes after hanging up; another call was received from a subordinate technician; not scheduled to come in; inquiring as to what was going on and why the Regional Manager was asking him to come into work on his weekend and 'override' us. At the advice of another technician overhearing the conversations; I took a written note of the above quotes from the calls.With continued inquiries for resolution on the aircraft; the oncoming day shift Lead informed Maintenance Control that the EO was still unworkable as it was and reiterated that the original temp repair proposal forwarded to Maintenance Control that included substituted hardware installation would be a fix deemed acceptable and believed conforming with standard practices that we would still be willing to sign off on. Giving in; the Maintenance Controller agreed to get the hardware installation added to a revised version of the EO along with an additional step for a cabin pressurization check that the day shift Lead smartly felt necessary for repairs performed on the pressurized structure of an aircraft. With assurances that the revised EO would include the agreed upon amendments; the day shift Lead and myself expedited the repair to the aircraft in an effort to make the scheduled departure pending timely receipt of the revised EO. The cabin pressure leak check of the repair was then successfully accomplished with only a small movement observed in the repair at a peak indicated differential pressure of 4.5 PSI; and no leaks or excessive loss rates noted. Upon departing the aircraft to accomplish paperwork closeout we were greeted by the oncoming flight crew; who had apparently been kept apprised of the ongoing situation and wanted to personally thank us for looking out for their safety.At XF:18z we received the approved EO XXXXXXXX Revision 1. Required paperwork was completed; signed log pages were sent; flight crew was briefed; and the aircraft was returned to green status at XG:10z. The aircraft subsequently blocked out of the gate at XG:39z for a delay from scheduled departure of 39 minutes. Why is this a safety concern? Upon later realization and review; I have found several possible deviations to Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs); the airline General Maintenance Manual; and uncertainty to the validity of the accomplished repair that should be investigated immediately as it may represent a serious safety issue to the aircraft. Having been so narrowly focused on getting the point across to the necessary parties involved in the tribulations of Dec Xth that the damaged part was indeed part of the pressure vessel of the aircraft and that a workable repair would have to be tailored to the additional physics involved with that part of the structure; I failed to realize the broader implications of what a repair to the pressurized structure of an aircraft entailed in terms of adherence to regulations; maintenance policy; and accepted practices. The FARs define 'Primary Structure: is that structure which carries flight; ground; or pressurization loads; and whose failure would reduce the structural integrity of the airplane.' Even though steps were added to Revision 1 of the EO to conform the repair to acceptable practices 'equal to its original or properly altered condition;' because the installation hardware was a reasonably close approximation of the original parts; the additional step of adding three layers of overlapping speed tape is in direct contradiction to the airline General Maintenance Manual policy for its use: -HIGH SPEED ALUMINUM TAPE- High speed tape is a convenient material for use as an interim repair for non-structural materials. Under no circumstances will it be used on primary aircraft structure. A Log Book entry is required when high speed tape is applied unless instructed to do so by an EO with DER approval.Under this policy; the use of speed tape in this manner is strictly forbidden and forgiveness when it comes to doing the maintenance under the provision of an EO only absolves the requirement of a log book entry for its use. However; even though agreement was made in Revision 1 of the EO for addition of attachment hardware and an added cabin pressurization leak check; the EO creator did not alter the original classification of the repair to acknowledge that the repair was in-fact being accomplished on an aircraft primary structure: 'The Main Deck Cargo Door Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is considered secondary structure. The time limited repair per this EO is minor; and the temporary repair per Part 1 does not affect the fit; form or function of the skin.'I would imagine this to be an oversight; and if it is; then an additional revision needs to be made which would at a minimum alter the category of the defect deferral and its associated time-limited re-inspections and permanent repair due date/cycles. If this is not an oversight; however; as this EO has been twice over reviewed and approved; and the MCD Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is indeed a secondary structure; then the original investigative cabin pressure leak test failed for a reason other than indicated (i.e. there is an existing failure of the primary pressure vessel somewhere internal to the Main Cargo Door). Which would in turn mean that a damaged secondary structure is now fulfilling the function of a primary structure pressure seal. I do not believe this to be the case; but; as the MCD is a modification from the original aircraft structure; the existing reference material available for my use to confirm the hypothesis that the cover plate is indeed a primary structure component is vague and uncertain. Tech Engineering likely has additional references not available at a line station that could perhaps shed light on the issue.Since issuing equivalent versions of the above safety report to both Airline and Company on [the next day]; Aircraft X has remained on a regular flight schedule with recurrent re-inspects per Part 2 of EO XXXXXXXX Rev 1; until receiving Part 3 Permanent Repair [4 days later]. I can currently find no record that any further investigation has been conducted.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Single air taxi pilot in IMC and icing conditions reported an alternator failure.

I departed ZZZ on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1. The aircraft had sat for roughly 3 days over the weekend before this flight and was difficult to start that morning (battery seemed weak). 40 minutes into the flight; the first symptoms of an electrical malfunction began to show up. I was roughly 15 nm from the IAF for the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ1 at 8;000 feet MSL; in actual IMC with light to moderate rime icing. I had just switched from ZZZ2 Center to the CTAF for the ZZZ1 airport when the auto-pilot for the aircraft unexpectedly disconnected. All of the lights on the autopilot control panel went dark; and the autopilot would not turn back on. Initially; I decided to continue the approach by hand and have maintenance check the autopilot malfunction on the ground. After briefly troubleshooting the autopilot; I returned to my instrument scan. At first glance; my HSI indicated that I was on Heading/Course. Needles were centered and heading bug was situated at the top of the instrument. But when I looked over at the Garmin 430 GPS; it indicated that I was off heading by 20-30 degrees. By the time I looked back towards my HSI; there was a 'HDG' flag starting to flicker in the top right hand corner. I looked across the panel at the co-pilot's instrument cluster and noted that the co-pilot's artificial horizon was flopped over; indicating a 45* right bank and 20* nose up attitude. The co-pilot's side DG was also off by 90* from my magnetic compass. As I looked back towards the pilot's side instrument cluster; my HSI began spinning around and around like a top.At this point; I had obviously determined that several of my gyroscopic instruments had failed; and I had difficulty determining which instruments were trustworthy and which were not. From this point on; I did my best to maintain straight and level flight with my remaining instruments and the Garmin 430 GPS ground track. I looked out the window at my wings (I was still in IMC and light to moderate icing [at] this point) and saw that during my troubleshooting I had enough ice accumulation that small 'horns' of rime ice were begging to grow on the leading edges and my de-ice boots were mostly white with a layer of ice. When I pressed the switch on the overhead panel to activate my de-ice boots; nothing happened. I immediately switched back to ZZZ2 Center and [received priority]; advising them that I had gyroscopic instrument failures and inoperative anti-icing equipment. I requested an immediate climb in an attempt to escape the icing conditions and find visual flight conditions before my remaining instrumentation failed; along with vectors back to ZZZ (which I knew had good VFR weather conditions...ZZZ1 conditions appeared to be worsening when I had last listened to the automated weather). ATC was extremely helpful and professional. Immediately offering any assistance they could; giving me no-gyro vectors towards ZZZ and approving a climb to 12;000 feet MSL. I had difficulty maintaining a heading and climb pitch-attitude initially; but got vaguely stabilized within a few minutes. Once stabilized; I noticed that the left alternator light was on; I attempted to re-cycle the alternator master switch twice without success. I then began to load-shed all electrical equipment which was not absolutely necessary for the continuation of the flight; and I advised ATC that I had experienced an alternator failure. I initially broke out of the top of the cloud layer and entered VMC around 10;000 feet roughly 15 minutes after the first indication of electrical failure. I had to request a higher altitude shortly thereafter as the tops of the clouds sloped higher towards ZZZ. ATC cleared me for a block altitude 8;000 feet to 12;000 feet; then eventually up to 14;000 feet; and authorized any course deviations necessary for me to remain in VFR conditions.Upon leveling off; I was initially concerned about what appeared to be a fairly significant performance loss. My first assumption was that it was due to ice build up on the wings/tail. In a level flight attitude; at 38 of manifold pressure and 2400 rpm (typical climb power) I was only getting 120 knots indicated airspeed. 160 knots to 170 knots indicated is more typical during cruise flight at a much lower power setting (30'/2300rpm). I alerted ATC that I was seeing abnormally low air speeds. But after a quick glance at my GPS (which was showing a 230 knots ground speed) I realized that the airspeed discrepancy was most likely due to pitot icing. ATC confirmed that they were showing me with a ground speed in the high 220's. By this point; the aircraft was out of icing conditions and flying just fine in VMC. So most of the potential danger had past. The last thing I had to do was search around for a hole in the clouds so that I could get back into ZZZ (there was an overcast layer between my aircraft and the ground). With the help of ZZZ3 Approach; ZZZ Tower; and several other aircraft in the area giving pilot reports; I found an opening near ZZZ4 and circled down for a visual approach into Runway XXL at ZZZ. The vast majority of the ice which had accumulated on the aircraft came off in the decent due to higher airspeeds and increasing temperatures. I landed without further incident; parked the aircraft; and immediately took down notes regarding the order of events while they were still fresh in my mind. I then called the Chief Pilot to relay what happened."

Captain reported returning to the gate and refusing an aircraft that had an uncontrollable cabin pressure issue.

This was a rapid pressurization. After single engine start; I asked the FO (First Officer) to accomplish the single engine after start checklist. We received taxi clearance to Runway XXL. I began taxiing about 50 feet and the aircraft began pressurizing immediately. Everyone on the aircraft began feeling their heads squeezed together. Immediately the EICAS gave a 'PRESN AUTO FAIL' caution. What would you do? Are you going to let the airplane keep pressurizing until it reaches 14;500 ft while simultaneously running the QRH and then aircraft drops masks mid checklist? I used my instincts and immediately stopped the aircraft; set the parking brake and pressed the 'dump' button near the pressurization panel to dump the pressurized air. I only knew to immediately do this because I've personally thought of this scenario plenty of times in situations where the boarding door was closed and external air condition was hooked up. I always thought to myself if the door couldn't open quick enough then I'd need to dump the air; so my instincts reacted as such when this actually occurred. This is not something I was taught; this is not something the company teaches; however it should certainly be a point of emphasis. Moving along; after I dumped the air; the aircraft began depressurizing as expected just enough for about 3 seconds and then immediately began pressurizing again. I unpressed the 'dump' button and pressed it again. Nothing happened. I did this instantly. Afterwards I pressed the manual pressurization button; and rotated it to 11 o'clock position and waited 2 seconds; nothing happened; I then rotated full clockwise but the aircraft kept pressurizing and I wasn't going to wait to run the checklist as the aircraft altitude kept climbing. I have read this checklist before and ran through this procedure on my own time once or twice due to curiosity; so I knew what to do personally. I then pressed the EMER CALL button to the flight attendant; and told him to immediately open the galley door. Keep in mind all of this happened within 15 seconds. I also told him the galley door because I didn't want passengers to panic and run out the boarding door thinking their heads were going to explode. This is how it felt. When the flight attendant opened the door; it slammed open; as expected; despite the pressurization knob fully rotated to the right. Then I ran the QRH. Keep in mind we were not losing pressurization; we were rapidly pressurizing; oxygen masks were not my immediate thought on the ground. The checklist says to don oxygen masks during rapid decompression. I made the PIC authority to open the galley door once the pressure would not dump properly because I knew it would completely depressurize the aircraft. After I ran the QRH; I called Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the Auto Pressurization; and have me continue with the aircraft to ZZZ; an airport with a field elevation of 3200 plus/minus 100 feet. One; I've never controlled pressurization manually in flight; and secondly I've never been to ZZZ; a high elevation airport. So I refused. Nonetheless; we went through the QRH; I ran through the proper steps from instruction from the book; and Maintenance. I did what the QRH said; which I actually did myself already; then I personally went to go close the galley door myself; in case it didn't properly pressurize. I at least considered running through the proper MEL procedure; however I was still not sold on taking the airplane. Once I closed the door; the same thing happened; aircraft began over pressurizing. I immediately opened the door again. I went back on the phone with Maintenance; after a quick discussion with my First Officer & flight attendant; I told Maintenance Control 'I will not take this aircraft.' He said ok; we ended the conversation; then I began coordinating with OPS for a gate return. I did not want to taxi with the galley door open; nor did I feel it was safe to close the door as well; so I simply turned off the #2 engine; the only one running; and asked to be towed back to the gate. I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch 'returning to gate; need new aircraft.' They responded 'copy.' After a few minutes a tug came; we were towed; I blocked in and I then I called Dispatch and explained to him the situation. He said he'd call me back. In a few minutes he did; he said he spoke to Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the issue and keep the same aircraft; I refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. No one knew what the actual issue was; and unless you felt your head being squeezed in an airplane uncontrollably on the ground; you wouldn't know how that felt. I can't imagine what it would have felt like if we were flying at 3;000 feet and the aircraft wanted to over pressurize to a higher altitude and the dump feature didn't work properly; because opening the door inflight; is obviously not an option. A few minutes later Dispatch called and said they'd reach out to the Duty Manager and call me back. The Duty Manager then called me; he said the same thing the Dispatcher said; to MEL the aircraft; and continue on the same plane. I respectfully refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. The Duty Manager then coordinated a new aircraft and I swapped to one about 30 minutes later. I must repeat; if you were not on the aircraft; you do not know how it felt. The crew was light headed; myself included; and the passengers had to have been as well. As a crew I felt we made the right decision; despite pressure to take out the same aircraft. About an hour later; when my new aircraft was being boarded; the previous aircraft was adjacent to us being worked on by Maintenance. In other words; it was not a simple MEL procedure. The aircraft was not safe to fly. Our new plane was just fine; we boarded; and proceeded to ZZZ safely and landed about 2 hours late. The QRH procedure is for inflight; and mainly focused on cabin depressurization; we were being over pressurized. There wasn't enough time to run a QRH all while solving the issue as the aircraft continued pressurizing on the ground. I wasn't sure how much time I would have. There were children on board; I immediately thought about everybody; and since I knew opening the door would solve the issue; I made the decision to open. I didn't know of any other checklist action item would actually stop exactly what was happening. There isn't even a tab here for cabin over pressuring. You had to be there.

MD-11 Captain reported a strong smell of 'oily fumes' and an auto-flight/FMS malfunction during cruise resulted in a diversion.

During normal climb out of ZZZ; passing roughly FL240; we got a single CAWS Overspeed warning; FMA indicated FMS speed; however aircraft had accelerated into the MMO range I Reduced the speed from Mach .81 to .79 and pressed FMS speed to edit a new lower FMS speed. Reaching cruise at FL350 returned to normal FMS ECON Cruise .83 Mach Two hours into the flight; in cruise with no changes to pitch or power with autopilot on; aircraft started to overspeed by roughly 15 kts beyond the MMO in a couple seconds Both Primary Flight Display's indicated the same speed fluctuation We were alerted by the CAWS and the aircraft started to climb The First Officer took the controls as he was first to identify the problem; turned off the ATS reduced the power I pulled the speed brakes and called for the controls; reduced the speed from .83 Mach to .80 Mach Airspeed spread was about 60 kts and we were at optimum altitude Once the aircraft speed and altitude were under control; I reengaged the FMS speed and ATS These previous events; helped influence my decision making for the primary event.......All three crew members had been in the cockpit; with the door closed; together since departure I got up to use the lavatory about an hour west of ZZZ1; 3 hours into flight As I opened the cockpit door I detected a very strong smell of oily fumes I turned on the lights on the courier deck and the main cargo deck Air was hazy I went to the cockpit and got my flashlight turned off the lights on the main deck opened the smoke curtain and confirmed the presence of blueish smoke on the main deck in my bright flashlight beam I asked the Load Master to please come back to the courier station and check She confirmed the presence of smoke and fumes I returned to the cockpit and I ran the Emergency Non-Alert SMOKE/FIRE/FUMES checklist As per the checklist; I determined the source to be the Bleed 3 as the smoke smelled oily; not acrid; and I've heard of this problem in the past on this aircraft; also the Dangerous Goods Form did not list any hazmat on board and all systems were still functioning normally I turned off Bleed 3 per the checklist and started looking at nearby airports in my iPad The smoke began dissipating slowly I asked the First Officer to please go back and make sure the smoke is not coming from a ULD He returned after a few minutes and confirmed the smoke was dissipating and it was not coming from any of the cargo He said it seemed to concentrated above the wing box but dissipating I was reviewing the previous logbooks and current logbook pages for any smoke occurrences during the previous flights to help come to a decision to divert per the Quick Reference Handbook or to continue per the Quick reference Handbook Before I could finish reviewing the logbook Autopilot 1 disconnected; the aircraft started deviating from altitude and we got a LEVEL 2 alert for FCC 1B FAULT; a master caution and my flight director disappeared I immediately switched to Capt on First Officer Flight Director and stabilized the aircraft; checked all the parameters and engaged Autopilot 2 I called for the LEVEL 2 FCC 1B FAULT checklist After the checklist was complete; I consulted with the crew and made the decision to divert to ZZZ1 as it was a Company flight; it was en-route; weather was good; we were very familiar with the airport and we have maintenance there I gave the controls and communication to the FO and began running Checklist I told the FO to advise ATC that we would like to divert to ZZZ1 for technical reasons We were 39 minutes from ZZZ1 and cleared direct to a point on the STAR We advised NCC via ACARS of our diversion On the STAR when we were passing 11;000 ft at 245 kts; we were cleared to 6;000 ft; I reduced the altitude to 6;000 ft on the FCP and selected IDLE and confirmed on the FMA The aircraft began to climb instead of descend; speeds were normal and aircraft was in clean configuration w/ local altimeter set I disconnected the autopilot and hand flew thelast 50 miles We were cleared for ILS On final as we set Flaps 15 we got a LEVEL 2 FLAP DISAG; this was expected as the right outboard flap had been 'X' out since the FCC Fault We set flaps 35 Flaps showing 21/22/20/X on both PFD's I elected not to extend the flaps further or retract and retry to extend them as the airplane was light and controllable; runway was long and insight; weather was clear and winds were light I elected to maintain MIN auto brakes however I informed the crew I was going to use all 3 reverse and to advise tower that we would be rolling to the end Before landing checklist was completed I announced 'no green box' due to flaps not beyond 25 degrees We landed with no further incident and taxied to the ramp. Excellent job from my First Officer and Load Master They were invaluable to me during the flight. I identified the haze/fumes when I left the cockpit to use the lavatory I found the upper deck full of fumes. [Probable cause of the] smoke was Engine oil leaking into Pneumatic system [Probable cause of the] FCC issue is unknown. Followed SOP; make decisions while weighing input of crew. [As my response] recommended Preventative Maintenance.

text:
B757 flight crew reported that a hydraulic system malfunction resulted in a diversion.

The left yaw damper was deferred on the initial paperwork. Upon logbook review at the aircraft; the mechanic informed us the deferral was cleared which left us with no MELs. Pre-flight and taxi were uneventful. Shortly after takeoff with the Captain as PF; the L HYD QTY EICAS illuminated; followed by the L HYD ENG PUMP EICAS. As we were handed off to Departure on the ZZZZZ 5 SID; I saw the L HYD SYS PRESS; RUDDER RATIO; and YAW DAMPER EICAS messages momentarily appear; but they quickly extinguished without an associated Master Caution (that I can recall). The Captain elected to leave the Flaps at 5 and bugged the speed back accordingly. Departure cleared us to 10;000 ft.; but allowed us to stay at 5;000 ft. to run the QRH checklists. ATC provided vectors in the vicinity of ZZZ while we worked the problem. At the time the QRH was referenced; we had two EICAS messages displayed. The L HYD QTY checklist did not have any action items. The L HYD ENG PUMP checklist directed us to turn the engine pump OFF. Since I had momentarily seen the L HYD SYS PRESS message and the Status page indicated a loss of fluid in the left system (magenta RF); we referenced the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist; but did not perform any of the actions at that time since the EICAS was not illuminated. As we discussed a return to ZZZ; the L HYD SYS PRESS message reappeared; along with the YAW DAMPER and RUDDER RATIO messages; an associated Master Caution; and the SYS PRESS light on the overhead panel. We accomplished the QRH checklist up to the deferred items and advised ATC. The controller passed word of the priority handling to The Company at the Captain's request while we completed the DIVERT ACARS; got performance data with the L HYD SYS non-normal; and set up for an ILS to Runway XX. While on extended vectors; we tried extending the gear normally which resulted in a GEAR DISAGREE EICAS and POWER XFER UNIT Status message. In accordance with the deferred items on the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist; we accomplished the alternate gear extension procedures. Once turned back towards the airport; we attempted normal flap extension from 5 to 15. The TE FLAP DISAGREE message appeared; so we again followed the deferred items for alternate flap extension. I sent for performance data reflecting the new non-normal (L HYD SYS WITH TE FLAP DISAGREE) accounting for the Flaps 20 Vref 20 landing configuration. With the QRH complete; the Captain called for the applicable normal checklists and we briefed the approach with attention given to non-normals (manual speedbrake extension before right thrust reverser deployment; manual braking; etc) and how a go-around would be handled (gear would remain down; flap speeds; etc). Once handed off to Tower; we relayed that we would not have nose wheel steering. Our plan was to clear the runway onto a high speed taxiway to be towed; but if we couldn't stop by XX; we would probably have to shutdown on the runway for tow. Tower told us the runway was ours with CFR standing by and said they had notified Company of the need for tow. We had a jumpseater onboard that is another 757 First Officer. He had plugged a headset into the observer panel for assistance as needed and checklist backup. The Captain queried the crew as to if we thought everything was in order as we approached the FAF. We were in agreement that all checklists were complete and we felt comfortable with the approach and landing. The Captain landed; manually pulled the speed brake lever; deployed the right reverser; and conducted manual braking. He cleared [the runway] where we were met by CFR vehicles. After performing the After Landing flows (except leaving the flaps at 20); the engines were shutdown for CFR to inspect the aircraft/brakes. Once cleared by CFR; the priority handling was terminated and we were towed into Ramp by Company. There was not any visible hydraulic fluid on the aircraft exterior when maintenance first looked. We performed a Shutdown/Secure checklist; conducted aquick debrief with the mechanics to include the wording of the Captain's logbook write up; and left the aircraft with maintenance as we were directed to tail swap and continue to ZZZ1 under a new flight number. As the crew van arrived; hydraulic fluid was leaking onto the ramp from the left side of the aircraft while the mechanic continued to evaluate the problem. I still do not know what the root cause of the problem was and/or if there was anything that could have prevented the loss of fluid in the left hydraulic system. I feel our crew worked well together to safely recover the aircraft despite the backside of the clock showtime and it being our first leg flying together. ATC and CFR were very helpful throughout the event. I think our training prepared us for situations like this (heavy system hydraulic loss) and CRM principles were used to efficiently handle the issue to the best of our abilities at that time.

Shortly after takeoff (ZZZ) and passing approximately 1;000 ft. AGL; we heard a caution aural and saw L HYD QTY EICAS Msg. There was also an audible thump sound and slight feedback through the flight controls (yoke). This was followed quickly by L HYD ENG PUMP Msg. We were flying the SID (I was PF) and the aircraft was in LNAV and VNAV. I called for A/P CTR CMD; confirmed the A/P FMA and that the A/P was in fact functioning properly. Initially; we remained on the SID while analyzing our problem. A quick check of the status page confirmed that the left hydraulic reservoir had lost a significant amount of fluid (high of .98 to low of .21; .30 after shutdown). We also had a momentary L HYD SYS Press message that extinguished and came back on later (on downwind). Considering an air turn back likely; I decided to keep the flaps at 5. We requested a level off at our initial altitude of 5;000 ft. We let ATC know we had a hydraulic issue and that we desired vectors for a likely return to Runway XX at ZZZ. With the initial 'aviating; navigating and communicating' complete we agreed that L HYD QTY was; at that point; our first priority. After running this checklist the L HYD SYS PRESS light came on continuously leading to the running of that checklist. Having reached the deferred items section of the checklist we briefly discussed contacting dispatch. I decided that a return to ZZZ was clearly the safest and best option and that direct notification by us would be more of a distraction than help. I decided to advise ATC and request ATC notify 'company' of our hydraulic system issue. This and quick divert message sent via ACARS; satisfied the notification requirement. We had good weather; a long runway (at a very familiar field) and were well below max landing weight. Before beginning the configuration process we completed our normal procedures; including after takeoff and approach checklists; and set up & briefed the ILS for Runway XX. We began configuring and quickly discovered that the PTU was not operating properly; requiring the alternate extension procedures for flaps and landing gear. After requesting and receiving landing data for our non-normal configuration (per checklist); we requested a vector to intercept final. With the assistance of our jumpseater we reviewed all the pertinent notes and made sure we had considered all the pertinent variables; no autobrakes; manual speedbrake extension on landing; R thrust reverser; only after speed brakes extended and no nose wheel steering (differential braking only) on roll-out. We notified approach and Tower of need to have aircraft towed to parking either from runway or after clearing runway (high speed taxiway). I planned to use differential braking to exit the runway; but wasn't sure how effective this would be. As it turned out; aircraft control was more than adequate for exiting via the high speed exit taxiway. After taxiing clear of the runway we stopped the aircraft and coordinated a quick inspection of the aircraft by crash/rescue and a tug to tow us to parking.

EMB-175 First officer reported a fumes event during initial climb resulting in a diversion.

The Captain gave me the plane and started making calls on COM2 which I did not listen in on. Operations attempted a Dispatch patch which didn't work; Dispatch via airnav; Flight attendant calls; and PAs. Meanwhile I was flying the plane with automation; getting vectors from ATC; descending (I believe we were around 30;000' when we decided to divert); and fielding ATC questions to a limited extent. We were able to go and stay VMC at some point during this time although it was night.Maybe 6 minutes later the Captain was back with me and he took the airplane. At that point I started working the box with a bit of help from the Captain. I was still also handling most of the ATC calls at that point. We ended up getting direct to a waypoint that put us on a base to final for Runway XXL. Shortly thereafter they changed it to Runway XXR. Unfortunately I wasn't able to send for the numbers until we were turning final. I ran what I could of the descent checklist as I waited for them to come back. As they finally came up; Captain said it was too late; he would use green dot as a reference for landing. I expressed that I was OK with that and pulled myself away from the automation. Either shortly before or after this the Captain commented a different strange smell in the cockpit; I verbalized smelling it as well but am unable to describe it accurately- maybe some kind of fumes. Remember at this point we had a real concern that there was a fire with a fuel leak despite the lack of alarms or EICAS msgs.The Captain executed a very nice landing and I continued to communicate with tower on the dedicated frequency. We pulled off and came to a stop. Captain asked for a fire truck to inspect the plane which was accomplished without any abnormalities or fire indications found. We then proceeded to gate in the company ramp. At some point during this latter taxi the smell dissipated from the cockpit. I suggested not turning the APU on as it could have been the source of our issues. Captain agreed and asked me to notify Ops that we wanted to taxi in and leave engine 1 on while they hooked up the ground power. I relayed this and it took a while but was eventually accomplished. We shut down and medics came into the forward doorway asking to assess/treat folks. The flight attendants seemed to be the only ones reporting headaches/symptoms from the incident; especially FA2. Both FA2 and FA3 did a great job throughout the situation. I was especially impressed with FA2 doing her job professionally while in obvious distress after the cockpit door was opened. The medics basically had to insist on taking her for evaluation while the Captain stepped in to the forward cabin and volunteered to perform any of her FA duties necessary while the passengers deplaned. I remained in the cockpit monitoring the systems.Captain demonstrated superb leadership and decision making skills this night and I feel very lucky to have been working with him during this event.We talked to a variety of ground personnel and mechanics after a quick debrief. One mechanic firmly believed that de-ice fluid was ingested in the APU and that caused the odor. Captain and I were skeptical as we had not de iced all day and had been in heavy rain. The mechanic showed me the aft of the aircraft and there did indeed appear to be a small streak of fluid (not water) on the belly forward of the APU inlet. However to me it looked like the fluid came from the APU as the fluid was more concentrated there and disappeared as the streak moved forward on the small belly fin for maybe 8'. I took a few photos which should be attached. It's also noteworthy that we had this same aircraft for the last 2 flights (about 4.5 flight hrs) which included an identical takeoff from ZZZ.Unfortunately it took over an hour for everyone; especially the FAs; to complete all the required phone calls and documentation. We were unlucky enough to wait over 45 minutes for ground transportation during which we talked to crewscheduling and the contacted the shuttle company multiple times. We all got to the hotel after X pm truly exhausted from the experience and without an opportunity to get any dinner. Surprisingly I wasn't the only crew member to mention trouble sleeping as I unwillingly replayed the events over and over in my mind. In hindsight now it's interesting to evaluate myself going from the adrenaline spike during the incident; to the fatigue crash afterwards; to the inability to relax when I finally got to the hotel room. The following day which was supposed to be my day off was a deadhead home. That afternoon I evaluated my condition and thought it appropriate to ask for a later start for my next 3 day trip starting the following day. I will evaluate myself again on the next day and ask for yet a later time/day to join this next trip if necessary.Despite all the great training I've had to it was a valuable experience to go through this in real time. It was interesting as this evolved from a transient cockpit odor to a de facto emergency landing. We do get mild transient odors in the cockpit from time to time without consequence and I really thought this would be a similar outcome. I fully expected the flight attendants to report the odor gone as we continued the climb out and found myself a bit surprised to be going into ZZZ2 even though we literally had just been discussing it before the decision was made. After extensive reflection I feel like we handled the situation very well. I do think in hindsight that we could have communicated even more during that extremely busy descent. We both debriefed about looking at the landing weight during the descent; thinking it was okay; and deciding it better to land even if we were slightly over weight anyway but I don't remember either of us verbalizing it in flight. We also didn't discuss our obvious decision not to hold and run checklists which we both decided was not the best option. There is an argument to be made that it we had our hands full safely getting the plane down ASAP and those discussions were OK to save until later. In hindsight we probably should have [communicated the urgency to ATC] at some point. Initially the Captain and I had some uncertainty as to how strong the fuel smell was in the aft cabin but decided it was time to go to ZZZ2 regardless. As soon as we described the situation to ATC they treated it as an emergency and we were busy enough not to discuss or bother officially declaring it.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
B737 flight crew reported multiple systems indicating failures; resulting in the decision to execute a return to departure airport and a precautionary landing.

Shortly after takeoff As the PF I experienced intermittent failure of both roll and pitch modes (with no flags; just the disappearance and reappearance in erratic random failures of pitch and roll indications separately) of my flight director during climb through approximately 6;000 ft. Obviously the auto pilot A disconnected and I was unable to reacquire it due to the erratic nature of the problem. Communicating to my FO (First Officer) of the issue; we recognized that his flight director appeared to be operating normally. This allowed us to use autopilot B to reassess our condition. With the auto throttle on with autopilot B the Number 2 throttle advanced rapidly approximately 5 knobs forward of the Number 1 throttle and I returned it to a symmetric condition (the auto throttle disengaged itself as well; Autopilot B still was working). While bringing the throttles to an asymmetric condition to stabilize the thrust setting the Stab Trim Light illuminated; the left fuel pump light of the center tank illuminated (approximately 22;000 lbs of gas in the center tank). We requested to level off at 16;000 ft. and 250 knots and indicated to ATC that we needed a few minutes to access a condition; that we would maintain our flight plan. We executed a transfer of controls to the FO making him the PF as he also communicated with ATC. After consulting the Quick Reference Checklist; it was clear the we had multiple failures not covered by the Quick Reference Checklist. In addition; the MA lights for both Flight Directors were alternating flashing in sequence. I Acquired the appropriate enroute Airinc VHF radio frequency from the chart and phone patched both dispatch and Maintenance Control. With no solution; both Maintenance Control and Dispatch agreed with my decision to divert back to ZZZ as opposed to continuing to ZZZ1 5 hours away in mountainous terrain with automation issues at night and a potential 12 hour+ duty day. FAs (Flight Attendants) were advised; ATC was advised (Requested priority handling and equipment requested to check brakes and tires); company was advised; and an announcement was made to the pax. We used the Landing Distance Normal Configuration chart for our aircraft to obtain landing distance as Saber wouldn't calculate for us the landing performance in our overweight condition at landing (approximately 161;000 lbs). It was my judgement to forego flying for however long it would take to burn 15;000 lbs of fuel to reach landing weight; so I opted to land overweight in light of the distance required from the chart. Once ATC cleared us on a vector heading for approach to land X in ZZZ; I assumed the PF role. Landing was inconsequential and smooth exiting X; X; holding short of X on X while ZZZ Fire assessed our brakes and tires. All normal; proceeded to Gate X.

On departure out of ZZZ; the Captain experienced intermittent failure of his flight director. Both his roll and pitch command bars would randomly disappear and reappear without any warning annunciations. Autopilot A disconnected and was unable to reengage as we continued the climb. As the Captain and I began to analyze the situation; we recognized that my flight director appeared to be working normally and the Captain was able to engage Autopilot B. A short period after engaging the autopilot; the autothrottles disengaged as a result of the Number 2 throttle advancing several knob widths forward of the Number 1 throttle. The Captain returned the throttles to a symmetric condition and the autothrottles were reengaged. We had been given a climb to 16;000 ft. and decided to maintain that altitude and our current airspeed of 250 kts. as we continued our flight plan route. The Captain transferred the aircraft control to me; and I kept the radios while he further analyzed the situation and referenced the QRG. I told ATC we were working an issue but required no assistance at this time. The autothrottles once again disconnected as a result of asymmetry and we elected to keep them off for the remainder of the flight. During this time we also notice the MA light for the flight director switches was cycling back and forth from the Captain's side to the FO side. Additionally; the left center tank fuel pump LOW PRESSURE light illuminated with over 20;000 lbs. of fuel in the center tank. Lastly; the STAB OUT OF TRIM light flickered despite any changes in pitch or airspeed. It was clear that we had multiple issues not covered by the QRG; and the Captain quickly tuned the appropriate ARINC VHF radio frequency and established a phone patch with dispatch and Maintenance Control. Since there was no clear solution for our situation; dispatch and Maintenance Control agreed with the Captain's decision to divert to ZZZ as opposed to continuing. This decision was made after the Captain and I discussed the threats involved: automation issues; night landing in mountainous terrain; long duty day. The Captain advised the FAs (Flight Attendants) and made an announcement to the passengers. He then took the primary radio back from me and requested priority handling with ATC in addition to coordinating for aircraft rescue and firefighting to meet the aircraft to check our brakes and tires since we would be landing overweight. The Captain briefed the approach and calculated the landing distance using the Landing Distance Normal Configuration chart for our aircraft since Saber would not calculate at our current weight which was approximately 161;000 lbs. I agreed with the Captain's decision to land overweight; given we had the landing distance; as opposed to holding for almost 2.5 hours to burn fuel. The descent checklist was accomplished; and the Captain took over as the PF once ATC cleared us on a vector for the ILS X. A 30-flap landing was conducted and a normal landing was made. We exited on X; X; and while holding short of X; aircraft rescue and firefighting checked our brakes and tires. With an all normal; we proceeded to taxi to gate X.

PA28 pilot on a night training flight reported the engine stopped working and they made a successful engine-out landing at an airport. Post flight inspection revealed the engine failure resulted from fuel exhaustion.

The flight where this incident happened was a night VFR cross-country from ZZZ to ZZZ; as the final leg of a cross country flight along the route of ZZZ-ZZZ1-ZZZ2-ZZZ; which was being conducted for the purpose of instrument proficiency for me; using a view-limiting device while accompanied by a safety pilot. Flight planning indicated that we had sufficient fuel for this mission; and indeed; I have flown this route several times with no issues in other similar aircraft. I was using planned fuel burn of 10 gph; in accordance with performance charts for [this make/model]; such as the one we were flying. We checked fuel state prior to the flight both on the gauges; as well as by visual verification on both tanks (both myself and my safety pilot) during the pre-flight inspection. Both tanks were visually noted by both of us as being above the tabs. The flight proceeded uneventfully until the final leg from ZZZ2 to ZZZ. Approximately halfway between the two airports; at an altitude of 6;500 MSL (a little over 3 hours into the flight); the engine developed roughness; then sputtered and quit. We had just changed tanks approximately 2 minutes prior; and I had adjusted the mixture slightly; so I immediately applied full rich mixture; turned the electric fuel pump on; and switched the tanks back. The engine caught almost immediately; and I was able to initiate a full power climbing turn in order to remain near the town of ABC; which I knew had an airport; just in case the engine quit again; since we didn't know the reason for the engine stoppage. After about 2 minutes or less; the engine quit again; and I pitched for best glide; and began searching for the airport; which we initially had difficulty doing; due to the obscuration of the airfield beacon by trees when approaching from the south. We attempted to use the CTAF to turn the runway lights up; and eventually were able to do so; and spotted the runway. Upon identifying my landing site; I then had my safety pilot read the emergency checklist for engine failure; while I performed the action items. We were unable to affect a restart. We then attempted to contact ZZZ Approach (just as this happened; ZZY Approach had handed us off to ZZZ; but before we could establish radio contact; the engine had quit the first time). Unable to reach Approach on the radio; we squawked 7700 on the transponder; then prepared for an emergency landing. We easily had the altitude to make the field; so I utilized S-turns and a forward slip to bleed off altitude for a straight-in approach to RWYXX. We landed safely; (a textbook short field landing) and egressed the aircraft. We could hear sirens as emergency responders from the city of ABC; both fire and police (having been notified by ATC) were en-route to our location. I notified approach via cell phone that we were safe on deck (all personnel on board; as well as the aircraft); and the first responders assisted with towing the aircraft to a parking area. Upon inspecting the aircraft afterwards; we discovered that both tanks were completely empty (both fuel tanks were still reading approximately 1/4 tank on the gauges when the engine first quit; and the left tank gauge continued to show this fuel state even after landing).
