According to pre-flight planning; we should have had about 1.2 hours of fuel remaining at that point of the flight; which would have allowed us to make it back to ZZZ and have our legal VFR night fuel reserve plus some; so this gauge reading seemed reasonable at the time (although I have never entirely trusted fuel gauges in aircraft; and this incident has greatly deepened that distrust)!My understanding is that the owner will be doing an inspection in the next few days to confirm that there are no fuel leaks or other issues that might have contributed to running out of fuel early. Assuming that no mechanical issues are found at that time; I believe that the following factors are involved:(1) For some reason I thought that fuel at the tabs on this plane was X gallons (Y per side); but I later found that in this aircraft it is Z gallons (A gallons per side out of a Y gallon tank). A contributing factor for this may have been that most of my recent flight time has been in a [different model] for which tabs are indeed Y per side. I may have confused this with the Y gallons per side TOTAL for this aircraft for full tanks; not tabs. (2) It is possible that this aircraft was burning a lot more than 10 gph. I was told afterwards that the aircraft burns more like 15 gph average if you are performing a lot of pattern work (and we had conducted 4 instrument approaches prior to heading home on the final leg). None of the [aircraft] publications that I have substantiate this type of fuel burn for an IO360 engine; but if so; than that would partly explain why we ran out of fuel early. I am not aware of whether this aircraft has any performance modifications that would increase fuel burn. A 15 gph burn rate; even for a short time; would definitely run us out much sooner than expected.Thankfully we were able to safely land engine-out at this small rural airfield; especially given that this happened at night in an airplane that I was relatively unfamiliar with. This incident reinforces the value of proper pre-flight planning and ensuring that accurate information is available in terms of fuel burn as well as fuel tank size; even when operating in the local area on a fairly short flight in terms of distance between points. It also reinforces the value of cruising at higher altitudes when over rugged terrain; especially at night. Lastly; it shows the importance of staying proficient at all aspects of an engine-out emergency. My thanks to all that assisted; from the approach controllers; to the first responders; as well as my safety pilot.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Instructor reported the aircraft became hard to control; causing a return to home base and a precautionary emergency landing.

Finishing up a training flight with a student in Class G Airspace my student advised he was starting to feel nauseous. I took control of the aircraft from my student using the 3 part positive exchange of flight controls. As I took control of the aircraft I noticed the flight controls were extremely stiff on the longitudinal axis (ailerons). When asking the student if he was blocking the yoke from moving he responded with no and I visually confirmed he was nowhere near any of the controls. After maintaining positive control of the aircraft I started looking around both yokes for a reason why there was such an issue with the roll function as well as looking out at both ailerons. I could not find any reason why I was having such an issue maintaining level flight. We had just completed turns around a point and I wondered if a bird or something collided with the underside of the right aileron at just the correct time that prevented me from turning the yoke right or if there was something that caught up the control cables inside the wing that was preventing this. I was about 15 miles and a 180 degree turn from ZZZ1 and about 20 miles straight to ZZZ. I decided that ZZZ was not only straight ahead but 95% could be over water and wetlands versus ZZZ1 which would put me over populations and wooded areas for a majority of the flight as well as the services available at ZZZ (ATC; ARFF; Line services; Maintenance and the aircraft's Home base). The decision was made and I continued straight towards ZZZ and listened to the ATIS while having the student look through the Emergency Checklist for anything that listed flight control issues. I also verified that the elevators and rudder were not experiencing any issues. I attempted to go further to the right but was met with more and more resistance and did not want to risk snapping anything or causing any further issues/damage. I contacted the tower and advised I was approximately 20 miles south of the airport with some sort of flight control issue and requested a straight in priority landing on Runway 1. Flying straight I would have intercepted the extended centerline on a very shallow 10-15 degrees. Tower advised me to continue and expect the request as well as asked if I needed anything. I advised I did not and was trying to work the issue while maintaining in control. About 10 miles out I realized that while I was maintaining control at 107 KIAS I had no idea what the aircraft would do as I slowed to approach speed of 66 KIAS. I also noticed that I was applying a considerable amount of right rudder to maintain straight flight. At point I made the decision with the unknowns there and having to be uncoordinated as I would be approaching the ground I would prefer Fire Services standing by as well as identify as an emergency to open up any further options that could be available as I may only have 1 shot at the approach once I get down towards that 66 KIAS. I advised my student to tighten his seat belt and that my arms were starting to get tired holding the airplane level that I would need him to use CRM with me and help with Power settings and flaps. At about 1;000MSL I told my student that at 800AGL I wanted him to release the top latch of my door and by 500AGL I wanted him to release the side latch so the door could be unlocked and we can focus on landing in the last 500ft. As I crossed the threshold at about 80KIAS with 2 notches (25 degree) of flaps and about 5 degrees of intercept of the centerline I had my student reduce the power to idle and maintained control through landing but did end up left of centerline.After the aircraft was fully on the ground rolling out I released the yoke which went full deflection to the left. I taxied the aircraft back to the FBO apron and shut down the aircraft. I had my Senior CFI meet us to have him look for a possible issue. After the aircraft was completely shut down I had him go and try to move the yoke which he did with no issues. Further investigation it was noticed that the autopilot (AP); Single Axis; roll knob was turned to the left. The autopilot was never a thought as upon hiring over a year ago I was advised by the then-Assistant Chief Flight Instructor that the Auto pilot did not work; was disconnected from power but not able to be removed from the bottom of the panel. I never thought anything of it because during night flights the AP never had any backlighting to show it had power. My senior instructor and I started up the aircraft and initiated the Autopilot which produced the same effect that I experienced in flight. We conducted a full check of all systems and found nothing else that could have caused the issue. We determined that the location of the AP the student could have inadvertently brushed the switch activating it with no knowledge as there are no lights to indicate it is powered or active. We also came to the conclusion that this incident was not a flight control malfunction as much as an unintentional activation of the AP as the AP did what it was told. Speaking with my Senior CFI we decided that I would personally verify any statements of inoperability from another pilot even if they are a superior with Maintenance and make sure the correct items are done for such items. I am also working on a full lesson for all of my students on the AP; how it works; issues experienced and multiple ways on how to shut it off until a decision could be made to keep the AP with it known active or make the AP inoperative and remove it from the aircraft.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Pilot reported electrical failure in flight; which resulted in a return to departure airport.

The mission of the flight was intended to be a discovery flight. The pilot observed the METAR and TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast) at ZZZ before the flight and determined the weather was sufficient for the mission of the flight. The pilot completed weight and balance data along with performance calculations before the flight for the aircraft along with full fuel and two people. The pilot then conducted the pre-flight on the aircraft; which had been hangered the night before. The specific aircraft had been flown once before by the pilot in a checkout flight. During the pre-flight inspection the pilot noted that the landing lights were squawked inoperative on the dispatch sheet and the parking brake of the aircraft was placarded as inoperative. During the pre-flight the pilot noted no other irregularity with the aircraft. Additionally the pilot noted that the alternator belt was taut and in place; all the aircraft lights operated correctly; the Pitot tube was properly heated when tested; and the flaps extended at a normal rate to its full extension. The PIC requested the fuel tanks to be filled to its fullest extent; which was done by a ramp worker; and the PIC noted that there were about 6 quarts of oil in the engine. Upon inspection of the electrical system; it appeared to operate normally. The PIC then entered the cockpit on the right seat; with the sole passenger sitting in the left seat. The PIC then gave the pre-flight briefing to the passenger and also demonstrated how to operate the flight controls and engine controls to the passenger. At this point the PIC then started the engine with the assistance of the passenger and then the PIC taxied to the run-up area. At the run-up area the pilot received the current ATIS and then performed the run-up as described by the checklist. The run-up proceeded without any irregularities discovered- notably the amperage gauge indicated that there was neither a charge nor discharge on the battery. The PIC then completed the run-up checklist and received the departure clearance. Shortly after; the PIC then received the taxi clearance and began to taxi to runway 8 via taxiway E1. The pilot then held short of runway 8 and proceeded with the before takeoff checklist and briefed the takeoff checklist and procedure. After contacting ZZZ tower; the pilot then took off from runway 8 and was given instructions to climb on heading 190. The pilot climbed out at Vy (74 KIAS) up to 8500 feet MSL. The climb proceeded as normal; the aircraft was handed over to ZZZ departure who instructed the PIC that they could fly at their desired heading and altitude. The PIC performed the climb checklist while simultaneously describing the function and purpose of the primary aircraft instruments to the passenger. Upon reaching the top of climb; the PIC began to set cruise power and pitch. The PIC also began performing the cruise checklist. Notably; the PIC saw a layer of a few clouds at the aircraft's 12 O'clock; and therefore turned left to navigate east of the clouds. At this point the PIC also turned on the pitot heat as the aircraft was navigating relatively close to the cloud layer and the surface temperatures were reported to be below freezing. (At this point this is where I believe the failure occurred. After review of the flight; I believe that this is a case of alternator over-voltage. At this time all the lights [NAV/STROBE/BEACON] were on; as was the pitot heat and the avionics system which may have been too much load for the system to handle.) In this middle of conducting the cruise checklist and navigating around the cloud layer; PIC received a call from ZZZ departure saying that they lost our transponder code and altitude on radar. They requested that the PIC reset the transponder; which the PIC did while also responding to departure. During the response transmission the PIC noticed that they could not hear their transmission through the headset and that they heard no reply from ZZZ departure.Shortly after; the PIC noticed the lights on the radio stack were flickering; which caused the PIC to suspect an electrical failure was imminent. At this point the PIC turned the aircraft to a circle pattern and reduced the power setting to economy cruise then began troubleshooting the problem. The PIC first checked the amp gauge and saw that it indicated there was discharge on the battery; then the PIC looked at the circuit breakers and saw that none of them were out of their regular position. After this; the PIC then turned off both the master switch and the alternator switch; waited 10 seconds; and turned it back on. At this point all the electrical systems on board the aircraft had failed. After failing to fix the problem the PIC then began to perform VFR lost-communication procedures. The PIC used their cellular device to call the FSS number and talk to the briefer; who then gave the pilot a weather briefing in the area along with valid SIGMETS; AIRMETS; and the local METAR at ZZZ. Shortly after that the call failed to FSS; but the PIC noticed that they had received a missed call from ZZZ TRACON on their cell phone. The PIC called the number back immediately and requested vectors back to ZZZ. The TRACON controller then provided a heading which the PIC flew while periodically giving altitude updates. When the field was in-sight; the TRACON controller gave clearance to land runway 3. The PIC then configured the aircraft for landing and performed a no-flap landing without incident. Upon landing the controller gave clearance to taxi to the FBO ramp via C; G taxiways. The taxi to the ramp proceeded without incident and the PIC then shut-down the aircraft and performed a post-flight inspection. It was noted that with the post flight there could be no clear cause of the electrical failure; and the alternator belt was still taut in place similarly to the pre-flight inspection.

A321 Captain reported recurring fume events which have resulted in flight crew experiencing physiological symptoms. Reporter questioned whether maintenance corrective actions are in need of review.

Fumes on flight ZZZ-ZZZ1. This report is to highlight the procedures used to resolve fume events. It isn't to report the fume event. In summary; after the flight and cabin crew smelled fumes during flight and after landing; Maintenance worked to resolve the problem. After performing various procedures; Maintenance said the problem was fixed three separate times. Each time; the flight and cabin crew pointed out that the fumes were still present. Even so; a manager from another department was brought in to see if she smelled any fumes-she did not. So; as the maintenance policy allows; the aircraft was returned to service; overruling six professional and very experienced flight and cabin crewmembers' specific and detailed descriptions of the characteristics of the still present fumes' smell; the locations in the flight deck and cabin where the fumes were detected and the air supply vent locations from which the fumes were emanating. Approximately an hour later; a flight crew reassigned to ferry the aircraft to ZZZ2 started the #1 Engine; smelled the fumes and refused the aircraft. The fume event began during descent below at 5;000 ft.; at 15 miles from ZZZ1 airport when I noticed musty smelling fumes on the flight deck coming from the eyeball vents on both the overhead and instrument panels. I recognized the smell from previous experience (along with information supplied by both Air Carrier and the Pilots Association); as being from petroleum based fluid being heated and entering the air conditioning system. Being close to the ground and landing; I wanted to find a solution quickly so I closed the flight deck vents to see if there was any change. There was not; so I reopened them thinking that if the fumes were transient that air flow might move the fumes through and off of the flight deck. I also started to feel slightly nauseated so I donned my O2 mask. After donning my O2 mask the nauseated feeling subsided somewhat. Landing was made without incident. At taxi speed I opened my window; turned off the air conditioning packs and taxied to the gate. I then spoke with the flight attendants to see if any of them had smelled the fumes. The flight attendant at Door 3L said that shortly before landing some passengers asked him about a smell in the area. Once they had pointed it out; he said he had then smelled the fumes. No other flight attendants reported smelling the fumes at their jumpseat locations during flight. I wrote up the fumes in the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logs); then completed and submitted a smoke; odor; fume form. When Maintenance arrived I described the smell of the fumes to them. None of the mechanics with whom I spoke (four I believe); smelled the fumes. From then until when the flight was cancelled at XA:00; one mechanic (of the four); acknowledged that he smelled the fumes 'slightly' and only one time. During this time; Maintenance completed procedure(s) three separate times and after each time said that they didn't smell the fumes and wanted to sign off the AML. Each time; my flight and cabin crew pointed out the smell of the fumes in the cabin and flight deck; so Maintenance continued their procedures. At some point after those three attempts to resolve the problem; one mechanic told me that the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that day. Soon after that; a manager from another department was asked to walk through the cabin and see if she smelled the fumes. After a bit I checked my schedule and saw that we were reassigned to take that same aircraft back to ZZZ at XC:00 on [Date]. That was consistent with the last I heard from the mechanic who said the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that night. Around XD:00; I saw that another crew had been reassigned to fly our aircraft to ZZZ2 at XE:00. I texted the Captain on that flight to be sure he was aware of the seriousness of the problem. He replied; stating that after they had started the #1 Engine; the fumes returned. He did not accept the aircraft. I then called [Pilots Association] Safety for some guidance. I am concerned because; despite all the procedures in place to determine whether the source of the fumes is eliminated; the methods to determine whether the fumes are present or remain:1. Expose maintenance personnel and possibly other people to the fumes and their potential harmful effects (isn't that what we're trying to avoid?).2. Allow using the olfactory senses of random individuals that; (a) may not be able to detect the smell of the fumes; (b) have never smelled the fumes and/or; (c) have no knowledge of the seriousness of the smoke; odor and fume events and their potential and documented health threats.3. Allow the complaints and input of those that do smell the fumes to be ignored or overruled by any randomly chosen person that does not smell them. It seems that the goal should be that if just one person still smells the fumes; the problem isn't solved and the aircraft won't be released to flight status.

BE-36 pilots reported a fire of unknown origin at engine start requiring evacuation and the airport ARFF to respond.

We had completed the pre-flight check of the aircraft and pulled it from the hangar at ZZZ Airport to the alley way between hangars.We had completed the pre-start checklist items; picked up the ATIS and our clearance to transit out of the SFRA (Special Flight Rules Area).The aircraft started normally. There was a single backfire after or as the engine started but not too uncommon. The throttle was retarded following normal procedures.Shortly after engine start the cockpit began to fill with an acrid smelling smoke from under the left side of the panel. The engine was immediately shutdown and we exited the plane. All electrical (master/alternator/ignition) was shut off.Co-pilot grabbed the fire extinguisher as we exited. After exiting the Tower was called. The Tower called the on-field fire company. Response time was about <5 min as the on-field company was sent to the wrong side of the field.We opened the engine cowling to see if we could identify a source and possible extinguish. No fire was evident in the engine compartment. The fire departments had not yet arrived.The prop began a very slow rotation as if the engine was trying to crank.We went to check to verify that the Master Switch was off. It was.Smoke from the panel was much heavier. Appeared to mostly originate from the pilot side.Close evaluation showed flames from top of the left side-wall upholstery.We used the fire extinguisher to extinguish the flames along the sidewall. The amount of extinguishing agent or time for a full discharge seemed less than expected (perhaps 30 seconds).Fuel valve was moved to Off.A person called indicating that the Emergency Locator Transmitter had activated. We began a search for the beacon to deactivate. Determined that it is behind the panel in the back of the passenger area behind the stretcher. Requires panel removal.Fire department from ZZZ arrives.They verify that there is no excess heat in area where the flames were extinguished or other locations.The mechanic we used at [Company] arrived and began assisting with assessment and possible causes and removal of the ELT.Fire departments determined that no action on their part was needed and departed. On the scene perhaps 30 minutes.No immediate cause was noted the A&P from [Company].We returned the plane to the hangar. We called [Company1] to see if they could determine any immediate cause. We were trying to decide if we needed to use [Company1] vs [Company2].The technician from [Company1] saw no immediate issues.We disconnected the ground side of the battery; wrapped and secured to make certain no contact could occur that might provide a power source.We left the airplane doors open or ajar to allow for ventilation and secured the hangar.The plan at this point was to have the aircraft moved to [Company2].

We pulled the aircraft out of the hangar; shut the hangar doors and climbed into the cockpit for the start. We completed the normal procedures checklist setting the parking brake; received our SFRA (Special Flight Rules Area) clearance and shut down the avionics for start and noted the time as XA:X0 pm. The engine was primed with the auxiliary fuel pump; mixture was set to full rich and throttle to full open. The ignition was turned to start and as the engine began to turn over it ignited; and the throttle was retarded to slow the RPM to approximately 1000 RPM. As the RPM was beginning to stabilize; there was a backfire explosion and almost simultaneously smoke began pouring out from the defroster duct? at the left side of the wind screen and from underneath the dash panel by the PIC (Pilot-in-Command)'s rudder pedals. The smoke intensified filling the cockpit and the door was opened to relieve the smoke. Since the smoke was continuing; the mixture was pulled; the ignition was turned off removing the key and the battery and alternator switches turned off. Co-pilot exited the aircraft to determine a cause of the smoke and as he was investigating; I pulled the fire extinguisher from behind the co-pilots seat. I then exited the aircraft while he continued to walk around the nose of the aircraft looking for any source of fire. None was noted and the smoke was ventilating and dissipating. I called the tower on my cell phone to notify them of our situation and asked for fire assistance. I told Tower we were [at] the hangars on the east side just south of the terminal building at hangar. Tower took immediate action to alert the airport firetruck and ZZZ City Fire Dept. We did not see any evidence of a fuel fire or flames exiting the engine compartment although we did notice that the propeller began to rotate slowly for a few terms before stopping completely. The engine compartment was opened and there was no evidence of any fuel or oil leaks or any fire or smoke damage to the engine compartment. We went back behind the right wing and looking through the cockpit door; co-pilot noticed flames between the sidewall and left rudder pedal. He activated the fire extinguisher and sprayed the area of the flame; extinguishing it.While waiting for the fire equipment to arrive; I called Maintenance to ask them to have a mechanic come over and evaluate the situation. Fortunately; their lead was on the way to the east side and he arrived to look at the aircraft. Shortly thereafter the Airport Operations Director was first to arrive on scene and supervised the arrival of the fire equipment. The airport team was first ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) unit on the scene and were very professional in evaluating the situation so that no unnecessary action was taken. The smoke gradually dissipated and the aircraft was checked for residual hot spots; none of which were found. The fire equipment returned to their stations and the aircraft was hangared until it could be moved to the local maintenance facility.

Pilot reported application of the wrong MEL complicated the flights unnecessarily.

In ZZZ we attempted to start number two engine using APU air and it spooled up abnormally slowly; and I noticed that the EGT seemed to lag. At 45% N2 the start stagnated and decayed until a 2.5% N2 decrease and Engine Fail indication on the ECAM. We stopped the start; then following guidance in our paperwork; we started number one (which also stagnated a little bit but then started normally) and then attempted a second start on number two using cross-bleed from the number one engine. We allowed the engine to spool up to 25.7% N2; then added fuel. At starter cutout; the engine hung again; dropping to about 43.2% N2 and hanging there before slowly spooling up to about 43.8% N2 when it timed out for the start and Engine Fail was indicated on ECAM again. Our Quick Reference Handbook said we could attempt a second start after the first hung start; but that maintenance action was required if the second start failed. At that point we requested a tug and BTB to our parking space. This is where Maintenance Control got involved. At first they suggested that we defer the APU bleed; however it was obvious to me that the air was not the problem (we used a separate source for each start); so I told him the APU bleed deferral was not sufficient. Then he suggested that a problem with the Integrated Drive Generator might be causing the hung start and suggested we defer that; and I agreed it could be tried. As part of the maintenance action during start the Inetgrated Drive Generator was disconnected and deferred; and the Airworthiness Release in the log book was signed off; then we continued getting the jet started and were on our way. During the flight the APU was running as required by the deferral; and at 36;000 ft. it automatically shut down. I attempted to start the APU; and on the second try; it started. I requested and descended to a lower altitude of 30;000 ft. and the APU operated normally for the rest of the flight. If I had not been able to start it; I would have had to advise ATC and divert. I wrote up the APU under a P code for momentary or transitory malfunction. In ZZZ1; maintenance checked the APU for any failure codes; did the repetitive inspection for oil quantity for the Integrated Drive Generator deferral; and signed off the APU. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed the situation and agreed that the APU was not malfunctioning and may have had a momentary problem with operating at high altitude. We accepted the jet for the leg to ZZZ2. With a fresh Airworthiness Release in the log book; we started the number one engine first; then started number two using cross-bleed at the request of maintenance. The number two engine came close to exceeding time limits; but did eventually spool up. We were filed for 33;000 ft.; and at that altitude the APU did the same thing--it shut down--and we were able to get it started again on the second try. We requested and descended to 29;000 ft. for the remainder of the flight. Again; the APU operated normally from there on; and again; I wrote it up with a P code for the shut down. I also made a comment in the logbook about the number two engine start; even though our flight paperwork said that comments for a successful start were not needed. There I made a note that the EGT from fuel introduction to the point where the start stagnated; then started to spool up; seemed abnormally low and was at least 50 degrees cooler at 45% N2 than the other engine. The stagnated start was evident from fuel introduction until after started cutout when it became apparent that the engine was not ready to continue the start on its own. The Integrated Drive Generator has nothing to do with the EGT during start. I suspect something else is going on here; perhaps a Electronic Engine Control problem with the fuel mixture at high altitude; or a sensor malfunction. On further reflection; I feel that the deferral of the Integrated Drive Generator was inappropriate for the problem we had; and I should not have accepted it. It created a problem where we could have been forced to request priority handling and divert. It is likely that whatever is wrong with our engine starts does not pose a safety of flight risk once we get the engine going; so it makes no sense to do a deferral that could compromise safety. Until this is figured out; the guidance needs to be specific and it needs to go out to everyone in the maintenance and crew pipelines and it should be operations friendly. My recommendation is that everything in the fuel system be checked in case it is causing the starting problem for cold engines at high altitude. I think that the bleed system is less likely to be the issue because of the low EGT I saw during all four start attempts on that engine. I also recommend that maintenance be able to attempt at least one more start before the aircraft is taken out of service; and that crew get more guidance concerning the problem. 'Maintenance action' is not enough to let a Captain know what to expect or what to accept. I also have felt for a long time that our systems manual has been scrubbed of a lot of detail about systems with which we do not directly interact; so we are less able to make informed decisions and instead have to rely on experience. That will not always save us from making the wrong call. Everyone in this situation acted in good faith; and I am not writing this report to cast any doubt on anyone. I only want to point out a safety issue that we can avoid in the future.

A319 flight crew reported while experiencing turbulence they were initially unaware their PA System and interphone warnings to the cabin were not heard due to the system malfunctioning resulting in frightened and angry flight attendants.

We departed on time for a XX minute flight. Climbing through 10;000 feet I chimed the flight attendants and we continued our climb to 21;000 feet. Center was telling me to expect bad rides all the way to our destination. So when we leveled off at 21;000 feet. I made an announcement stating that the ride was going to be rough and that I would keep the seat belt sign of the entire flight. I also asked the flight attendants to remain seated for the duration of the flight as well or so I thought. The ride was not good. Continuous light occasionally moderate turbulence. The arrival is challenging on a good day and today was no exception. We were dealing with a complex arrival; turbulence; icing and multiple changes to speed and altitude. We were cleared to descend via the arrival with no speed restrictions with about a 90 knot tailwind.We would be early. Around the time that we started our descent I noticed that someone was trying to use the door code to gain access to the cockpit. I immediately declined it and made sure door was locked. The Pilot Flying and I both thought that was strange so I tried calling back to a Flight Attendant to see what was going on. That was the first indication something was wrong. When I turned on the speaker for the cabin I could hear an audible cycling noise. When I tried to chime the flight attendants I couldn't hear the chime and I could not hear any voices on the interphone. I tried to make a quick announcement but nothing was coming out back in the cabin. As the Pilot Flying and I were extremely busy managing the descent and approach we heard a knock at the door and could faintly hear a voice. Pilot Flying turned around and saw a note on the ground that said INTERPHONE INOP.I wanted to get up and grab the note to try and write something back but we were too busy. A few minutes passed. The cockpit door lock code was entered again and I denied it a second time. I tried to yell as loud as I could that we got the message. I think they must have heard that time because they stopped knocking on the door. We landed and began our taxi to the gate. After clearing the active runways I had Pilot Flying call maintenance and inform them that our Cabin Interphone and Public Address system was inoperative. We taxied to the gate and shutdown. After the shutdown checklist was complete and before the forward door was opened I got up to check on the A Flight Attendant and see if everything was OK. He was visibly upset. After the passengers got off the other two Flight Attendant's joined us up in first class to discuss what had happened. A Flight Attendant said that it was the scariest flight of his life. He said that after we had hit a rough patch of turbulence the cabin lights in the plane started to cycle on and off. They were still doing it after I went back to talk to them. He then had tried to call me to see if everything was OK but couldn't reach me. He thought that maybe we had lost pressurization and that we might have been incapacitated. He tried the door code to maybe get a peek inside to see if we were OK. He left a note under the door in hopes that we would grab it and write back. Only after the last time that he tried the door lock and I denied it did he hear me yell through the door. The other two flight attendants were also upset that they couldn't communicate with me. I spent at least 15 minutes with them trying to explain why I couldn't respond to them even though I wanted to.Trying to unlock the cockpit door without my authorization put me on high alert. This is not something I expected. If this had been a different flight with more time I would have taken their note and responded to it and sent it back. That would have been the best way. I tried yelling through the door; but it is loud in the cockpit and only on the second time did they hear me. If we had lost pressurization the masks in the back would have dropped and they would have felt it in their ears. The first time I denied his access to the cockpit door he should have known we were OK. I cannot just open the cockpit door without knowing who is behind it. My first priority is to fly the aircraft. I just didn't have enough time to respond to them the way they wanted me to.I tried to address all of their concerns and I did understand that they were upset. I wrote up the Public Address system as well as the Interphone system with their input to give the mechanics all they needed to fix the system. Maintenance came on board and reset the system. I tested the PA and both forward and aft intercoms with the Flight Attendants and in front of maintenance to make sure everything worked. Maintenance signed off the system and we than headed back. After our initial conversation about what had transpired I thought all Flight Attendants were OK just a little rattled but good enough to continue. If I had known they still had reservations about what had happened I would have immediately responded to them. My crew always comes first.

During our descent on the arrival we heard a knock on the cockpit door. We turned around and saw a note that was slid under the door stating that the interphone was inoperative and there were lights flashing in the cabin. We heard the Flight Attendant said that he was trying to get a hold of us. We never heard him prior to that as this was a 30 minutes or so flight and we were busy from wheels up. The Captain told him we were landing soon. When we landed Maintenance was contacted. Upon arrival at the gate the Captain met with the flight attendants to discuss the event. I went to do the walkaround. The mechanic came and fixed the problem. The interphone and Public Address system was tested before we left the gate and they worked.

B737-800 Captain reported a fumes event during gate de-icing; which resulted in a cabin crew replacement due to physiological symptoms.

I am submitting this copy of a fumes report submitted following a SOF event that occurred following deicing at the gate at ZZZ as a report. The only thing I might add pertaining to legalities is that after the event when we elected to attempt to fly the leg a second time before Maintenance took the plane out of service; that decision was made after conferring with the Duty Chief at Maintenance Control who had consulted with Maintenance following the SOF event. We had been running the packs with the APU for a long period of time after the passengers deplaned; and then did an engine run on top of that to blow out the entire air conditioning system and had no further issue with deicing fumes. The plane was only subsequently removed from service because it came to light that there might be an IOD claim from one or more of the flight attendants (3 of whom elected to deadhead home on the very same airplane they'd been working on when we had the fumes event) 'This is a report of a fume event that occurred post-deicing at the gate at ZZZ. A separate Fume Event form was also submitted. This is the third such occurrence I have encountered following ZZZ deicing in the past 2 years. In the previous 2 occurrences the effects were much less pronounced and not deemed a hazard because their duration was brief and the cause obvious. In those two cases when the aircraft was reconfigured post-deicing; when the packs were reinstated there was an immediate introduction of visible deicing fluid fumes entering the flight deck; with a much less pronounced but slightly noticeable effect in the cabin that did not warrant any action or alarm. In both cases the packs were turned off and cockpit windows opened followed by an eventual attempt to turn the packs back in one at a time with no further issues. In this case the same thing happened only to a much greater and somewhat alarming degree. When we ran the reconfiguration checklist using the HOT app in this event; turning the APU bleed on reinstated the packs which caused an immediate introduction of thick deicing fluid smoke into the flight deck. My memory of the next couple minutes is a blur because it felt like there were several things demanding my attention and not a lot of information to triage their importance and make a proper best decision given all the variables present. The cockpit smoke was so thick that I could barely see the First Officer and had to feel for my oxygen mask to find it. At some point the packs were turned off; oxygen masks used and the cockpit windows opened. At that point my primary concern was how bad did it get in the cabin? Based on past experience and the current magnitude of the problem; I suspected not nearly as bad as the flight deck but probably getting everyone concerned. Almost immediately the flight attendants called and said the cabin was hazy and what was going on? I said it was deicing fluid and tried to ascertain their assessment which while alarmed didn't suggest it was dire. (The QRH was never considered as the smoke/removal procedures are inflight procedures and rely on using the packs). At this point I was weighing the possibility of evacuating into frigid; arctic conditions with high winds onto a glycol-covered ramp (including 2 wheelchair passengers) vs getting the jetbridge up to the aircraft ASAP (as soon as possible) in case an [immediate] deplaning was deemed advisable. I asked the First Officer to contact ramp control to get the jetbridge attached immediately and tried to think of a way to provide some relief to the cabin air situation. I called the flight attendants back and instructed them to disarm all their doors and to the extent possible crack them open a couple inches to get fresh air into the cabin. That turned out to be unsuccessful because a tailwind was blowing the APU fumes from back to front so that idea was abandoned pretty quickly. Based on my previous two experiences I began wondering if enough time had gone by and perhaps turning the packs on might actually help to bring fresh air into the cabin so I experimentally flipped on the left pack only; but the smoke returned and I immediately turned it off again. It felt like a Catch-22 situation. I knew the only way we could clean out the air was to run the packs but I didn't dare turn on the packs again with the passengers on board. The jetbridge was eventually attached during which time I had assessed the cabin personally and there was a faint lingering odor but nothing I considered alarming. After the passengers were off I asked the flight attendants to self-assess whether they were okay to continue or did they want some medical evaluation and they all said yes they could continue. At some point I contacted the Duty Chief Pilot and after he consulted with Maintenance they suggested doing an engine run. It was at this point that the gate agent informed me that the flight attendants; who had also deplaned; that the flight attendants 'did not want to take this airplane'. We eventually did run both engines at the gate; using both APU and engine bleeds to blow out the pack air until we were satisfied that there were no further issues with fumes. At some point 4 standby flight attendants were assigned and we reboarded the aircraft and departed. My strategy this time was to take the APU completely out of the equation and we requested and received permission to deice at the CDF instead. Halfway into this deicing I was notified something to the effect that the previous flight attendant crew was claiming an injury on duty and because of that Maintenance was therefore taking that plane out of service. We eventually returned to the gate and deplaned to a different aircraft. As I reached the new gate boarding area I saw an off duty [Company] pilot [Name] waiting to board and I asked him for a candid assessment of his impression of what the cabin situation seemed like; and he confirmed my initial suppositions; namely that it was noticeable but not alarming. He likened it to the kind of haze that might be initially experienced when turning on the packs in very humid conditions; but nothing like the thick smoke we encountered in the cockpit. Once again we had to deice but the CDF was closed by then; so I modified our post-deicing procedure to turning the pack switches off prior to reinstating the APU bleed; and leaving them off through both engine starts and then turning them on after the APU bleed was off at the conclusion of starting the engines. We finally departed uneventfully.' I believe the cause of the fume event was 'inadvertent introduction of Type 1 deicing fluid into the APU intake'. I have one recommendation that I will personally use from now on; namely what I mentioned earlier which is not running the packs until they are set for engine bleed as the air source following deicing. I also have to wonder why this has happened 3 times now (all at ZZZ). Clearly there needs to be more emphasis on protecting the APU inlet door when spraying Type 1 fluid. I don't know their procedures; but maybe spraying in brief spurts above the inlet door from back-to-front might help; or just avoiding the area altogether and clearing it by hand in the worst case scenario; but I'm picturing the usual visual of Type 1 fluid cascading down the cockpit windows like a car wash; and if that is going on in the back of the fuselage that can't be a good thing.

B737 flight crew reported a loss of B system hydraulic fluid; followed by the loss of multiple hydraulic pumps resulted in a diversion.

Normal takeoff and climb out. We went to FL400 for cruise altitude. We got to cruise; made our PA turned off the seatbelt sign. I was Pilot Monitoring. FO (First Officer) said;'uh oh we have a light on the HYD overhead.' I looked up and ENG2 engine driven pump said low pressure. I canceled the master caution and got out the QRH. Simple checklist; select the HYD pump switch to off. End of checklist. We pulled up the hydraulic display on the center screen. B system 106%; normal pressure. We started a what if dialogue. We agreed it was OK to continue with present condition. We looked up Loss of System B in QRH; and discussed it. We looked at flight plan divert circles and discussed scenarios. After 5-10 min the system B quantity started to decrease; slowly at first. I asked ATC for a descent to FL 320. Now the System B started to decrease rapidly. We knew we were about to loose Hyd Sys B. We selected Autopilot A to fly the aircraft; still descending; we were now over Location X but before ZZZZZ fix. We texted Dispatch we were going to lose System B and wanted to confer if we should divert or continue; Note-Loss of SYS B checklist did not say land at nearest suitable airport. We were almost to FL 320 and the ELEC 1 low pressure light illuminated; as the system quantity reached 0 and system pressure was 0;pump switch off per checklist. We got a few more lights and confirmed we had a complete loss of system B. Unbelievably we now got an ENG 1 hyd low pressure light illuminate; pump switch off per checklist. ELEC 2 HYD pump only hydraulic pump now functioning. It held autopilot A. We looked at each other and said lets head to ZZZ1; we had previously talked about divert points and where to go if the situation had gotten worse which it did. During this time we noticed A HYD quantity decreasing from 90+% to low 80's(we thought we might loose A too)I requested a descent and a turn direct to ZZZ1 from Center for a hydraulic loss. He gave us a different heading and said to expect to hold for sequence. We were now clearer to the controller and requested priority handling. The lead FA dinged us and asked if everything was OK; I told her no; type of situation; and to prepare the cabin for a divert to ZZZ1; I asked her to have the cabin ready in 10 minutes; no evac prep necessary. We got direct from ZZZZ Center; reprogramed the FMC and let dispatch know we were diverting. We started in on the loss of System B checklist as we were making a dive for ZZZ1. We ended up taking a vector to lose altitude. We completed the loss of system B to the ALT Flap extension. I then called back to the FA confirmed TEST; no evac; trucks would be standing by; we might seem like we were landing faster. I made a PA to the passengers. The FO did an excellent job of flying the airplane first; great CRM working with me on the checklists; with ATC ; keeping me in the loop where we were when we were being pulled from so many directions (We were getting pulled from ATC; Dispatch; FA; PAX; checklists...). We completed the ALT Flap extension and then landing checklist. The landing was normal for a flaps 15 landing.After the parking checklist; we debriefed. ZZZ1 station manager entered the aircraft and said they might have an aircraft swap if we could fly to ZZZ2. Sent Maintenance report. I talked to the FO and cabin crew and they all wanted to continue and fly to ZZZ2. We called dispatch and he elaborated on the possibility of us flying to ZZZ2. All the crew members wanted to finish the flight to ZZZ2; so we started in on this plan. I spoke with the Operations Manager and the ZZZ2 Chief Pilot for clearance for all of us to continue to ZZZ2. We did have to also fill out a simple report and give copies of our licensed to the [local] authorities. We informed the passengers. The plan did come together and we did an aircraft swap and an uneventful continuation to ZZZ2.

In cruise; the System B Engine Pump 'Low Pressure' light illuminated. The Captain (non-flying pilot) accomplished the QRH checklist and the pump switch was deselected. Hydraulic quantity in the 'B' system was over 100%. Approximately 5 minutes later the 'B' system quantity starts to rapidly drop to zero. After reaching zero; the 'B' system Electric Hydraulic Pump unexpectedly illuminates 'Low Pressure.' We also receive the associated caution light for the flight control system. While the Captain was completing 'Loss of System B' checklist and we were discussing our options (ZZZ1 vs ZZZ2); we received another caution light for System 'A' Engine Pump 'Low Pressure.'We immediately decide to divert to ZZZ1. The Captain advised ATC; and notified the Dispatcher over ACARS. We completed the checklists; notified the Flight Attendants; and informed the passengers. There was a very clear division in the flight deck workload. The Captain worked the problems; communications with the company; and in cabin communications. I flew the aircraft and communicated with ATC. This workload division not only works well in the simulator but also in real life.We completed the 'Loss of System B' deferred items and Alternate Flap Extension procedure. We shot the ILS in ZZZ1 and landed without incident. Clearing the runway we taxied to the gate. The System 'A' Electric Pump continued to function and we fortunately had no other problems.This whole situation was extremely similar a recurrent training scenario that we had not that long ago. Having 'seen it before' was strangely reassuring.

B737 First Officer reported an inflight engine shut down and loss of hydraulic fluid resulted in a diversion.

At cruise altitude FL380 approximately 40 minutes into the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 the Engine 2 HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE light illuminated. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) performed QRH Non-Normal procedure and selected the associated HYD PUMP switch OFF. No further action was required at that time. I don not remember exactly what Hydraulic Qty and Pressure values were at this time but I recall that they were relatively normal as the Electric Hydraulic Pump remained functional.Approximately 15-20 minutes later; the Engine 2 OIL FILTER BYPASS indication illuminated on the Upper Display Unit Primary Engine Indications page. The Captain performed the ENGINE OIL FILTER BYPASS QRH procedures. The OIL FILTER BYPASS light remained illuminated after closing the Engine 2 thrust lever which directed us to the ENGINE FAILURE OR SHUTDOWN QRH checklist and the required shutdown of Engine 2. We elected not to attempt a restart of the engine. As PF (Pilot Flying); I continued to fly the airplane. I disconnected the autopilot and auto throttles and hand flew the airplane; adjusting rudder trim to approximately 13 units of left trim in order to maintain wings level; yoke level.We advised ATC and requested a descent to FL240 due to Engine Out Altitude indication of FL245; and slowed to 233 kts. per the Engine Out speed indication. Center cleared us to descend; as requested. I descended in LVL CHG to FL240. Shortly thereafter were handed off to [adjacent] Center. Initially we elected to continue toward ZZZ1 and were cleared direct to ZZZ1 by enter. After approximately 10-15 minutes of hand flying and after reaching FL240 I engaged Autopilot A (Autopilot B was unavailable due to the non-normal events).The Captain communicated with the flight attendants; made a PA to the passengers; and coordinated with flight attendants to have a deadheading Captain join us on the flight deck as an additional resource/additional crew member (ACM). This was the Captain I had flown with from ZZZ4-ZZZ the previous day and we therefore had the added familiarity and comfort of having just flown together. The Captain attempted to contact Dispatch via both ACARS and on Comm 2 via a frequency that was received in an ACARS message. We could hear Dispatch calling us but they could not hear us talking to them (possibly due to our low altitude?). ACARS availability was intermittent in our location. At some point later on; Center informed us of the frequency that Dispatch was trying to communicate on. We told Center that we had been trying to contact Dispatch on that frequency to no avail; and asked them to relay to Dispatch that we probably had little additional information to share with them beyond what had already been successfully exchanged when ACARS was available and beyond what Center already knew about our situation. During this period of time; the Captain and I periodically exchanged communication roles as necessitated by the multiple overlapping tasks required to be completed; while the deadheading Captain also assisted with some communications to passengers; to Dispatch; and reviewed and confirmed the QRH procedures we had followed; as delegated by the Captain (PM).Approximately 10-15 minutes after shutting down Engine 2; performing associated QRH procedures; and dealing with intermittent communication issues with Dispatch; we discussed and confirmed the fact that ZZZ3 was actually the closest suitable airport and asked Center for direct to ZZZ3. Prior to that decision; given our location over the Gulf; our direct route to ZZZ1 had been taking us relatively close to what would have also been a direct route to ZZZ3. Therefore; there had been no significant delay in getting us on a course to our nearest suitable airport ZZZ3. Weather at ZZZ3 was procured; Dispatch was successfully notified of and supported the decision to divert to ZZZ3; Flight Attendants and passengers were notified; and ACARS divert communications were completed. Initially we had elected not to balance fuel but after the center fuel tanks were empty; we elected to balance fuel; opening the crossfeed valve and turning off Engine number 1 fuel pumps.The Captain discussed with me and the ACM Captain whether or not we would elect to exchange controls at some point and it was agreed upon that the Captain would fly the approach and landing. I recall that transfer of controls occurred while at FL240; approximately 10 minutes prior to descent to lower altitude. Non-Normal landing distance was calculated by me (and backed up by the ACM) and other One Engine Inoperative Landing checklists were reviewed. I made a PA to the passengers explaining that they could expect a relatively normal landing at ZZZ3 with the exception of possibly seeing fire trucks there as a precaution. Below 10;000ft. I completed the portion of the One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist for configuring for a Bleeds Off landing. Despite having calculated non-normal landing distance; normal landing data was also procured (as suggested by the ACM Captain) in order to determine whether or not any special engine out missed approach procedures existed; which did reveal a missed approach procedure of flying runway heading to ZZZ VOR.While on a final base leg vector to final approach for the ZZZ3 ILS at 2;000 ft.; the Captain called for Flaps 1. However; the flaps did not extend when selected. We discussed why that might be occurring; trying to determine whether or not it might be associated with our original HYD LOW PRESSURE situation which had initially been resolved by turning of the engine drive pump and utilizing the remaining electric pump. We informed Approach that we had a flap issue and requested vectors away from the approach. I selected the SYS page on the Upper Display Unit to observe Hydraulic indications and saw that System B Hydraulic Qty was 0 or close to 0 and Pressure was low; if not also 0 (I do not recall the exact value). In post flight discussion with the Captain we discussed that there may have been a time (when flaps 1 was selected?) that a Master Caution light illuminated; we both looked up at the overhead but did not notice any new lights illuminated that were not already part of our previous non-normals. The Captain also recalled that when I had performed the Master Caution Recall as part of the After Start Checklist; the annunciator panel lights had not necessarily all illuminated without one or both of us having to push on the panel; as is often the case; and therefore it is possible that when/if the Master Caution light illuminated during the high workload single engine approach phase of flight; we may have failed to see a HYD indication on the annunciator panel or if it did illuminate; we might have considered it to be associated with the original HYD LOW PRESS non normal. Postflight; we discussed the possibility that it was the demand placed on the hydraulic system by the selection of flaps in conjunction with some other cause of a leak that caused the hydraulic quantity and pressure to go to zero at that time. In any case; given confirmation of 0 HYD QTY on the SYS page; we now performed the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH checklist and procedures which eventually directed us to the Alternate Flap Extension procedure.Once we had completed and reviewed the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH checklist and procedures; and the Captain discussed his plan for configuring flaps (taking into account the additional time required for alternate flap extension); I asked the ACM to reference the deferred items (e.g. landing checklist) for ONE ENGINE INOPERATIVE APPROACH AND LANDING while I referenced the deferred items (e.g. landing checklist) for LOSS OF SYSTEM B; to make sure they were the same or comparable and that we did not miss anything; given that I could only run one landing checklist and we simultaneously had two separate non-normals with deferred items. When ready; we were cleared for the approach. We successfully extended the flaps to 15 usingthe alternate flap extension procedure. Upon contact with ZZZ3 Tower I informed them of our special request in the event of a single engine missed approach per the landing data information.The approach and landing by the Captain were excellent. He stopped the aircraft on the runway with manual brakes per the QRH procedure. ARFF equipment came to the runway and personnel examined the aircraft prior to our taxiing to the gate. We left the flaps extended in case Maintenance wanted them in that position and informed ops and station maintenance of their position. We discussed with a mechanic some of the details of the non-normal events. We had to wait for customs to get ready for us; which caused a delay in deplaning. I took advantage of that time to go to the cabin to talk to the flight attendants and First Class passengers to see how they were doing and talk a little about our situation and answer questions while the Captain continued discussion with mechanics and Chief Pilot; etc.One final note I would like to add is that we received outstanding; professional support from all ATC facilities during the flight and from Flight Operations (Chief Pilots; Safety Committee; etc.) postflight; and our flight attendants were totally professional and did an outstanding job. Utilization of the deadheading Captain's input and support was extremely helpful; too. Thanks to everyone who supported us.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Flight Crew reported a repeat failure of the Take Off Warning System and a failure of trailing edge flaps to retract caused an Air Tun Back and a precautionary emergency landing.

Arriving at the aircraft and checking the logbook; I noticed that the last crew had written that the Takeoff Configuration light and horn activated on takeoff (speed of activation was not noted). I surmised that the crew rejected the takeoff and subsequently swapped out of the aircraft after returning to the gate and the aircraft was not flown afterwards. The corrective action was a check of the Takeoff Configuration Warning System with no faults noted. Since nothing was actually corrected; the Captain and I discussed the possibility of it activating again on our takeoff. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the Forward Cargo Bin C. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. We were relatively full on this flight and our V1/VR speeds for Flaps 1 on Runway XXR were 125/135. The engine start and taxi out were uneventful with the throttle burst yielding no takeoff warning. On the takeoff roll at approximately 130 knot (5 knot after V1) the takeoff warning horn and light activated. We elected to continue the takeoff. The initial climb was normal and we discussed that we would be writing this up in ZZZ1. The Captain called for 'flaps up' at the appropriate speed and I moved the flap lever to UP. We had a few distractions from ATC due to hold-down altitude that was cancelled. Before I moved the landing gear handle to OFF; I checked the flap indicator and noticed that the flaps were still at 1 with the LE FLAP EXT green light illuminated. After confirming that the flap handle was up; I told the Captain the issue and that we need to keep our airspeed below 250 kts. and level off to handle the problem.After notifying ATC that we would need to level off; they gave us vectors for terrain while we ran the QRH for Trailing Edge Flap Disagree. Since the QRH doesn't really address the disagreement when attempting to RETRACT the flaps and only deals with setting the flaps for landing; we turned our attention to coordinating the air return. Dispatch was advised of the return as well as Station Ops in ZZZ. Our current gross weight was a little over 130;000 pounds so we extended the gear to add drag and burn off excess fuel for landing. The F/As (Flight Attendants) and passengers were notified of the return. Since this was a flight control issue; we [received priority handling] and notified ATC that we were requesting [Runway] XYL but would need time to reduce our landing weight to 128;000 pounds. We felt this was the safe option as time was not an issue. We then ran the QRH; ran the performance calculation for the Trailing Edge Flap Disagree QRH; and then the brake cooling module. The flaps extended normally with the Alternate Flap system to 15 degrees. The only slight issue was although I read the section directing the flap lever to be moved to the final flap position (15); we were sidetracked by discussing slowing during the extension and this was not done until after the QRH was completed. This allowed us to see our Flaps 15 maneuvering speed. After the delay vectors were complete and we were below the maximum landing weight; we made an uneventful landing on [Runway] XYL. Brake cooling allowed us to take right to the gate and the ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) trucks followed. No other issues occurred. We swapped into another aircraft and continued the pairing.

The aircraft was an originator. The previous day a takeoff had been rejected because of a spurious Takeoff Config Warning and the maintenance resolution was no faults noted. The F/O (First Officer) and I discussed possible reasons for a false warning lasting a few seconds; which refreshed our memories of the warning system and thankfully prepared us for a repeat occurrence. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the forward cargo bin. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. On takeoff; approximately two seconds after the F/O's V1 call; the configuration light illuminated and the warning horn sounded. The F/O called VR; and we lifted off. The light went out and the horn stopped about the time the wheels left the ground. The F/O's performance and adhering to procedure during this event was flawless; which combined with our earlier discussion allowed the situation to be handled easily. We briefly mentioned writing the issue up again in ZZZ1. I called for Flaps Up; from their takeoff '1' setting. F/O moved the flap lever to Up; and then moments later told me the flaps didn't go up; and instructed me not to go over 250 [kts.]. We were still at about 200 knots; so no airspeed issues. I told F/O to tell ATC we needed to level off and maintain low airspeed. Initially we told ATC we would follow the SID and get back to them. ATC gave us a terrain clearance altitude. We confirmed the flaps were not up. I called for the QRH and we agreed that 'Flap Disagree' was the appropriate checklist. The checklist starts off by saying 'to prepare for landing' so we paused the checklist; agreed we were not going to ZZZ1 with flaps out; and I messaged Dispatch we were returning to ZZZ; told ATC; and received clearance to return to ZZZ. I notified the F/A (Flight Attendants) and told the passengers we were returning to ZZZ. We ran the QRH for Flaps Disagree; the procedure went mostly uneventfully. We were at 130;000 pounds; so we took delaying vectors to burn fuel to 128;000 [lbs.]. We checked the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; no issues. We did [receive priority handling]. We landed Flaps 15 and taxied to the gate. Positive takeaways. The CQT training from (year)?; (year)? that emphasized flap malfunctions prepared us well to handle the stuck flaps. Negative takeaways. The QRH for Flap Disagree was obviously written with a failure occurring during approach in mind. For our situation of failure on takeoff; the procedure kept us with the flap handle up until we had returned to ZZZ and were preparing to land; which meant we had flaps out; but no maneuvering speed. We know that Flaps 1 speed is 180 knots approximately; but it would have been one more item in our favor if we had moved the flap handle to match the flaps to give us the normal sight picture on the displays. While we were extending the flaps with the alternate switch; between watching the flap gauge and calls from ATC; we momentarily missed the instruction in the QRH to move the flap handle with the flap movement. We followed proper flap speeds as flaps were extending; but that that was because of our experience; not the display. The QRH should have the instruction to move flap handle with flaps before the actual instruction to move the flaps so that crews can discuss the handle in advance. We ran the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; and then tried to run again for Autobrake 2. The brake cooling module did not work the second time. We recalled a recent (Company communication piece) about Dispatch doing something to mess up performance calculation results; which could be rectified by requesting landing data again; but that did not work. Something in the performance calculations needs to be corrected so that brake cooling can be run more than once. Brake cooling was not an issue; even with Autobrake 3; so this was a small nuisance. Based on passenger comments; F/As did a great job. F/O's performance was excellent; our teamwork together allowed the situation to be handled easily.

Captain reported refusing the aircraft after discovering that the nose strut was leaking after service due to strut extertion not within limits.

Upon arrival the inbound crew advised us that the nose strut might possibly be low. I advised them that we would look at it on the walk around and that we would write it up if necessary after doing the walk around. Prior to boarding with the only occupants on board being the two flight attendants and myself; my FO (First Officer) went out and did the walk around; he motioned for me to come down and look at the strut which was nearly fully collapsed and not showing any chrome. Not having a ruler or protractor available we took an informal measurement. The distance between the top and bottom was two fingers or less; which was certainly less than two inches. At this point; I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control to advised them of the situation; at which point Contract Maintenance was dispatched. I made an entry into the logbook stating that the nose strut was nearly compressed and needed to be serviced. Once Contract Maintenance arrived; he originally rolled out the tanks; as if he were going to inflate the cylinders; he attempted to open a valve in the nose wheel strut area and then after some difficulty stopped. He then made a phone call to Maintenance Control. After this phone call; he said that per the AMM (aircraft maintenance manual) the measurements that he took indicated that the strut was showing 2 inches and was legal for dispatch as outlined in the AMM as is and that he was to sign it off as instructed by Maintenance Control. At this point we boarded; and just prior to closing the door; under all prudence and caution; I decided to do another inspection of the nose wheel strut to find it fully collapsed and actively leaking foamy fluid. I contacted Maintenance Control and advised them that the strut was compressed and leaking foamy fluid; which I then entered into the logbook. We deplaned and Contract Maintenance then added nitrogen to the strut and signed it off again. At this point; the on duty pilot; Name 1 called me to gather more information on the situation. I informed him of all the events that had occurred up to this point. He then asked me why I would do a preflight walk around with passengers onboard and he stated because we aren't really sure of what the strut compression should look like after passengers had boarded and additionally why would I need to do that after I had a legal sign off. I informed him that in the interest of safety that I felt it was OK to do a walk around after a maintenance procedure and; as well as to comply with the CFM (company flight manual) guidance for exterior inspection; which is to ensure that gear struts aren't fully compressed and that there are no fluid leaks. I also added that we should still be able to see some chrome on the strut and that there shouldn't be any leaking fluid. After the Contract Maintenance inflated the strut we then began to board again as we waited for the book to be signed off. As the FO and I were briefing; the Contract Maintenance asked me to step outside. After stepping outside; the Contract Maintenance guy pointed out the strut which may have been inflated to the legally required two inches and but was leaking a solid stream of foamy liquid and not just a couple bubbles as Maintenance Control contends. I then contacted my Dispatcher Name 2 and Maintenance Control. They then advised me that they would remove the aircraft from service and schedule us to take the RON aircraft that was coming around XA:15pm. I also sent pictures of the compressed strut and leak to Maintenance Control. I attempted to send the video too but was unable to do so because of the file size. The following morning; I was contacted by Chief Pilot Name 3; who asked if I was OK with how everything turned out and to get my side of the issue. He also said that I was scheduled to fly the airplane several more times the following day and would I be OK with taking the aircraft. I told Name 3; that I'm perfectly fine flying the aircraft as long as it's legal and safe; which in this case would mean the strut would be showing a normal amount of chrome and not streaming foamy liquid from the cylinder. He also shared an email outlining the events from Name 2 which directly contradict several key facts from the evening. 1. The inbound crew didn't write up the aircraft. I wrote up the aircraft three times. 2. When Maintenance came back there was foaming bubbling liquid coming from the strut which can be be seen in the pictures and videos that I took or are visible on the ground which appears wet from the leaking fluid. Name 2's email incorrectly characterized this leak as a couple small bubbles. The cause narrative for this series of events is pretty straight forward. I feel like my Dispatcher was very accommodating and I feel that the real issue here lays with how Contract Maintenance; Maintenance Control; On Duty Pilot and indirectly Name 2; Maintenance Control; Maintenance Director interact with the pilots after the fact. Contract Maintenance from the very beginning expressed his hesitation with the situation once he saw the foamy liquid coming from the cylinder. Finally; his insistence that I look at the leaking cylinder after we boarded and he once again expressed his hesitation and ultimate concern about the issue thus giving me a moment of pause. I had the opportunity to speak to Maintenance Control several times and they didn't really seem to understand why we wouldn't go because in their opinion; because they signed off on it that it was good to go; even though it was leaking. The On Duty Pilot questioned why I would do a walk around after Maintenance was performed; expressing that we didn't know what the nose strut would look like after boarding and why would I do that even though I had a legal sign off; as if I was supposed to accept the sign-off carte blanche. I expressed to him that I needed to be not only legal but safe and that I could do a walk around whenever I felt it was needed on confirm to expectations set forth in the manuals. I didn't see that email from Name 1; until Chief Pilot contacted me to inquire if I was OK with flying the aircraft on my next trip. I told him that I was was fine with flying the aircraft in the future; as long as it was in serviceable condition; which would mean showing a normal amount of chrome on the strut and not leaking fluid. The concerning part of Name 2's email is where he ends with 'This is bad when Maintenance is using appropriate AMM references for the checking of proper servicing being refused with a legal sign off; but we are taking the delays for no reason at this point.' This sentence is challenging because it assumes that I'm making a refusal for no good reason and that the sign off were legal to begin with. If it had only a couple bubbles as his email suggests then I would have certainly taken the sign off but upon receiving the sign off and seeing the stream of foamy fluid still coming from the cylinder; along with input from the Contract Maintenance and my First Officer we needed to again assert our concern with the aircraft. Fortunately Name 2 wasn't there; he doesn't know the extent of the issue and his comments are a direct challenge to the safety reporting culture that the Company has developed.

EMB-175 flight crew reported a cabin fumes event during approach descent.

Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the Flight Attendants that there was an odor in the vicinity of row X. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning or acrid smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row X; to whom it was very noticeable; which was also confirmed by FA 'B'; but only when they walked up to row X. There was no visible plume anywhere in the airplane. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.The FO was flying the airplane (PF) so they took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. The comment about a fuel smell drove the pilots to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; while we requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated; clearing other aircraft from our path. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit [Runway] XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of runway. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down (left-hand-side) engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down (right-hand-side) engine #2. Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I 'Deice' and Type IV 'Anti-Ice' fluid; with engines running; at the X Pad.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. FO also said that after landing they briefly noticed an odor.We could have [advised ATC] earlier on in the event. This would have allowed us traffic priority earlier in the descent (and speeds above 250 KIAS once below 10;000); getting us on the ground sooner and reducing the overall time of pax/FA exposure to fumes.We flew the same airplane the following day; and the airplane was cleared by Maintenance with no defects found. Nothing was wrong with the airplane itself. Fumes remaining localized in a certain area of the cabin suggests internal point source emission rather than external ingestion or airplane system malfunction. However; at time of writing; we still do not know; definitively; what caused the fumes.The FAs are commended for their prompt notification and accurate description of the nature and extent of the fumes. FO is commended for flying the aircraft while coordinating with ATC and requesting ARFF; while the CA ran checklists and coordinated with the FAs; then flying the approach almost to minimums. Working together seamlessly is key in these situations; and the CA commends the crew for a job well done.

Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I and Type IV fluid; with engines running; at the South De-Ice Pad.Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the FA's. I (the FO) assumed it was the FA's notification that they were seated. Instead; they communicated to the CA that there was an odor in the vicinity of row x. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row x; to whom it was very noticeable. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.I (the FO) was flying the airplane (PF) so I took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. Since the CA was communicating with the FA's; I trusted his lead on necessary checklists to run; as he had the first hand information on the situation in the cabin. During this time; we had entered IMC conditions; and I was flying the airplane and working the radios; receiving several heading; altitude and speed changes during this time.The comment about a fuel smell drove us to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan).
