Name FA-3 kind of took over and made some announcements or was listening to the Captain; when he was calling me. The Captain reported the fumes/odor; and a mechanic came onboard. The boarding was complete; but the Captain notified the agents of the problem. I needed some fresh air; so I went to the jet way door; opened it; and took a few breaths; but a customer service supervisor; I think; told me to close the door immediately; as in a few minutes some machine was going to be turned on; 2 gates away from ours; and the smell would have come to the jet way from the open door. I did not smell anything outside; but I closed the door immediately; as I was instructed; well before the machine 2 gates away; was turned on; so there was no way that any smell/fumes could have come in through the door. The Captain made an announcement that the passengers needed to deplane; and everybody deplaned. We deplaned as well. I immediately went to sit down; as I felt dizzy. I took a bottle of water with me; to keep me hydrated. After the flight kept being delayed further and further; it was finally delayed until the next morning; to allow the mechanics to work on the plane. The Captains were given the name of the hotel where they were going to layover; but it took over an hour for the Hotels and Limo department to work on our hotel stay. We waited and waited and finally decided to go with the Captains; hoping that Company would put us in the same hotel. When we went outside; still not knowing where we were staying; a van driver flagged us and told us we were going to stay at the hotel with the Captains. As we were driving; I received a phone call from ZZZ Flight Service; Name; confirming that we were staying at the hotel. After a good night sleep; the next morning; I felt much better; however; both of my hands were shaking; and; when I put my contacts back on; I realized that they were foggy. The driver who took us to the airport told us that the plane was fixed by the mechanics. The plane we boarded was; in fact; the same plane we had the day before. When I looked in the logbook; I read that the mechanics could not reproduce the problem; and that; therefore; nothing was done to the plane. They wrote that it could have been a smell/fumes coming from outside and reaching the plane from a door left open. As I described above; the fumes/odor started on the plane long before anybody operated any machine or equipment outside. There were no fumes/smoke/smells outside. In the morning; though; I did not smell the smell from the day prior. However; I felt the presence of the fumes; as by the time we were taking off my throat became scratchy again. Name FA-3 didn't look that good; either. As soon as she came onboard; she did not have the energy she displayed the day prior and sat down immediately in a first class seat. I asked her if she was feeling OK; and she said she felt tired. She did not feel like herself. She said she could not sleep well; as she felt heaviness on her chest. She thought that maybe she ate too much food during the flight; but that now she realized that it was not what she ate. I told her that it could definitely be an increase in blood pressure or other symptom related to the fumes. As the flight progressed; she went to the back. I continued to serve in first class; and; twice; I couldn't even speak; as my throat became really scratchy. I went to the galley to drink some water and felt better. When we arrived in ZZZ; I felt better; but; at night; I had headache; so I had to call sick for the trip I had the next day. After a good night sleep; I felt much better. I thank the Captain for reporting the problem; however; I don't think that the plane is fixed. The problem was not fumes or smell coming from outside but something wrong with the plane; probably an oil leak causing toxic fumes and odor to come in the cabin. It would be nice if they could check and try to find the leak. I do not feel safe flying on this airplane. As far as the operations went; there was a lot of confusion with our hotel accommodations and with communication from the Company to us. The next day; there was also a lot of confusion regarding the new departure time; as the flight info on our tablet; Company; and the information the Captain's had showed all different departure times. Communication between the Company and the crews really needs to improve. Scheduling should contact us directly; instead of relying on automated methods of communication.

Flight Crew reported a safety cone was ingested by a running engine after a ground crewman approached too close to the engine.

Landed Runway XX at ZZZ; taxied to gate. Didn't have 2 minute cool down; there were no marshalers at Gate XX. I was trying to find the Ops frequency and contacted Ops to see if we were still at Gate XX; at which point we saw marshalers going to Gate XY and started marshaling us in. I was watching them and didn't trigger to turn on the APU. Marshalers parked us; said chocks were set and captain pointed at the screen; and I turned the APU on (both engines still running at this point). Both engines were at idle. Around 30% spin up; felt a shunt and heard a noise from the right side of the cabin. Captain asked what that was; I thought it was the APU conking out (plane had been written up for a recirculation fan issue when we got it; and the only change we'd made was the APU turning). Captain asked if it was a baggage cart that had hit us or something; so I started looking around. Looked out and saw ground crew looking around and looking at engine 2. After the APU reached 100% and the engines were shut down; I (First Officer) opened the window and asked what happened; to which the ground crew said a cone went into the engine. Captain immediately sent message to Dispatch and was on the phone with company as I waited for the jet bridge to connect so I could do my walk around.When doing my walk around; asked the ground crew person who was handling the cone what happened; he said he 'got close to the engine; then something didn't feel right - like the cone was pulling'. He said he then 'pulled back; and that's when the cone got sucked into the engine'. It was an orange cone connected by a pipe. The cone closest to the engine had been sucked in. I did notice the ramper in question had Bose headphones around his head but not over his ears when I was talking to him. Don't know if that was a factor.On walk around; found most of the cone behind the intake; pieces in the stator vanes; and debris strewn across the ramp. Pieces found behind Left Main Landing Gear; and about as far back as about 30 feet behind the tail of the plane. No damage noted to landing gears or tires. Captain came out and also assessed the damage; and we informed the next crew of the situation as well.APU could have been turned on sooner to allow engine to be shut down quicker. Ramp crew should wait to approach engines until they're shut down.

We landed in ZZZ on Runway XX. The taxi to our planned gate; Gate XX; was short. The engines had not passed the 2-minute cool-down prior to entering the ramp. As we entered the ramp area; no rampers were at Gate XX; but they were starting to walk out to Gate XY. First Officer then tried to reach Operations via radio at least twice but didn't get a response. Simultaneously; I was being marshalled to Gate XY so we proceeded to park at Gate XY. I parked at the gate without incident and set the parking brake. I looked down and noticed the APU had not yet started and pointed it out to the First Officer. Between the cool-down period; trying to verify the gate; and watching for obstacles on the ramp; the APU had not yet been started. The engines were idle while the APU was starting. At approximately 20-30% APU; we felt an impact on the right side of the aircraft; followed by a loud noise. I asked what happened. There were no EICAS or gauge indications of a problem. The First Officer thought maybe the APU malfunctioned during the start and I asked if a baggage cart impacted the aircraft. Around this time the marshaller started looking toward Engine 2. When the APU reached 100% I shut both engines down. The First Officer opened his window and asked what happened. The ground crew indicated that ENG 2 had ingested an orange traffic cone. I immediately sent an ACARS to dispatch and called Maintenance to report the incident. The First Officer conducted his walk-around and assessed the ENG 2 damage; taking pictures which he sent to Maintenance via e-mail. Upon his return; the First Officer provided the following explanation from the employee who placed the cone:The ramper allegedly explained that as he went to place the cones in front of ENG 2; two orange pyramid-shaped traffic cones connected by a white plastic pipe; he felt the engine start to ingest the cone furthest from him. He stepped back but the cone didn't stay connected to the pipe. The First Officer noted that the ramper responsible for cone placement was wearing a Bose headset. This is extremely uncommon. So uncommon that I've never seen a ramp worker with a Bose headset or similar headset capable of playing music. I do not know if anything was interfering with the ramp worker's ability to properly hear the aircraft engines. After the APU was off and the airplane was connected to the GPU; I conducted a visual inspection of ENG 2 and called maintenance with an update of the ground crew's explanation of how the cone was ingested. I made a video recording of the fan blades. During this time; the ramp worker was telling the First Officer that he wasn't sure whether or not he should have told us to shut-down the engine when the cone was ingested. Ground crew should be trained to recognize when an engine is on and when to notify the crew to immediately shut the engine down. The ramp worker could have been killed due to his lack of training in recognizing an operating engine. Engines can be running at the gate for any number of valid reasons and ground crew should be trained when to recognize an operating engine. Ground crew should be properly trained in hand signals for an abnormality. Pilots could wait to taxi into the gate until the 2-minute cool down passes and the APU is operational to further prevent these kind of incidents.

Pilot reported landing gear failed to indicate extended and during alternate extension procedures; communications problems and failure to follow check lists resulted in the landing gear collapsing on landing roll out.

I am the owner of a Mooney M20E and have >300 hours in this plane. The flight in the late afternoon was a demonstration flight for a friend of mine who is considering beginning pilot training. He has done informal training many times over several years including with me; and has excellent instincts and innate skills that indicate he will be an excellent pilot. In addition; he has significant knowledge about airplanes; airplane systems and general aeronautical/ aviation information. Weather conditions were VFR and not challenging in any way. There were some mild clouds and precipitation in the area but we had no difficulty avoiding them throughout the flight.I flew left seat and handled all engine controls and critical phases of flight; takeoffs; landings; radio calls; etc. He had controls for much of the enroute time and legs of traffic patterns. We did standard maneuvers; mostly practice traffic patterns and landings at ZZZ1; which is close to ZZZ and is the most commonly used training field for many pilots out of ZZZ; including myself. We did three touch and goes and one full stop/ taxi back at ZZZ1. There was no indication of a gear problem for any of these several extensions or retractions. I have very recently done solo training flights with similar or greater numbers of gear extensions and retractions in a similar span of time with no indication of problem. After close to an hour of flying; we returned toward ZZZ for our final stop. We entered a long right base for Runway XXR; and at the appropriate time put the gear switch down. For the first time ever in this plane that I know of; there was a gear extension problem. The gear motor activated and could be felt extending the gear. It seemed mostly normal; but perhaps a little louder/ more forceful than usual. It stopped abruptly; it seemed to have taken a usual amount of time; but the gear on this plane do normally extend quickly and I could not be certain the motor had run as long as usual. The two gear down lights (one on the panel and one on the floor) did not illuminate. The gear actuator circuit breaker had popped out. I tried resetting the circuit breaker twice; but it did not stay in. The gear switch had no effect at this point; as expected with the circuit breaker tripped. The feel of the plane in flight felt as though the gear were down with the expected amount of drag.I advised ZZZ tower that we were breaking off the approach for troubleshooting of a gear problem; and headed generally north of the field in coordination with the controller. I pulled out the Owner's Manual; and my passenger assisted in reviewing the manual gear extension procedure; with which I am very familiar. I have practiced this on the ground a few times over the years at the time of annual inspection with the plane on jacks. I have also practiced it in the air at least once in this plane.With my passenger reviewing the steps out loud for me; I extended the gear manually. The hand crank did not reach a stopping point and the gear down lights did not illuminate. I checked the visual floor indicator; which is there as a backup in case of electrical failure; and the 'GEAR DOWN' sign was visible as normal when the gear extend; with the alignment bars lined up normally as per my memory of how they typically line up. Many additional cranks on the manual extension handle on several more tries had no further effect on anything that I could tell. We were concerned we might have a broader electrical problem of some type leading to failure of the indicator lights; even though the gear appeared to be fully extended. I checked another indicator light on the panel in the same cluster as the 'Gear Down' light (the 'Ram Air' light); which was working properly. I could find no other signs of electrical failure on board. There was no smell or sign of smoke.At this point; I contacted ZZZ tower and coordinated a low pass down Runway XXR to get a visual check of the gear. The tower controller was ableto see the gear well and reported all three appeared to be fully extended. The plane was performing well and maintaining control was not an issue. I was able to aviate; navigate and communicate easily and without difficulty; and to go through the appropriate manual gear extension procedure with plenty of time and focus. My passenger remained very calm; focused and helpful throughout. Neither of us became anxious or nervous; and we were able to communicate well and work together well. He was an asset to me functioning as part of the crew; even without formal pilot training. The ZZZ controller(s) likewise were extremely responsive; helpful and professional.I did not seem to have any additional options to try to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate. I was fairly confident that the gear were fully extended. We were in no immediate danger; and there seemed to be no other emergency reason to land prematurely; although the possibility of some larger electrical system problem remained in my mind. As such; I decided that spending extra time in the air for additional attempts at troubleshooting was no longer wise and that we should land safely while conditions were good.The landing on Runway XXR was smooth; well controlled and uneventful. The wind was nearly straight down the runway and was light. I most often land with no flaps; and chose to do so in this case as well. I made sure to land with excellent technique; touching down gently just above stall speed; well aligned with the center line and with minimal control inputs. I made sure not to use the brakes; and I elected not to use the elevator for aerodynamic braking; as I wanted to avoid any unnecessary forces on the gear. I allowed the plane to roll out long on the runway; and all appeared to be going well. I let the tower know that I intended to roll out long due to the unknown status of the gear. Runway XXR is 7;500 feet long; I touched down not far past the numbers; and rolled out nearly to taxiway 1 for a total rollout distance of about 3;500-4;000 feet.After we had dissipated most of our forward speed without incident or sign of additional problem; I began a very gentle right turn toward the 'high speed' exit for taxiway 1. At that point; the plane began to settle toward the ground toward the left; with the front and right settling down very quickly after. The prop struck the runway and the engine quit; the plane skidded about 30 feet and came to a stop at a mild angle off center line. The impact with the runway was surprisingly soft from our standpoint. I quickly shut off the master switch; magneto switches; and fuel selector; and we exited the plane quickly and easily. There was no fuel spillage; smoke or fire. Neither of us sustained any injury of any kind.Using a heavy boom truck; we were able to gently lift the plane off the runway via the engine mount. I was able to easily manually extend the gear fully; and again was unable to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate despite the gear being verified fully down; and the manual floor indicator properly aligned. While being towed away; the plane again settled to the ground toward the left when initiating a fairly gentle slow turn to the right. This time; only the left gear folded.At the time; shortly after; and for the next day or two I believed that I had properly pushed the crank forward to engage the manual gear extension mechanism and allow the handle to work properly. This is one of the basic few steps needed in the manual gear extension procedure; and I had done it many times. It is a small handle and lever located at approximately the left side of the left pilot's knee; and is easily reachable with your left hand. After reflecting on the events and going back to visit the plane; in fact I had not properly pushed that lever all the way forward. It appears that the manual gear extension mechanism will apply enough lowering force even when not properly engaged to allow the gear to fully or nearly fullyextend; but without the crank properly engaged it appears that you cannot get enough force to fully lock the gear in place.At the time of the [event]; although I and my passenger were under good control and responding well to the situation; I was approaching or beyond 14 hours since I had woken up and gone to work early that morning. I believe that pushing the end of my duty day; as well as familiarity with the procedure and not double checking myself that I had followed every step properly were contributing factors in my failure to fully lock the gear. I believe I could have prevented the gear collapse had I followed the checklist and double checked every step.We have not yet jacked the plane and examined all of the relevant components. Whether or not there is some other structural damage to the gear extension mechanism or any of the components involved; and whether or not we are able to ultimately demonstrate that the gear down lights were or were not in fact working; it does not change the fact that I did not properly complete one of the necessary steps on the checklist for manual gear extension. I also failed to catch this omission with a thorough review of the procedure and circumstances after the gear lights failed to come on. I allowed myself to give too much weight to the possibility of an indicator failure and did not continue to troubleshoot more when I have the ability to do so. I also believed that my familiarity with the procedure was sufficient that I did not consider that I might have omitted or failed to properly complete a step.As I reflect on this; it gives me a sense of humility and a reminder of my own fallibility; and reinforces that I need to double check checklists and critical steps at all times. My belief that my left hand had done what it was supposed to with respect to the one missing step was simply inaccurate. I could have and should have caught the error with a careful review of the circumstances; and there was not an emergency pressing need to get the plane on the ground immediately. I will carry this lesson for the rest of my life. Fortunately; no one was injured; and the mechanical and financial damage to the plane are the only costs. But it is still a humbling fact that I did a basic part of managing my aircraft incorrectly and caused damage as a result. In another circumstance; I or someone else could have been hurt with such an error. I will redouble my efforts to be meticulous for procedures; checklists; and review of critical items at all times. In addition; I will be more careful with respect to aircraft operations beyond 12 or 13 hours since waking up in the morning on any particular occasion.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
PA-44 instructor pilot reported a cross threaded oil dip stick caused a loss of oil inflight; leading to an inflight shut down and air turn back.

During the preflight of the aircraft; my student performed the inspection. He called me in when he was having trouble removing the oil dipstick of the right engine to inspect oil level since it was secured very tight and was hot to the touch. I came out there with a napkin to use as an insulator for our fingers and managed to loosen the dipstick by using both my hands. I checked the oil level and handed the dipstick to the student for him to do the same. He placed the dipstick back in and secured it; and I doubled checked that the stick was secure by loosening and retightening it. I then proceeded to run my own quick check of the aircraft by verifying the oil in the left engine and checking the fuel quantity onboard. We found no issues with the aircraft and proceeded with the flight.About an hour into the flight; we were in the south practice area performing Vmc demo with the student at the controls. During the maneuver; I had noticed an oil slick starting to form off the right engine. For the maneuver; we were operating the right engine at full power while the left was idle. To make sure we are all on the same page; I pointed out the slick and had him start turning back to ZZZ. I instructed him to scissor the throttles; go full power on the left engine and idle the right engine. I immediately called up our dispatch and informed them of our engine trouble while they coordinated preparations at the school; airport; and rescue services as part of the company procedures. About three minutes after we idled the right engine; the oil temperature was rising to the limit. Since we were holding 3;000 feet at the time with an idling engine with good performance; and I did not want to risk having a seized engine I elected to shut the engine down and feather it. We informed dispatch; and then followed the appropriate checklist. And elected to continue to ZZZ since they still needed time to prepare the field for our arrival with emergency services; familiarity; and long runways available. On the way back; I shifted my attention to the student and briefed what happened; and what we are going to do from now. During this time; I had him at the controls flying while I ran the checklists with him. I briefed that I would have him fly to ZZZ but once we start maneuvering; I will take the controls for descent and landing. As we were nearing the field; dispatch called us requesting we circle the field if performance allows for a few minutes while they still waited for rescue to arrive. Once we were about 3 miles south at 3;000 [feet]; dispatch called again telling we do not need to circle anymore; and that the airport will not call rescue. I really did not want to stay in the air longer than we needed to; and changing the plan now would have increased risks; I opted to continue to land. I took the controls at this point; and since we needed to lose altitude; I decided to fly a normal pattern and flew down to make a normal 45 entry for runway 20. Runway 20 was the longest runway with most favorable wind conditions. The landing was successful. The airport was closed for our recovery; and we planned to shut down on the runway and get a tow; but I was nervous about another aircraft behind me on short final; so I used the remaining speed of the aircraft to turn off onto the taxiway at about 10 knots.During the post flight inspection; we could not see anything out of place other than the oil streaks. We checked the dipstick and saw that it had slightly loosen but appear to be seated. But when maintenance performed their inspection; they determined the oil dipstick was cross threaded. They determined this was the most likely source of the oil leak. Only about a quart of oil was lost in flight.I think obviously the biggest factor here was the dipstick not secured properly. I was not aware how easily the dipstick could be cross threaded. The biggest learning moment for me was paying closer attention to how the dipstick is seated. In the specific aircraft; the dipstick sits directly on the engine block; and you can only easily see the dipstick from a top view unlike other aircraft I operate such as the other [aircraft type] where the dipstick is sits on a pipe that protrudes from the engine where the dipsticks cap is visible from the side. I think what also did not help was the fact we used a napkin to hold the dipstick during the preflight; which also visibly covered it. I think from here on out I am going to make sure some gloves are accessible and emphasize to my students the potential risk of cross threading.However; I am concerned about the airports handling of this situation. It was revealed when we landed; the airport management seemed to have not deemed our situation important enough to call in fire rescue as a precaution. They also have seemed to do a poor job of closing the airport as aircraft were still taking off and landing even when they announced multiple times over the radio the airport is closed. When I landed; a aircraft was flying not too far behind us in the pattern; and I had to move the aircraft on a single engine off the runway out of concern they would land on top of us which added the risk to us. But in the end of the day; the aircraft made it back in one piece; and most importantly my student and I made back safe.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Flight Crew reported the First Officer's sliding window opened on takeoff roll; causing an air turn back and a precautionary landing.

As Captain; I was the Pilot Monitoring and the First Officer was the Pilot Flying for this flight. On the take off roll at approximately 90 to 100kts; I hear the First Officer make the comment 'There seems to be a lot of airflow through this window'. I glanced over and to see from my point of view that the window appears to be closed. I shift my eyes back to the runway centerline; airspeed and engine instruments while thinking about what he said. At approximately 110kts; it becomes loud with high airflow into the flight deck. The First Officer shouts 'My window is open'. I quickly glance over to his side to see he has his left hand on the control wheel and is holding the R 2 flight deck window closed by the window lock lever with his right hand. I immediately took the controls. At this time we are approximately 120kts just prior to V1 (129). I took a quick glance at my First Officer and back to my instruments; I saw that we were Vr + 8 to 9kts. I then rotated. I saw a positive rate of climb and shout 'gear up'. The First Officer assumed pilot monitoring and raised the landing gear. I shouted 'Can you crank the window closed at all?' He responded 'No; it won't close'. At this point; Tower had advised us to contact Departure. I selected the Center Autopilot; VNAV & Heading Select with a heading of 360 as assigned. I opened the speed window and remained at Flaps 5 to prevent the airplane from accelerating. I figured the faster we would go; the louder the flight deck would be and the more the First Officer would struggle to hold the window in position. The First Officer shouts 'I can't hear anything from ATC.' Around 3;400 ft. I contacted Departure and informed them that we need to stop climb and return to the airport because we have a flight deck window opened. We were given a left heading of 270 and to maintain 4;000. We performed the after takeoff checklist. My First Officer states 'I can't hear anything from ATC but what do you need from me?' I responded 'ATC is giving us vectors back to ILS RWY XX. If you can; get flight deck performance for Runway XX and set us up for the ILS RWY XX; I'll do a quick brief; then we will do our Descent and Approach checklist.' With one hand still on the window crank; the First Officer did just that and along with his flow. ATC gave us another vector and asked if we need more time. I told ATC that we were not ready and asked to continue heading at 270 and 4;000. Once we were set up; briefings and checklist were complete; I advised ATC we were ready for the approach. Since I was flying while doing the radios myself and the First Officer with only one free hand available; I decided it would not be prudent to be heads down and message Dispatch through ACARS. I felt the priority was to fly the plane and get us safely on the ground. I informed ATC 'We [request priority]; 2 souls on board and approximately 4 and half hours fuel on board'. ATC asked the nature of the [situation] and I replied 'We have a flight window cracked'. I meant to say cracked open; however; the noise from the airflow was a little distracting. ATC gives us an intercept heading of 100 and clears us for the approach. We were stable; fully configured; and all checklists were complete prior to the final approach fix. At 800 feet AGL we broke out of the clouds. I had the airport in sight and disengaged the autopilot. A normal landing was made at approximately 265;000 lb. We informed Tower that we did not need assistance and taxied to parking. Upon taxi in; I do not know if the First Officer closed the window or left it in its previous condition from flight; opened. Perhaps he left it alone so that Maintenance could inspect. I wrote up that the First Officer R2 flight deck window opened on takeoff/climb and I waited for them to inspect. There was no damage or defects noted.I honestly do not know if it was a Flight Deck Window malfunction or if it was ever truly locked. Both of us had opened our Flight Deck Windows on the ground during preflight because the APU was off and the temperature was in the 70's. About 30 minutes prior to block out; I started the APU and we closed our windows. In the Before Start portion of the checklist; I verified my flight window was closed and locked with strut at a 90 degree position. I heard the First Officer respond 'Closed and locked'. I could see his Window Lock Lever was in the forward and locked position; however; I could not verify if his decal showed 'CLOSED' nor if the strut was at a 90 angle simply because of the angle from where I was sitting in the Captain's seatI think that in the moment; the First Officer did a great job of prioritizing aircraft control in such a critical phase of flight. To be in the high speed regime of takeoff; so close to V1 and to keep 'aviating' while a huge startling distraction occurred was commendable. He also; kept his head in the game and jumped to the pilot monitoring duties without delay. He prompted me for the after takeoff checklist as we were about to level off at 4;000. If I could have done one thing over; I would have shouted 'My controls' in a louder voice. I didn't take into consideration that the First Officer could not hear well at that point.I'm also appreciative of our Company training video made by Boeing of a flight with the flight deck window opened. I'm glad that I was shown to me during my 767 upgrade training. I never thought I would be in that situation but thankfully I had some idea of what to expect. The plane will be extremely loud and distracting but it will safely fly.

During takeoff my window opened immediately after the CA (Captain) called '80 knots; thrust set.' I was PF and saw the window rolling aft. I grabbed the window handle with my right hand while continuing to fly. I maintained runway centerline and described what happened by shouting cross cockpit to allow the CA to have the information and make an appropriate reject decision. About 10 knots before V1 the CA took the aircraft. I couldn't hear him verbally call V1 due to the cockpit noise and open window. Perhaps I didn't hear him call V1 because he had already taken the aircraft. Regardless it was loud and my audio panel wasn't set up to compensate for the noise.When the aircraft rotated I immediately assumed the role of Pilot Monitoring. He shouted to raise the landing gear and I did. The CA flew and took the radios because I had shouted cross cockpit that I couldn't hear ATC well enough to communicate. Both of us had to compensate because of the noise. The CA selected heading select and turned left to our assigned heading of 360 and elected to select VNAV and Center Autopilot Command almost simultaneously.The CA requested to stop climb around 5;100 MSL and informed me that we would return to ZZZ. Around this time I had determined that as long as I held the window with a good amount of strength it wouldn't roll open. I adjusted my interphone and ATC freq to Max volume so that I could hear. I then asked the CA if he was ready to run the After Takeoff Checklist and we did. Everything from that point forward was standard and in order except that the CA had to turn the Standby Attitude Indicator to ILS mode because I had one hand holding the window; the CA [advised ATC]; and did the radios. After we landed all roles were normal and the taxi in was standard.This situation is dynamic. I think perhaps a better verbal transfer of aircraft control on takeoff roll but we effectively handled the situation. I thought the CA was going to reject the takeoff. By the time he processed what was going on he decided it was safer to continue the takeoff. It was loud and we coordinated the best we could in this situation.

A320 Captain reported that a component was inadvertently switched off after the other pilot left the cockpit for a lavatory break and a multitude of warnings and ECAM messages went off as a result.

Inadvertent switching off of IR1 mode selector which deactivated that associated ADIRU. ADR and IR data not available. This occurred during flight one of day two of an initial Captain upgrade. The trainee came off the B777. He has been with our company for many years. The three legs of day one was extraordinarily busy. It was immediately clear to me during those three legs he had studied hard during training and had mastered much of the material. On the first two legs of day one I had a LCA (Line Check Airman) in-training watching me conduct the line check as part of that LCA's upgrade training. I commented to the new LCA not all trainees will be so well prepared as this one.This flight was leg four of the IOE and the first flight of day two. Our transportation to the airport was 15 minutes late and there was a detour so we arrived at the aircraft about 30 minutes prior to departure. Normally; I introduce myself to all the FAs (Flight Attendant). However; because we were on IOE; [we] were somewhat late to the aircraft and on Release 6. I only introduced myself to the FM. I felt I did not have time go to the back to introduce myself to the FAs assigned to the rear of the aircraft.We had been in the seat for approximately 3 hours. The upgrade Captain requested I ask the FM to prepare the meals and that we would then take a restroom break when the meals were ready. I did so. The FM called us about 25 minutes later to state the meals were ready. The upgrade Captain offered me the opportunity to use the Lav first. I declined and said he should go first and I would then go. The door chime rang and then I heard a knock. That knock is not standard. However; it occurs occasionally with legacy Company 2 flight attendants. We put on our masks. I saw the upgrade Captain move to get out of his seat; stand up; and let the FA in while he then left the cockpit. I noticed nothing odd about his movement out of the seat and to the rear of the cockpit. I saw out of the corner of my eye the FA was standing near the rear of the cockpit just behind and to the right of the Captain's seat; a normal position for a relief FA.My concentration then focused on something else. I think it was because we were getting ready to enter a large area of convective activity. I might have been looking at WSI and comparing that to what I was seeing on the weather radar. Why my gaze was generally focused forward and right I am not sure; but it was. I planned to brief the relief FA about this weather and its possible effect on their service in a few minutes. It was at that point; maybe 30-45 seconds after the upgrade Captain had left the cockpit; that for lack of a better description; 'all hell broke loose.' The cockpit went from a completely benign environment to one of confusion. The startle effect was in full force. The first warning was a continuous repetitive chime and the warning lights flashing. I immediately looked at the E/WD (Engine/Warning Display) and noted about 4-5 ECAMs listed; primary secondary and independent failures in both red and amber. I silenced the CRC (Continuous Repetitive Chime) by pushing [the] master warning light. That silenced the CRC. However; there still was an aural alert going off that I could not silence; which created a fair bit of consternation on my part. I look at my PFD and saw the FMAs were wrong. I then saw the AP (Autopilot) was off and that there was nothing where I expected to see the AT (Autothrottle) condition. I noted the aircraft climbing slightly and corrected that. I knew the AP disengaged for some reason but didn't know why. I thought about engaging AP 2 but then thought that may create new problems; so I elected to hand-fly until the ECAMs were sorted out. I saw we were no longer in NAV but again; wasn't sure why. I did see that the aircraft didn't diverge much from the 'green line' so lateral stick inputs weren't necessary. At this point ATC called to ask us something about recycling the transponder. We wereon speaker at that time; I responded we had a problem and to standby.I then noted the airspeed increasing and pulled the TLs (Thrust Lever) back; I didn't want to add an over-speed to our problems. This silenced another aural sound. I do not recall seeing a Thrust Locked ECAM or FMA which I thought would have been the source of the alert I couldn't silence. I glanced at the Captain PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display) and saw they didn't look right.The aircraft was reasonably stabilized now but; in my mind; because the ECAMs were displayed; the situation wasn't. I then told the FA to recall the trainee Captain to the cockpit. He opened the door; looked and then closed it; and said he was in the bathroom. I told the FA I knew that and I wanted him back in the cockpit now. He then had the FM knock on the Lav door. The trainee Captain returned to the cockpit and the relief FA left. The trainee Captain was incredulous when he looked at the E/WD. I told him I was hand-flying; had the aircraft and radios; and that he was to handle the ECAMs. It was at this point I noted we were about 20 knot slow; well within flying speed but slow for planned speed. I had overcompensated for my worry of overspending the aircraft. I pushed the power back up. Airspeed had fallen out of my cross-check. The trainee Captain methodically and correctly went through the ECAMs. As I recall the first several ECAMs had no action items; one ECAM had us switch the air data switch to three. At some point during this; ATC stated they now had data on us and asked if we needed assistance. We told him we were completing a procedure and to standby. Once the status messages were read and the ECAM procedure completed; I reached up to engage AP two. It did so. I armed the AT and then moved the TLs to the climb detent to engage it. Our ATC clearance was to proceed direct to a fix so we reinserted that. I don't recall having to pull or push to capture our assigned altitude but I can't be sure.It was now maybe 4-5 minutes after the initial event where I could take a breath. I recalled the ECAM and saw the ADR 1 fault. I then looked over to the ADIRS panel and saw IR mode selector one was in the OFF position. It; of course; was on for the flight up until some point in [the] last few minutes. I asked the trainee Captain if he recalls hitting the switch with his head or back as he left his seat. He said no. I then thought perhaps the switch was defective. This aircraft came to us as a through flight. We did not have to turn them on so we had no knowledge of how that switch felt by turning it on. We again discussed it and he stated he didn't recall even touching the overhead panel while leaving the seat.Because I didn't introduce myself to the FAs at the rear of the aircraft prior to the flight; I wasn't sure which FA came to the cockpit during our break. I asked the FM to ask the FA who came to the cockpit to call us on the interphone. That FA did and I asked him if he recalled touching anything on the overhead panel; he stated he did not. What I found unusual was that during the event; the FA seemed very nonplussed by the cacophony of sounds in the cockpit. I would have expected a FA to at least ask what was going on; but maybe he was somewhat shocked by what he saw and heard during his short time in the cockpit.The trainee Captain and I discussed that I would write up the ECAM and then conference Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control to provide further details of what we thought may have occurred. I wanted the switch looked at but also didn't want Maintenance to search for a problem which might not exist. I ACARS'd Dispatch with the request and he set up the conference call. The communications with Technical Support Maintenance Control were reasonably good and he captured exactly what I wanted him to know and he appended it to our write-up. Since the Captain's displays were significantly degraded; we switched PF/PM roles. Fromthat point we continually deviated for weather; were put in holding; and changed our alternate three times. We over-burned by almost 5500 lb on this flight; more than on any flight I have been on in [an] Airbus. It was an understatement to say this was a busy flight. I don't know how this happened. The final flight of the day was a termination. As the trainee ran that checklist and turned off the IRUs; he stated he couldn't believe how he accidentally managed to switch that style of switch - pull and turn - off by getting out of the cockpit.I am disappointed in myself for not more thoroughly reviewing the flight manual for ADR 1 fault after things had settled down. We did not have a GPWS TERR FAULT light and no ECAM direction to switch it off so it remained on. We discussed that threat in that we were now the aircraft's GPWS system and to be cognizant of the terrain. We also discussed changing the transponder to position 2 but did not do so because there was no ECAM direction to [do] so and ATC noted no anomalies in our reporting. Also; once I saw the IR mode selector switch in the off position; I should have considered reviewing the NAV IR fault non-normal even though we didn't have that ECAM. I did not do a word search in the flight manual for ADR. Had I done so; I would have seen that there may be RVSM limitations associated with its failure and should have gone to the FOM for further information. I recall many years ago; our Line Manager at the time; wrote up in his weekly update a similar event. As I recall he wrote the trainee somehow managed to hook the window shade into that same switch and turned it off. That of course didn't happen here.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Air carrier flight crew reported experiencing a Stabilizer Out of Trim problem during climb out. They completed the appropriate QRH checklist and performed an air turn back.

I; the CA (Captain); was PM (Pilot Monitoring); the FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). During the climb-out phase in level flight in mildly hazy VMC at 17;000 MSL at 290 KIAS with Autopilot B engaged the Master Caution; the 'FLT CONT' item on the CA-side SAP ('6-pack'); and the right half only of the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light illuminated. Press-to-test of the 'Stab out of trim' light showed both bulbs operable. After establishing that FO was actively remaining the PF; I performed 'Stabilizer Out of Trim' QRH procedure with the result that the autopilot electric trim and both pilot yokes trim switches were inoperative in both directions. I notified ATC that we had a mechanical problem that would eventually result in [requesting priority] and landing at a nearby airport; probably ZZZ; but for now we were content to remain at 17;000 slowly outbound from ZZZ while we worked the problem. Knowing we were also over landing weight; nicely under control; and still had a lot of checklists to run; I had no desire to rush into diving towards some final approach fix before we were ready to land. I performed the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH procedure with the result that manual hand-cranked trimming was possible in either direction; albeit against unusually high resistance and with a 'cogging' feel as if pushing against a powered but stalled electric motor. This was true even when the aircraft was in-trim. One pilot could move the trim using one arm; but two pilots using one arm each worked much better for anything more than a couple turns of the trim wheel. We found that one pilot could both hand-fly and crank the trim; but tended to make unwanted aileron inputs while doing so. So it was doable in a pinch but not smooth. The forces required to turn the trim wheel did not appreciably reduce as we later slowed & configured. In the course of reading & discussing or doing the 'deferred items' section of the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH I started to activate the GPWS Flap inhibit switch. The FO stopped me saying we were above the 250 KIAS speed limit at that time. That sounded familiar to me; but no such limitation is stated at that point in the QRH. Nevertheless; we chose to delay activating the GPWS flap inhibit until we had slowed to first configuration speed around 220KIAS. Discussed with [the] FO whether ZZZ was the best divert option and which runway to use. ZZZ & longer Runway XXL was the unanimous choice. By that time we were a few miles south of [the] VOR on a south-southwesterly course for ZZZZZ; roughly 100nm from ZZZ.I then performed the 'Non-routine Landing' QRH procedure; alerting ATC for a return to ZZZ XXL with ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) standing by. Coordinated with ATC for return via direct arrival for ILS XXL. Asked Company explicitly to alert ZZZ Approach & Tower of the intended non-standard XXL landing. Notified Dispatch via ACARS report. Briefed FAs via intercom; and passengers via PA on the situation; my expectations; and their roles. We selected the non-standard landing Runway XXL based on that runway being much longer than the more typical landing Runway XXR. That was a minor miscue; because I/we had not considered the effect of the large displaced threshold. Which I now consider insignificant. For landings eastbound the difference is 2500 feet and would be significant. Lesson learned: the big runway length number on the 10-9 page can be significantly misleading; take the time to dig into the 10-9A details page. The fact that was our takeoff runway and within Jepp FDPro I'd used the green highlighter to extend the highlighting all the way to the takeoff threshold didn't help. What had been useful to help direct my taxi to the correct threshold for takeoff became mildly misleading when evaluating which runway to land on. Which was not a side effect I noticed at the time or had considered previously. Still working as PM I performed normal divert preparations and top-of-descentprocedures: Reconfigured FMS & ACARS for ZZZ arrival; obtained ATIS; set up radios and performed approach brief; landing assessment; etc. Notified ZZZ Ops of our return by direct radio call to obtain a gate assignment.We discussed that we'd be a little above the normal max landing weight; but the already requested priority covers for that administrative requirement; and the runway available was nearly double what the QRH procedure's performance chart said was required. Performed descent checklist and before landing checklists and flows as normal. Throughout the evolution the FO kept us neatly in control; tight on the FD despite sometimes having to hand-crank the trim himself; caught a few radio calls I missed; and demonstrated overall high situational awareness and excellent systems knowledge. This is especially impressive for someone fairly new to the airplane who is just back from 6 months of furlough. During descent below 10;000 ft approaching downwind we changed control to CA as PF w FO as PM. We sighted the field while on base. During the turn-on to final I was using visual lookout primary; backed up by the LNAV purple line and the ILS. There was a moment of confusion as the ILS and LNAV came together before I was aligned with what I had thought was the landing runway. Having landed on XXR dozens (hundreds?) of times over the decades; that habit was unhelpful for a few seconds before we got fully established pointing at the correct runway. We then realized that Runway XXR is concrete and very easy to see in mildly hazy conditions while Runway XXL is asphalt and much harder to see. In fact XXL was invisible until we got closer in following the LNAV & LOC. My general habit on any landing involving parallel runways is to verbalize seeing all the relevant runways by name and explicitly saying which one I'm aligning / aligned with. E.g. 'I see XXL and XXR. I'm aligning with XXL.' For whatever reason that verbalization didn't occur; with sorta predictable results.Intercepted final outside intermediate fix in level flight at 3;000 ft. Configured to flaps 15 early and slowed gradually to Vapp of approximately 160KIAS before glideslope intercept at final approach fix. FO kept the airplane nicely in trim on my requests.Made a flaps 15 slightly overweight (approx. 148K#) approach and landing to a smooth touchdown on ZZZ Runway XXL just shy of the 2000ft marker. Upon stopping made a PA to reassure the passengers & remind them the safety vehicles would be seen around the airplane. ATC gave us an alternate frequency to contact ARFF on. Which surprised both of us a bit. Once we were communicating with ARFF I requested they inspect us for hot brakes or damaged tires. ARFF found normal brake temps and no tire damage. At ARFF's request I released them at that point and we taxied normally to [the] gate.Following shutdown the FO attempted to manually crank the trim to the usual post-shutdown 5 units from the 8-9 units we'd used at touchdown. At zero airspeed the trim was still 'cogging' and almost as difficult to move as it had been in flight. So we left the trim at the landing setting for Maintenance's edification. Which point we discussed with the Chief Pilot who met the flight and again later with the maintenance folks who also met the flight. I made appropriate aircraft maintenance log book entries for the stab trim failure and for the overweight landing. Spoke with Dispatch by phone before leaving aircraft per FOM. The next morning I filed the required report. In all I think this event worked out pretty close to textbook; minus the small glitches identified above.The main electric trim failing was the causal factor. Everything else is just details.1. Subsequent research on the ground shows that activating the GPWS Flap Inhibit switch is called for in 11 different QRH procedures; and in the Flaps 15 landing procedure. Only the 'One Engine Inoperative' QRH procedure and the 'Flaps 15 Landing' procedures mention that limit; the other 10 QRH procedures do not.I do not know whether those differences are deliberate or an oversight. Suggest someone on the 737 fleet team look into this. If the difference is deliberate there probably ought to some verbiage available in QRH or [procedures] to explain the rationale so others don't mistakenly apply a remembered restriction where it's not intended. 2. We were both surprised to see that only half of the 'Stab out of trim' annunciator illuminated. Which left us wondering at first if we had a warning system malfunction or a trim malfunction. I surmise now that the right bulb is connected to FCC (Flight Control Computer) B and the left is connected to FCC A. And that had the Captain been PF; we'd have seen the left half illuminate instead.However it works; the details of left & right are not documented in [manual] where the annunciator is described. At a minimum there should be a statement like 'Only half of the annunciator may illuminate. That is still a valid indication of an out-of-trim condition.'3. Overall; from the 'Stab out of trim' annunciator illuminating to touchdown was about 30 minutes. From reviewing the ACARS logs I know it was at least 28 minutes and less than 35. As the CA / PM / QRH operator I was working quickly and diligently almost the entire time to accomplish all the non-routine and normal procedures in full without hurrying. Had we turned back even a couple minutes earlier the airplane would have been approaching the airport before we were fully caught up and mentally transitioned from handling an [urgent inflight situation] to performing a normal low-stress; albeit flaps 15; landing.Given the reality that following all the procedures fully takes nearly 30 minutes; I believe we do a disservice to pilots in the sim; rushing around the traffic pattern with an engine out. That encourages hurrying; doing QRH steps without really thinking them and their implications through; etc. We fight how we train; and we're training to hurry. I question the wisdom of that.Further I question the wisdom of planned arrival fuels that only allow for approximately 30 minutes to flameout at traffic pattern altitudes. The so-called FAR '45 minute reserve' is 45 minutes at cruise; not 45 minutes at traffic pattern altitude with e.g. flaps stuck partly extended. I now conclude that performing a major QRH evolution discovered in the arrival traffic pattern while down near Company planned arrival fuels would necessitate skipping a lot of steps or giving them at best a lick and a promise.I believe it is unwise to plan arrival fuels that tightly. Yes; we commonly have additional hold and / or Dispatch fuels. But each of those may legitimately be burned in delays encountered before the [urgent situation] appears. This saves Company a lot of money on the many flights that don't turn out worst-case. But it really sucks to be the pilot who draws that short straw; and is faced with either doing a rushed job of handling the [situation] or running out of fuel.That's planning; in extremis; to fail. An industry-leading FAR 121 carrier should not be planning to fail. In extremis or otherwise.

At a level off of 17;000 ft we noticed stab out of trim light. I was the PF so it was my aircraft. The Captain ran the stab out of trim QRH checklist which lead to the QRH stab trim inoperative checklist. We did not regain electric trim. Manual trim was what we were left with. Then the non-routine QRH checklist was performed. The manual trim wheel was difficult to work for both us even when the plane was near an in trim condition. Speed was slowed to about 270kts from about 290kts then. [ATC was advised] and we planned and set up for an arrival back to ZZZ. I flew the aircraft and worked the manual trim while the CA performed checklists; set up for the arrival and approach; and the briefings. Manual trim did not become much easier until on approach when aircraft was slowed to approach speed; however even then it was difficult. The CA took the aircraft and I became the PM. The landing was nice and smooth. Once on the ground using the manual trim wheel to reset the stab trim to 5 units was still very difficult.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
B757 flight crew reported an APU fire warning after takeoff and returned to the departure airport.

APU fire return to field. Boarding and pre-flight normal. Once the packs were turned on the cabin cooled down easily; but we were not able to get the flight deck under 80 degrees until after engine start. Taxi was also normal; from [the gate] onto Taxiway 1; Taxiway 2; and to RWY XXL. To fly the departure up to and maintain 3;000 ft. Takeoff normal (full thrust takeoff per Maintenance request on maintenance release). On the climb out approaching 3;000 ft; in LNAV; we hit ALT CAP (Altitude Capture); and PNF (myself) rolled the speed to 230 knots. Right at this moment the APU FIRE EICAS message displayed; and the Fire bell alert sounded. Captain took both flight controls and radios; put the auto pilot on and addressed ATC. [Advised ATC] and requested an immediate return to the field for landing. I ran the APU QRC paper checklist. Which reads; Pull the APU Fire handle and rotate to the stop for 1 second. I completed the QRC items; and then turned to the electronic checklist to complete the full APU FIRE checklist. Which stated 'Choose one: APU Fire warning light stays illuminated (which it did); land at nearest suitable airport'. Captain then handed flight controls and radios to me; so that he could consult with the Flight Attendants and the Company. After doing so he took back over the role of PF (Pilot Flying). Captain then made a turn with ATC instruction back toward field for a downwind to RWY XXL. Still level at 3;000 ft. ATC requested where the fire indication was. We set up for an ILS approach; with appropriate frequency and FMS arrival selection for XXL. We were then given a descent to 2;000 ft. by ATC as well as a turn to base leg. Captain began to slow to configure for landing. Using speedbrakes to slow the aircraft. On this turn in the descent with Flaps 1; while retracting speedbrakes; and the MCP (Mode Control Panel) speed in the window set to minimum flaps 1 speed; we had a momentary shaker activation; less than 1 second; and I immediately put out Flaps 5 and we continued to slow and configure from there. We were cleared to maintain 2;000 ft. until established; and cleared for the ILS approach. We continued to add flaps to 15; then 20. Gear down; flaps 25 and 30 without event. Landing data was requested for landing on XXL; overweight 235k lbs; Auto brakes 2 was set for sufficient stopping distance. Also performed a small dip low on GS for touchdown to use full runway length. We touched down with 200 fpm descent. Rolled to Taxiway 3. Exited runway at 60 kts. Continued onto Taxiway 2 to hold short of Taxiway 4. At this time the [it was] assessed that no heat was found in the tail or any other part of the aircraft. The flight attendants also assessed no smoke or heat in the cabin. The decision was then made to taxi to a gate expeditiously to deplane passengers and get maintenance on board. Taxied to the gate; shut down the left engine to allow the jet bridge to be attached to the airplane; then shut down the right engine once ground power was established.

APU Fire Indication after takeoff. Flight was the first segment on day one from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was the flying pilot for this leg. Loading and boarding were normal with a mostly full flight. The cabin of the aircraft had been cooled nicely; but we were having a bit of a challenge cooling down the flight deck; with temperatures hovering in the high 80's. The ZZZ weather was 340/10; 10SM FEW 040 SCT080 BKN250 28/18 29.86. We pushed off the gate on time. [We taxied] to Runway XXL and contacted Tower. We accomplished the before takeoff checklist items and were cleared to takeoff Runway XXL on the ZZZ Departure. The maintenance release noted that a Max power takeoff was due; so we did so; at a TOG weight of 238;192 lbs and the flaps 5. During takeoff roll as we accelerated; water dripped out of the overhead panels which was interesting; we took off; cleaned up the gear and flaps as scheduled. Somewhere between 2;000 ft and 3;000 ft. in the climb in a left hand turn to heading 290; we had a Master Warning and an EICAS annunciation APU Fire. I continued to fly the aircraft; took the radios; and while the First Officer accomplished the APU Fire QRC. It is important to note that the fire light remained on and did not go out after running the QRC with no other indications of a fire. Also; it is important to note that the APU was shut down on the ground after engine start during the after-start checklist; and had been off for approximately 20 minutes. We ran the appropriate checklists; notified Dispatch and spoke with the flight attendants. The Purser was informed that we had an APU Fire indication and was asked if there were any fire indications in the aft cabin? They said they did not have smoke but noted a slight odor (possibly the fire extinguishing agent that was fired into the APU during the QRC). I told them to prepare the cabin quickly as we would be on the ground in 8 minutes. My FO (First Officer) and I spoke about the overweight landing; briefed the approach; and identified the ILS. We planned a flaps 30 ILS to Runway XXL at a weight of 235;000 lbs. as 235;000 lbs. was below our performance limit weight of 259.9; so a 30-flap landing was appropriate. Fortunately; we discussed the possibility of an overweight landing prior to takeoff; so we were already familiar with the requirements. Although we suspected an erroneous APU Fire warning; time was still a driving factor as the fire indication never went away. We maintained 250 kts for as long as possible then configured using flaps and speed brakes to slow the aircraft. We were configured with flaps 1 and were decelerating with the flaps tracking to 5 and the speed brakes out. We decelerated to flaps 5 maneuvering speed; and just as I started to retract the speed brakes for literally a split-second I heard a sound that was so brief I could not tell what it was. The FO told me that it was a split second of the shaker due to the boards being out at the flaps 5 maneuvering speed. We continued configuring with gear and flaps 30; accomplished the landing checklist. We flew the ILS to Runway XXL with the autopilot and auto throttles engaged until 500 ft when I disconnected the autopilot. I disengaged the auto throttles around 100 ft. I briefed that I would slightly duck under the glideslope with a planned touched down early in the landing zone.We touched down approximately 1;200 ft. down the runway with auto brakes 2 selected. The touchdown was extremely smooth with a VVI (Vertical Velocity Indicator) of less than 200 fpm. During the landing roll; we queried the Tower to see if they could see any smoke trailing the aircraft; and they said all looked normal. We rolled clear of the runway on Taxiway 3 and stopped on Taxiway 4 where the ground personnel looked us over. The ground personnel informed us that they could see no indications of a fire and that their thermal imaging scan showed no heat in the APU area. We ran through our after-landing flows and taxied to the gate. We shut downthe left engine so they could start deplaning the passengers. When ground power became available we secured the right engine and secured the aircraft. I proceeded into the cabin to chat with maintenance; passengers etc. Maintenance opened the APU area and said that they suspected a faulty fire loop; as there was no evidence of a fire. Maintenance later found that a faulty APU fire control panel was the cause of the warning. Also; the total flight time from wheels up to wheels down was 11 minutes. That is extremely fast when considering all the factors to evaluate. All in all; I feel that this was a well-executed event; and resulted in the safe return for passengers and crew.

result_labels: Flight Crew Returned To Departure Airport
text:
Flight Crew reported loss of equipment cooling on the ground did not change after takeoff; resulting in systems losses and an air turn back and precautionary landing.

When we arrived at the airplane the flight deck was around 34 degrees; but it soon cooled to around 28. Everything else was normal until the Captain stepped out to use the restroom. As soon as he sat down the ground crew pulled the ground power; but we had not yet switched over to the APU; so everything shut down. The Captain switched to the APU; but the right FMC did not start back up; and we got a R FMC FAIL status message. After about five minutes it did come back on without incident. We pushed back and started normally; but after about two seconds after I selected the status page on the lower EICAS we got a PACK 1 status message. The Captain reviewed the procedures; but because we had already blocked out and did not get any EICAS messages we continued. After starting up with the packs all off the flight deck warmed up quickly; but we knew as soon as we took off it should start cooling. At around 1;000 ft. the Tower gave us the Departure frequency and I checked in successfully. By the time we reached 5;000 ft. we were concerned by how little airflow there was; and the observer pilot asked for the ECS page to verify that the airplane was pressurizing. It seemed to be normal; and we monitored the air; but still figured as we climbed the flow would increase. Around FL180 Departure called us on guard and said; 'Aircraft X; if you can hear this transmission contact...' The Captain and I agreed that she hadn't called prior to that and I dialed in the frequency. I couldn't reach them; so I asked for another frequency. I didn't realize how much the heat was affecting me; but on the third frequency I asked the Captain to attempt to call. When he transmitted; I could hear that his call wasn't going out; and I finally recognized that we had lost the left comms. I didn't want to change the right radio from guard; because that seemed to be the only way they could reach us; so I used the center radio and was able to reach ZZZZ Control. Shortly after that we got an EQUIP COOLING EICAS message; and the third seat pilot began to run the checklist; and I asked for a level off altitude of FL300. ATC came back with FL290; but we were at FL288 and empty; so I said we would do our best. We ended up climbing to FL295 before we could get level; and promptly descended back to FL290. At this point we began to discuss returning when we noticed that the secondary attitude indicator was leaning to the right; but our wings were level; so we all agreed we should return. We told ATC we needed to return and explained that we were having equipment cooling issues. They assigned us the arrival and Runway XXR; but the workload was continuing to accelerate; and we were all sweating profusely; and told them we would like to get vectors to the ILS for XXR. I gave them the fuel remaining; souls on board; and tried to explain that we were safe; but needed to return soon. We completed all checklists; and uneventfully landed; taxied; and parked the airplane. I didn't realize until we were on the ground how much the heat in the flight deck was affecting me. Even with the lack of traffic in the vicinity; I am surprised how long it took me to recognize the radio failure. In the future I will be more cognizant of the heat and it's affects not only in seeming to increase workload; but also decreasing focus and clarity.

I had gone to the lavatory on the ground prior to departure. Before I returned to my seat; the external power was pulled without my permission; and the power to the aircraft was interrupted; as I sat back down; I selected the APU power source and after waiting a bit; the R FMC would not come back. We called Maintenance up and the FMC returned to normal. We ensured all of the data that we had input was correct and then continued onward to push. The aircraft was extremely hot; and we know that they had just established air as we were arriving at the aircraft. The interior cabin was at 36 Celsius and we agreed that the aircraft should cool after takeoff. After starting we noticed a Pack 1 status message; but there was never an associated EICAS message. We followed our checklists and proceeded with taxi. After takeoff; the airflow never increased and the FO (First Officer) selected the EICAS page as we all were wondering if we were even pressurizing. The gaspers were blowing at about 5%; but cool air was coming out. It was still extremely hot in the aircraft; and the 3rd observer seat first officer said that he had hardly to no air coming out of his gasper. At around FL250; we began receiving radio calls on 121.5 and it was at this time with trying to transmit out; and different frequencies that we realized the radios were not working; except for the center. The Pilot Monitoring was able to get the right radio to work intermittent; and immediately we got the Equip cooling EICAS caution message. I continued to fly the aircraft while the crew ran the QRH and attempted to maintain contact with ZZZZ. At this point; we all agreed the best course of action was to return to ZZZZ. We were given a level off to FL290 after an initial climb clearance. We were given this rapidly; as were already in a climb; but I arrested the climb and descended back from FL295 to FL290. We were given vectors and further descent. At this point with descent power; there was almost no airflow. We [received priority] to get on the ground as safely and quickly as possible. My standby instruments were also showing erroneous. We landed in ZZZZ without further incident. After touchdown; the airflow suddenly increased to normal. Maintenance was briefed with the logbook; but I was not given the nature of the aircraft's issues before we headed back in to rest.

EMB-145 Captain reported refusing an aircraft twice when maintenance declined to address the discrepancy and maintenance control pressured him to reposition the aircraft to where the parts were available.

I was assigned Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 to reposition a plane that needed a mechanical issue fixed. Upon receiving the aircraft; I noticed the flight deck was unusually warm. The cockpit indication showed 32-33 degrees. The side window vents blew coolish-lukewarm air; and the gasper was blowing HOT air. The side vents air flow was weak and the gasper had strong air flow. I proceeded to write up the aircraft and have Maintenance look at it. After Maintenance did an inspection; they signed the aircraft ok for service with the cockpit indicator still reflecting 33 degrees and feeling unreasonably warm/hot. Surprised that it was signed 'OK for service;' I asked one of the technicians if he agreed with me the cockpit felt hot; he replied 'Yes; I would say it is warm.' I then asked if he agreed the gasper was blowing hot air; and although the side vents were slightly cool to lukewarm with weak airflow; it was not enough to cool the cockpit. He looked away without maintaining eye contact and replied '...well…we have to get this plane to ZZZ1. We don't have the parts here.' I then asked a second time why is the aircraft signed off as 'OK for service.' I received about the same reply. Eventually I was told 'it's your prerogative but it feels fine compared to outside. We are saying it's ok for service.' Shortly after; he left so I then called Maintenance Control and told them the temperature control knobs left in auto were not sufficient to cool the plane at any position; and that if you moved the knobs to manual; it was blowing out warm air immediately followed by hot air within 5 minutes. Maintenance Control replied that he didn't understand as the technician said it was 'OK for service; and only 25 degrees in the cockpit.' My statement to him was 'Absolutely not. It is right now indicating 32 degrees and nothing is fixed. Did you want me to send you a picture of the temperature?' I did not receive a reply as we talked about what the issue could be. I stated to Maintenance Control; 'I have seen this before multiple times and I think either a duct connection is loose; or there is a tear or leak somewhere; did you want me to send a picture of the cockpit temperature to show you what is indicating?' I still received no reply that he wanted evidence so I then asked him for the number I can send it to. When provided and after I sent a picture; he replied 'CABIN temperature looks pretty normal for a summer day' but mentioned absolutely nothing about the cockpit. He thought the plane was 'heat soaked' but I reminded him it had already been running for an hour and a half. I was then instructed and proceeded to run ground air inside the cabin and directly point it at the cockpit. It dropped 8 degrees from 33 to 25 in 20 minutes. I then had the ground air disconnected and within 20 minutes the cockpit heated back up to 31 degrees; and 5-10 minutes later it was again at 32. After writing it up a second time and being told from Maintenance Control it's still probably just 'heat soaked'; the same technician from before came back and I told him what we did. He replied while mumbling something about 'maybe we got some parts lined up and we'll take a look.' The First Officer and I went back inside to cool off and let Maintenance work on it. After 5-6 hours of Maintenance continuously working on the plane; I called Maintenance Control to get an update. Apparently; the technicians did in fact discover a leak(s); and were proceeding to put a sleeve(s) on. An hour later it was still not done (about 6-7 hours of continuous work since the second write up). I then was removed from Aircraft X by scheduling.Cockpit indication and hot feeling in the cockpit.Hot airplane that would not cool down without external air and feeling pressured to take a hot airplane to ZZZ1 for service.Refused the aircraft twice.The main concern is current maintenance practice. I was able to get the technician to agree that it was warm inside the cockpit even though he signed offthe aircraft as 'OK for service' because they could not find anything wrong. I will give the benefit of the doubt that maybe the technician relayed bad information to Maintenance Control and read the temperature of the cabin instead of the cockpit; however; he still told them it felt fine when clearly the temperature control knobs were not functioning properly. There was a second technician that stated the same about it being OK for service. Since the first write up; Maintenance Control had me troubleshoot it for up to 4 hours with/without the technicians. After going through 2 large bottles of water; sweating profusely; and being asked to run the ground air into the back of the aircraft instead of the front this time as it was probably still 'just heat soaked;' I said no and needed a break. Also; I mentioned that based on experience it was probably a leak or tear. Sure enough; after having the technicians look at the aircraft a second time; this is what they found and worked on for several hours. The fact I refused the aircraft twice and they 'found an issue' the second time leads me to believe they knew all along. Especially considering the fact the technician admitted to me that the cockpit would not sufficiently cool but yet signed it off and told maintenance control it was fine. A chief pilot called me to get more information and while I did not feel pressure from him directly to take it; it was clear that the company for one reason or another needed to get this plane to ZZZ1. Again; I did not feel pressure from the chief pilot directly; but I could not help but think everyone in Maintenance knew this plane could not get stuck in ZZZ. I also believe that troubleshooting for Maintenance up to 4 hours is excessive when it was clear the aircraft was not heat soaked but instead was not self-sufficient to cool on its own. I am not a maintenance technician nor one with the most experience; however; I felt undermined from the technicians signing it off and Maintenance Control having me go through the motions of 4 hours of troubleshooting and not one person taking my advice that I had seen this exact issue multiple times. More believably I was ignored and every trick was pulled just to get the aircraft to ZZZ1; i.e.; being told constantly by Maintenance Control we can get the aircraft cool enough with PC air so that we can depart but then reminding them the packs are not working properly and keep heating the plane up. Regardless; the technicians constantly tried to tie the issue to me implying that I was the problem and ultimately it was my call. If this was the case; I do not see why they would have had to work on the aircraft for several hours following my second write up.

A321 flight crew reported ECAM messages appearing and experiencing flight degradation due to Maintenance performing improper procedures around an MEL and inactivating the wrong spoiler pair.

The aircraft in question was operating with MEL 27-XXX open; Spoilers #2 or #4. After engine start on both legs; an ECAM message was received regarding the spoilers but this was disregarded as a result of the MEL. Upon further reflection; these messages should have triggered further investigation on my part; as the presence of such an alert was not mentioned in the MEL. However; I had noted a write-up in the MEL about spurious messages - made by a Check Airman - which was subsequently signed off by Maintenance as essentially being unimportant. The aircraft had flown 4 legs the day prior with the MEL active. Also; at the time of this incident; I had approximately 100 hours of experience in any Airbus aircraft.The first leg of the day was flown uneventfully. Immediately after takeoff on our second leg of the day with the same plane; an ECAM caution and audio alert was triggered for a F/CTL SPLR FAULT. The message subsequently cleared itself; but then a few seconds later; would trigger again. This cycle repeated itself approximately every 20-30 seconds for about 20 minutes; until the flight reached FL270; where the message stopped cycling and instead remained. Initially; after exiting the sterile period; ACARS messages were sent and a brief exchange ensued. An emergency return to ZZZ was offered as an option; but given that we were well above maximum landing weight and the ECAM did not require us to land as soon as possible; I elected to continue the climb.Upon reaching cruise altitude; I transferred the flying duties to the FO (First Officer) and verbally contacted Dispatch and eventually Maintenance Control. Maintenance had no inflight suggestions and stated that they would look at it when the plane is on the ground. At this point; the Dispatcher and I discussed our options. Since the ECAM mentioned FUEL CONSUMPTION INCREASED and FMS PRED UNRELIABLE and we still had just under 3 hours to go on a flight planned to land with just 8;000 LBS of fuel; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ1. Dispatch changed our destination and we proceeded to an uneventful landing in ZZZ1. An emergency was not declared.
