While on the ground in ZZZ1; one of the responding mechanics reported to me that he discovered that the MEL procedures were not properly complied with when the item was deferred and that Spoiler Pair #2 was inadvertently deactivated instead of Pair #4. Apparently; the aircraft had flown 4 legs in this condition prior to our operating it. He mentioned to me his concern that on the [day prior]; a previous crew; the previously mentioned Check Airman had also apparently experienced a similar condition; wrote it in the logbook; only to have Maintenance simply clear the entry by writing 'info noted.' He expected that the aircraft would be taken out of service to fix the underlying issue. However; the decision was made to clear the write-up that I made and allow the deferral to continue. Based on the information that was relayed to me by this Mechanic; it appears that the initial error of deactivating the wrong spoiler pair was attempting to be covered up. This is very concerning.My relative inexperience with Airbus aircraft allowed me to be lulled into a false sense of security when it came to ECAM messages that appeared to relate to the MEL item. Seeing a write-up about spurious messages being handled the way it had been also led me to believe that there was nothing out of the ordinary; when realistically; there was a major error made by a certificated Mechanic. In retrospect; what was displayed on the F/CTL page should have alerted me to a problem; with both Spoiler Pairs #2 and #4; but I assumed that this was the same display that the mechanics and all of the other pilots who operated the aircraft before me also saw. The MEL does not give us specific guidance as to what should be displayed on this page with the MEL active; but I presume that the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) procedure referenced should tell the Mechanic whatshould have been displayed.More information in the MEL document detailing what exactly should be displayed on the SD (System Display) and what messages the crew should or shouldn't expect for a given MEL. Also; if there was indeed an attempt to cover up a maintenance error; I think this case should be used as an example as to how to properly correct an error.

After takeoff we got an ECAM for flight spoiler fault that was reoccurring. We had this aircraft on the previous leg and got the ECAM and cleared it but this one kept returning. We still thought it was associated with the MEL on the Aircraft Spoiler Surface 4 INOP but Spoiler Surface 2 was also INOP. The Captain had reviewed the logbook before the previous flight and seen another crew had this happen and Maintenance had signed off [that] it was normal for the MEL. The Captain got in touch [with] Maintenance through Dispatch and they wanted us to divert to ZZZ1. We diverted and landed uneventfully.I think Maintenance improperly deferred the Spoiler Surface 4 and after a crew wrote it up; did not verify it was correct. The MEL should have had us view the Flight Control page instead of the HYD SD page for amber information of #4 Spoiler ONLY amber or #2 Spoiler ONLY.

ATR 42 First Officer reported that ATC advised flight crew after takeoff that the aircraft may potentially be missing a tire as a main tire and wheel assembly had been found on the runway; resulting in a immediate precautionary landing at the destination airport.

This report concerns the unscheduled separation of the #4 - outboard right main wheel - from the aircraft on takeoff from Runway XX in ZZZ. We began the trip receiving the aircraft from the previous crew at the gate in ZZZ1 one leg prior. There were no abnormalities on the pre-flight; no abnormalities that had not been cleared; and no major abnormalities of any kind recorded in the logbook or in the previous logbook that was in the can for the aircraft. The previous crew verbally told us that it was performing well when we received it from them. The first leg; ZZZ1 to ZZZ; operated smoothly with nothing out of the ordinary occurring. The post flight after that leg revealed no discrepancies of any kind. We pushed back from ZZZ; and our taxi route towards Runway XX included left- and right-hand turns as well as brake applications; and the aircraft continued to operate normally with no signs of any abnormality on the wheels.When we performed the takeoff; shortly after we selected the landing gear up; Tower called us and told us it looked like we lost a tire on the runway. The takeoff was so smooth that we weren't sure if we had in fact lost a tire as we had no indication in the cockpit of any system abnormalities; and the aircraft felt like it was operating normally. We knew there was construction around the runway in about the position we would have lifted off the ground at; so I thought that perhaps it was misidentified construction debris - although we hadn't seen any debris on the runway prior to takeoff. We asked them to perform a runway inspection to determine if it was our tire while we contacted Dispatch to obtain some identifying information about it; as well as to make a plan of action in case it was our tire. We contacted ZZZ Operations after some attempts; and asked them to remain at the airport to assist in identifying the tire and in case we needed to return to ZZZ.We decided not to relay to Dispatch through Operations because we initially had trouble reaching them and we believed that their Operations radio was a handheld and would not have good signal at altitude and location we would need to hold at. We decided to continue climb so that we could contact Dispatch through AIRINC. We discussed the possibility of flying by ZZZ Tower to have them identify if we were missing the tire and which one it was; but at that time we were still not sure that it was our tire and we were unsure if we would have enough fuel to do that and still proceed to ZZZ1 if that was what Dispatch wanted us to do. We made the judgement call that Dispatch would most likely have us continue to ZZZ1 due to the long runways; good emergency services; and having the finest Operations and Maintenance staff there to assist. We continued to climb along our filed route while ATC attempted to identify the tire. Shortly after that; we advised the Flight Attendant (FA) of the potential situation and that we were most likely continuing to ZZZ1; and we would wait to advise the passengers until we were sure and close to ZZZ1 to avoid panic. She said that she would take the time to review some information in her manuals. We chose to continue at a speed of long-range cruise or slower - 180 IAS being the safe speed used when structural damage is suspected - because we were unsure if there was debris on the wheel assembly that could become dislodged and damage something else; or if losing the tire had already damaged something.It took about 30 minutes to 45 minutes for us to make contact with Dispatch after that. We attempted AIRINC; Station Operations on 4 or 5 different local frequencies; relaying through company aircraft; or through another frequency. We attempted using different transmitters in case there was debris from the tire that had damaged an antenna. We were unsuccessful; so ATC attempted to call Dispatch. This took time because ATC was attempting to call using an old company number with an old area code. It was further delayed because we werebeing handed off to new controllers periodically and we had to apprise them each of the situation and have them attempt to make contact. ATC did make contact and Dispatch instructed us to continue towards ZZZ1. After that; we were advised that it was in fact our tire. We requested priority handling and continued to ZZZ1. After this determination; it took roughly 15 - 30 minutes longer for us to contact Dispatch on AIRINC.We had time with a low workload in cruise because we couldn't contact Dispatch through AIRINC yet; so we used the time to review our manuals and the QRH for the related procedures. In the QRH we decided that the Landing with Abnormal Landing Gear Procedure was the most applicable. We began to brief and discuss this procedure while trying to make contact with Dispatch through AIRINC. When we did make contact with Dispatch; [they] advised us that they thought it was the #1 wheel - the left main outboard. We told him that the procedure called to induce a fuel imbalance and to burn off as much fuel as possible before landing. We asked his opinion of going into holding on the way in to ZZZ1 to do so; and he agreed.After this determination was made; we said we would call back again and terminated the call because our radio transmitters made it very difficult to talk to ATC and Dispatch at the same time - there appeared to be interference or override between VHF 1 and 2. We began cross-feeding fuel to make the left side as light as possible and briefed the FA assuming that the #1 wheel was the one we had lost. We told the FA that there was a good chance that it would be a normal precautionary landing and that we would most likely come to a stop on the runway; or exit the runway if able; but most likely would not taxi to the gate. We decided to request for fire trucks; busses; a tug; and a GPU to be standing by. After we were done briefing the FA; we continued to discuss the procedure for approach and landing. The first step of the checklist was to notify the passengers; so we used some time to create an agreed-upon script to brief the passengers without inducing panic - which I would later administer when we were holding near ZZZ1. We noticed that this procedure appeared to be designed to cover both structural landing gear issues as well as tire and wheel problems. We were not sure if we had structural problems or not resulting from the loss of the wheel; so we briefed the procedure including several decision times - such as what we would do if the gear extended normally vs. if the gear did not extend normally vs. if we lost the hydraulic system when the gear was extended; etc. The result which did occur which we briefed was that the gear extended normally and the remaining tire; brakes; and steering operated normally for the landing.The decisions which we briefed involved in this were as follows. We left the GPWS switch in the on position because that switch's function is to silence alerts when the gear is not sensed down and locked. No fuel imbalance was established; and with our and Dispatch's agreement due to the relatively light weight of the aircraft; small practical difference the imbalance would make; and for ease of procedure application in the interest of safety. We did not pull the emergency gear extension lever due to the gear extending normally and indicating locked down by both indicating systems. Our understanding is that the emergency gear extension handle simply opens the uplock boxes; which had already been opened successfully; and that pulling the emergency gear extension handle could potentially impede us during egress if an evacuation was needed. We discussed at what time the bleeds should be selected off for approach. I had never selected the bleeds off in this aircraft in flight before; so the Captain and I had different opinions about when it should be done. We ended up selecting them off at 500 ft.; which I now agree with in hindsight. The remaining items of the checklist would be completed after we were already on the ground. We briefed that we would complete these steps if there was some kind of fire; severe damage; or loss of control evident at touchdown; but we would otherwise move slowly and discuss these steps due to the potential hazards of aircraft control involved with performing them.While we were discussing this; Dispatch called on AIRINC again and corrected that we had actually lost the #4 - outboard right main wheel - rather than the #1 as said earlier. I asked him if he was sure and made sure that Maintenance had checked the serial numbers on the wheel to be positive. After Dispatch told us this we re-briefed the Flight Attendant for the #4 wheel.After we were all thoroughly briefed; we began our delay vectors around ZZZ1 to burn down to roughly 2000 lb. as instructed by Dispatch; I gave the PA to the passengers. When we had burned enough fuel; we began the ILS to Runway XYR - the longest and most familiar runway for us in ZZZ1. The gear extended normally and we saw no abnormal flight characteristics or any system abnormalities. On touchdown; as briefed; I began using the tiller to steer the aircraft early; and we felt it pulling slightly toward the right. However; not nearly enough to warrant the emergency engine shutdown. We were able to control the aircraft throughout the rollout to maintain centerline. We chose not to try to turn off the runway as it would be a left turn-off; which would put the most weight on the right side; and we were unsure of the quality of braking that we had. We used reverse only until we were at a slow walking speed and only then used brake application to bring the aircraft to a stop on the runway centerline abeam the XX taxiway exit where the firetrucks and Operations were waiting.Tower gave us the discrete frequency to use. The firetrucks came onto the runway and asked us to shut down the #2 engine so they could inspect. We complied and they said the remaining tire seemed to be in good condition and asked us if we wanted to exit. We said no; we would like to deplane the passengers and then be tugged. While Operations was setting up to deplane the passengers; we briefed how we would manage shutting down the #1 engine in order to deplane; and requested the GPU to be connected so we could deplane with lights on without killing the batteries. When the GPU was ready; we connected; Operations pinned all 3 gears; we shut down #1; checked the after-landing and -parking checklists; called the Flight Attendant; and then began deplaning to the busses. While the passengers were deplaning; Operations connected the tug. When the passengers were clear we prepared to sit in the cockpit while Operations tugged us to Gate XX. We monitored the tug process; arrived at the gate; and began conducting the postflight inspection and filling out the logbook. I completed the logbook while the Captain called the Chief Pilot to begin debriefing.I suggest that Station Operations be provided with better radio systems; or that the ACARS system be utilized in our aircraft. It was difficult for us to establish a reliable communication with Dispatch due to a combination of poor-quality radios and not many base stations being occupied due to the time of day. A communication with Dispatch was very necessary in order for Maintenance to verify which tire was missing so that we could adjust our procedures.

A321 flight crew reported after taking the runway for takeoff and setting power; they received an ECAM message ENG 2 FAIL and rejected the takeoff; securing the engine and discharging the engine fire bottle. They required a tow back to the gate due to loss of nose wheel steering.

TOGA APU bleed on config 2. Cleared for takeoff; at about power stable and 1.5 EPR Engine 2 FAIL message (no fire indication) and single chime. Notified ATC of reject and needed to clear runway. Started ECAM procedures; at the same time another airline notified us over air that we had a fire on our number 2 engine. We then proceeded to extinguish fire with push button and squib. After finishing up procedure and coordination with CFR to make sure no fire was present we set up to be towed back to gate with no further incident.Apparently; Airbus is having issues with this config for takeoff. TOGA APU bleed on.Coordination with Airbus on reliable and safe max effort takeoff configurations.

Day 3 of a 3-day; early departure; last leg home. Gate XXX; short taxi to runway XXR. Allowed the engines to warm up for three minutes while on the ramp to get the five minutes required before takeoff. Winds were reported 280 degrees to approx 300 degrees. From previous experiences from flying the Airbus in and out of ZZZ; the winds can switch to a tailwind component very quickly when they use runway XXL/R for departure; so I expected a potential tailwind.We were cleared to line up and wait on runway XXR. The aircraft was lined up with the center line and the parking break was set. Control was then given to the FO as we awaited takeoff clearance. Once it was received and we read it back; we immediately experienced a single chime; which normally would indicate that perhaps the airplane was not configured for takeoff. Upon looking at the ECAM; we had an ENG 2 FAIL ECAM alert. Normally when we encounter ENG FAILs in the simulator; we are presented with a master warning and three chimes. This was a singular chime. I immediately told the FO we needed to clear the runway as there was a 90 degree taxiway (1) on the right side of the runway just 50 yards or so from us. FO advised tower we needed to clear for a warning.At this point I initially thought this might be a false warning. There was definitely a surprise factor to all of this. As we were clearing the runway (right turn) at taxiway 1; I glanced at the EGT and it was red. At the same time; another airplane that was getting ready to take the active runway said he saw fire coming out of out right engine. I stopped the aircraft on taxiway 1. I had the FO call for the CFR vehicles. The FO wanted to run the ECAM procedure; but I had him check the Quick Reference Card first as I remembered there was either a quick action or ECAM exception procedure that needed to be run prior to executing the ECAM procedure. The FO started to look that up... I called back to the cabin and asked the flight attendants to check to see if there was any smoke in the cabin or any sign of fire coming from the engine. The answer was that there was no evidence of fire or smoke; from the #3 or #4 FA. When I returned to the FO; he said the QRC procedure he found was for an ENG FIRE on the ground. After considering a possible evacuation; my focus shifted to getting the engine shut down. Since we had no indication of a fire from the cockpit (other than high EGT) nor any evidence from the cabin; we ran the ECAM ENG FAIL procedure and elected to discharge a fire bottle into the #2 engine. I made a PA to the passengers telling them we exited the runway due to an alert we received in the cockpit and to expect some emergency vehicles come around the aircraft. The fire trucks were not present at this point; so we asked the other airplane if they could see any evidence of fire. They couldn't see from their vantage point; so I taxied the aircraft South on taxiway 2 to taxiway 3 (50 yards?) to see if they could see any evidence of continued fire. They still could not see; so I stopped the aircraft at taxiway 3 and waited for CFR to show up. No fire indications in the cockpit; such as aural fire warning or ENG FIRE ECAM; other than the excessive EGT with the ENG FAIL ECAM.Once CFR arrived; communications were hampered as they were not on a dedicated frequency yet. I queried the tower and they gave us the right frequency to be on; when they arrived. CFR scanned the aircraft and did not find any hot spots. At this point; we had finished the ECAM procedure and were looking for any follow-up procedures (which is the next step in Airbus; non-normal methodology). The FO couldn't find them. They used to be in the QRH and were on [specific] paper... easy to find. Since a previous; major QRH revision; they are no longer on [specific] pages but are found within the QRH itself. I told the FO not to worry about finding them... that much of the material was not going to be applicable. I redirected our focus back to the STATUS page so we could discuss the current situation of the airplane. The big thing was that we had no nose wheel steering; so we summoned ops to get us a tug and advised CFR to follow us under tow. It took an inordinate amount of time to get a tug out to us (maybe 30 minutes or more); but seemed like hours. Made several PA's explaining that we were still waiting on our tug.Eventually towed back to the gate. Maintenance met the aircraft and asked about EGTs; duration; and the fire bottle status. I told them I remembered seeing an EGT of 669 at some point... maybe for 30 to 60 seconds. AML entry was made indicating all of this.When all of this was occurring during a short amount of time; I originally thought that maybe this was a false alert (only a single chime). After exiting the runway and realizing the extent of the emergency; I thought that perhaps we had the presence of flames due to a compressor stall; exacerbated by a wind that may have shifted to a tailwind.After returning to the gate; I was in contact with the Fleet Captain... who asked if the APU was ON for takeoff. I replied that it was. In Airbus world; you can do a Max power takeoff and run the packs from the APU; freeing-up the engines; giving you a little more power for takeoff. That was the case this morning. The Fleet Captain indicated that the ENG FAIL ECAM was caused by having the APU bleed ON. Apparently; this causes back pressure on the engine bleed and is a known issue. Tech Ops is increasing ground idle to prevent thisAfter speaking to the Fleet Captain; he mentioned that the QRC procedure (requiring completion before doing the ECAM alert) entitled ENG FIRE on GROUND is a procedure used when there is no electrical power to the aircraft. It is a procedure that is to be used in that situation. Perhaps I misunderstood him as our conversation occurred after the adrenaline started settling down a bit; but maybe it needs to be explained to the flight crews (the correct use of that particular QRC procedure).Also; the FO had difficulty in finding the ECAM follow-up procedures; to the point where I said we need to move to the final step of assessing the STATUS (page) of the airplane.Finally; communication from the tower on how to communicate with CFR/ARFF when they arrived could; be improved upon. In retrospect though; we never said the word 'emergency' to them. My instructions to the FO were to get the trucks rolling now... not very clear perhaps and maybe was a factor in the initial comm problems with CFR.Advised the Duty Chief that we were done flying for the day. The adrenal rush was subsiding and he was very helpful in accomplishing that for us.

EMB-175 flight crew reported two gate returns and an aircraft swap caused by a landing gear no dispatch EICAS message. The flight crew reported concerns over communications issues with Maintenance and Dispatch.

Taxiing out we got the EICAS message LG NO DISPATCH. We returned to the gate because the GRG (Ground Reset Guide) requires the procedure to be ran at the gate with engines; APU and hydraulics off and we also needed ground power as well. Captain wrote up the discrepancy as well as the corrective action. Dispatch was informed and they passed that info to mx at the captain's request including the AFML (Air Frame Maintenance Log) page number. The GRG was successful at resetting and we left the gate. When cleared for T/O on the second attempt we received the EICAS message LG NO DISPATCH again while lining up on rwy XX. We returned to another gate because we could only reset using the GRG once. The captain wrote it up again and called our dispatcher and what sounded to me MX as well. We deplaned; I did a walk around and we swapped airplanes and departed with no further issues.I should've double and triple checked with my captain that MX was called. Don't assume anything. Write it down. Make a list what needs to be done and triple check it. Call Chief Pilot if need be; to double the crew that nothing was undone.

We received EICAS message 'LG NO DISPATCH'. Followed procedure with QRH guiding us to GRG.The GRG states that it must be accomplished at the gate with GPU on; and the APU & engines off. Proceeded to gate and followed GRG successfully. Kept dispatch informed and for new numbers due to different FOB (Fuel On Board); and asked to forward message to MX control; including all information and logbook page; via ACARS.On second taxi out all was good at first; but upon reaching rwy XX we received the same EICAS message. Being allowed to do the GRG once only; we had to go back to the gate. After keeping again everyone informed (ATC; FAs; passengers; and dispatch); and after securing the airplane at the gate; I proceeded to write it up. The gate agent asked for more information and I informed him that I will coordinate with dispatch. After being informed of a plane swap and the deplaning in progress; dispatch tells me that he will call me back after talking to his supervisor to verify that plane swap.In that moment I initially decided to call MX control to inform directly of the new open write up; but then received the call back from dispatch again; verifying the plane swap; at the same time of informing him from the happenings and procedures we had to do and as why.In that moment I must have assumed that either dispatch forward the information again to MX control or even that I did it already while waiting for the call back; but have actually not done it.Upon landing in ZZZ I talked to the Chief Pilot about this; and agreed that MX control always needs to be informed asap; yes; and that with all the circumstances I must have assumed myself that I did it but had not. I immediately called MX control to inform about the new write up. The first they got from dispatch; yet the second one they saw it while on the plane; prior to my call.Usually; I am on top of these things; especially with priorities (like inform MX control first; as more important); yet with all the communication back-and-forths; in addition to prior information fwd via ACARS; and subsequently talking to dispatch while just prior wanting to call MX control; I assumed very wrongly that I informed MX control.While they got notified after we landed in ZZZ; I keep thinking of the consequences; like what if another crew would have a repo flight that night and arrives at that grounded airplane with open write up and not being able to do their flight? Etc...What I have learned from this is several things: if I have to call MX control; do it right away; another caller can call back again or I will call them back after informing MX; but first things first! And while fwd the message via ACARS to MX via dispatch; take the time to call myself; even if the passengers are delayed already; just do it. Also; I shall not assume that I have kept everyone informed. Take a moment to reflect and think back the steps. Did I inform dispatch? Check! Did I inform crew; ATC; pax; etc.? Check! Did I personally inform MX control? No; do it right away! And if they are informed already; now they are informed twice; ok; but I made sure it is done correctly.What I have learned from this is not to assume anything; but to double check that all steps have been done and procedures followed; even if this means that; like in this case; MX control would get notified several times with the same information; but I will make sure that I will do this right away; keeping the priorities in place.Also; despite a long delay and coordinating with crew; GA; dispatch; etc.; to keep focused on pending tasks without assuming these have been done; knowing that in all the confusion; there is always something that was missed out; and to go through all steps until everything is being confirmed as accomplished. Slowing down and taking the time to do the things right and prioritize them; and not getting myself distracted that could lead me to think that a current procedure I am on just got done.

MD-11 Captain reported flight control computer issues during approach resulted in loss of all autoflight capability. Pilot also reported the aircraft had been previously refused due to flight control computer malfunctions.

Descending through approx 12-13;000 feet for landing at ZZZZ; my FMS timed out as they occasionally do. Gave it a few moments to catch up and then selected the FMC1 prompt in the upper left hand corner of the FMC. Not only did it not reset; there was no standby option listed and I then noticed my First Officer's FMC had also lost all data. On a descent into ZZZZ at about 10;000 feet I decided it would be best if I assumed control of the airplane and we did a positive transfer of control. At about the same time I glanced over at the approach chart for ILS XXR went to the NAV page and manually entered the frequency and inbound course for ILS runway XXR. We had a Level 1 alert to set field altitude manually and I tasked that duty to my First Officer. I also said I had the radios at the time. I called ATC and informed them we had lost most of our normal navigation equipment; that we would be unable to proceed directly to any fix and that I would need vectors to join the runway XXR localizer. Passing 10;000 feet I would estimate we were approx 20-25 miles from the field. Several times the flight director was commanding directives that did not comply with our ATC directives so I was forced to turn it off as it was a distraction. The autothrottles also were not responding in an appropriate manner either and rather than trying to fight them I disconnected them as well. Conditions at the field were day VMC. On a vector and once cleared for the approach approach mode armed although I doubt it did any good I looked for the localizer to come alive and when it did I attempted to track it manually. There were a couple S turns as I was in real time having to adjust my scan away from looking for a flight director and towards just a localizer needle and a heading and trying to bracket it. Things became more stable as we continued down the localizer until we had the runway in sight still at many thousands of feet above the ground I transitioned to line up visually and then cross checking my localizer it showed right of course and I realized the piece of pavement many miles in front of me was the taxiway not the runway and shifted back to the left onto localizer at I would estimate 2;500-3;000 ft AGL. We probably should have asked for a visual approach at that time but we were too busy to even think of it. Now hand flying the airplane fully manually with no automation nor flight director assistance at around 2;000-2;500 feet I would estimate I leveled the airplane as the glide slope was approx 1 dot below us to join it. I did not even look at the approach plate to see were intercept altitude was as we were in visual conditions and I was too focused on maintaining manual aircraft control to be distracted looking away from the panel. ATC did ask us several times during the approach are you stabilized. We had the situation under control so I told me First Officer tell her yes. We were fully configured on glide slope and localizer with landing checklist complete by 1;000 feet AGL (actual more like 1;500-2;000 ft). There was a high speed foot on the airspeed indicator but no low speed foot. Based upon our landing weight and my prior experience in the airplane I flew the approach at 165 knots flaps 35. The approach and landing from 1000 feet AGL to touchdown was uneventful. This airplane had recent prior multiple flight control computer malfunctions that caused a prior crew to have a sudden pitch down moment according to the prior Captain. My goal was to get it on the ground as soon as it was safely possible and try to separate the automation from control of the aircraft to a reasonable extent.When we lost all our navigation data from both FMS so close to the airfield and with day VMC conditions at the field and my First Officer focusing on another checklist and given the recent history of this airplane; I decided the safest course was to revert back to old school flying and not waste time trying to manage the problem through running an extended Dual FMS Loss checklist and focus our efforts on getting the airplane on the ground.The prior day I witnessed two aircraft mechanics on this same jet in conflict over whether the airplane should be returned to service or not. One mechanic thought there was only 1 flight control computer having issues the other thought both computers were malfunctioning. One mechanic said the airplane was AOG to me 2 times. After that I went into the cockpit to observe their trouble shooting. One mechanic was simply trying to clear the fault in the CFDS (Centralized Fault Display System) the other wanted to know why and wanted more time to diagnose it. When one mechanic said to me the airplane is AOG a 3rd time I took the extraordinary step of calling the Duty Officer and telling him I was not crewing this airplane until the mechanics were given some time to troubleshoot and requested we be placed into rest. After minimum rest we came back to the jet and I spoke with the mechanic that was objecting to the return to service the previous night and he now seemed comfortable releasing the jet to fly.I personally witnessed one mechanic trying to pressure another to push the jet back on the line and I commend the mechanic who resisted. I don't know what happened after we left the airplane to then make him comfortable having it signed off; but I was told there would be 2 replacement flight control computers sent to this jet after I left it. Not sure if that actually occurred. I know we have a business to run but one of the mechanics told me at least one of the flight control computer issues was a repeat write up. Maybe we need to give more time and attention to issues that are repeatedly written up with a common problem source.

Flight crew reported difficulty in raising the trailing edge flaps and elected to divert instead of risking a grounded aircraft at an outstation.

Crew departed late due to brake accumulator issues on previous aircraft; and a potential one on this aircraft.Ground Ops were completely normal and the FO (First Officer) had no problems deploying the flaps to 3 for takeoff.Takeoff was normal and as we were turning to an assigned heading; we reached the cleanup altitude. I called for flaps 1 and noticed that the FO had some what I felt was minor difficulty bringing the flaps up to 1. This is not unusual; a hand slips; or the lever used to move the flap handle out of the detects isn't gripped correctly for easy retraction. I thought little of it.When I called for flaps UP; the raising was again delayed; and I noticed my FO reaching around with his right hand to put both hands on the flap lever to get it up. We talked about him having trouble getting them up; and I flew the aircraft only to ensure that I did not over speed the flaps. Eventually he was able to get them up which I saw on the speed tape on the PFD and I verified on the display; and flap handle position.We discussed what had happened a bit but decided to focus on safely exiting the terminal area and getting to altitude since the aircraft was now in the safe; and proper configuration. We made a plan to contact Maintenance Control at cruise and notify them of the problem and get advice about continuing the flight.After reaching altitude; the FO told me what he had encountered and explained how difficult it was to move the lever that released the flap handle from the detent to raise the flaps.A phone patch was initiated with dispatch and Maintenance Control and we discovered that our radio 2 wasn't able to receive over long distances. We ended up substituting radio 3 for radio 2 and temporarily disabling ACARS to complete the phone patch. Maintenance Control was very helpful on the phone patch and felt like he knew what the problem was. Maintenance Control was asked if he felt the aircraft should continue to ZZZZ; and he wanted it to go to a maintenance hub. As a Captain; I agreed with that thought process and asked the Dispatcher to bring in the Ops Manager so that we could all agree on a plan of action. We could have landed the aircraft at ZZZZ if there had been a flap malfunction; but the aircraft would have been stuck there quite a while.Eventually after consideration of landing lengths; the close to overweight landing weight of the aircraft; and the potential for wet runways in ZZZ1; that the best and safest place to divert the aircraft would be ZZZ1 in case the flaps would not deploy normally. Consideration was based on the worst case; flaps up scenario.Destination was changed with ATC once the plan was agreed upon by all parties and the phone patch was terminated and ACARS restored.Maintenance Control was asked via ACARS if we should leave the flaps down after landing and they asked them to retract them as much as we could.Fortunately; the landing in ZZZ1 was uneventful. The flaps deployed normally. Upon taxi-in. The flaps were retraced to position 1; where the handle binding began to be very difficult to overcome.Upon arrival at the gate; after shutdown; I tried to move the lever that releases the flap handle from the detent and found that it was impossible to move with just one hand.

We were doing a flaps 3 takeoff from [Runway] XXL. After the acceleration altitude; and above flap retraction speed; the pilot flying called for flaps to 1. I noticed; while moving the lever from 3 to 1; that the flap lever was nowhere near as smooth and free moving as it usually is; rather; it was quite difficult to move. As we accelerated through flap 1 retraction speed; it took considerable effort to get the lever out of the detent. I mentioned it to the captain who quickly made sure to raise the nose and not over speed the flaps as I used both hands to get the flap lever compressed and moved to the up position. The flaps moved as expected; with no issues; the flight control page showed normal; and the hydraulic page showed normal. We continued the climb out of ZZZ; and when reaching a safe altitude; I took the controls and radios with ATC; while the captain initiated an incredibly detailed conversation with dispatch and Maintenance Control. After exhausting every bit of information we could give; and every insight Maintenance Control had; the decision was made with dispatch and everyone in planning that they were talking to; to divert to ZZZ1 instead of potentially having a flight control issue on landing in ZZZZ; on a shorter runway; at an international station; and then leaving the plane there. We didn't [request priority] but asked approach to slow down early to get the flaps out and make sure they extended. We had planned every contingency for having to go around and then [request priority] if they didn't; and were ready to run whichever QRH abnormal procedure would have applied based on where the flaps ended up. On the approach; the flaps came down just fine and a normal landing was made. After landing; we planned; with maintenance approval; to attempt to retract the flaps but to stop if they locked again and not force anything. The lever was much less stiff from flaps full to flaps 1 than earlier; but again locked at the detent there. We left the flaps at 1 into the gate; let ramp know to tell anyone they could; and had maintenance meet us there. Sounded like they were going to replace the entire flap lever section.

EMB-175 flight crew reported a forward cargo compartment fire extinguishing system armed light and elected to continue the approach to landing. There was no evidence of smoke or flames when the compartment was opened by ramp personnel.

On the approach into ZZZ; already cleared to land via Tower and under visual conditions; we got a blue message on EICAS that stated 'CRG FWD FIREX HI ARM'. Me and the Captain discussed our options and decided that continuing to land would be our best option. I called the flight attendants in the back to make sure they didn't smell any smoke or realize any abnormalities which they both confirmed they hadn't! The blue Message on the EICAS actually was cleared away prior to our landing. Upon landing; we advised operations of what happened and told them to proceed with care. once at the gate; the Captain wrote the event in the logbook for further inspection by maintenance.

We planned and briefed a visual approach to [Runway] XXL. About 20-25 miles from ZZZ; we were cleared by ATC for the visual approach to XXL. We immediately turned direct for the visual approach.Shortly after crossing the far (north) shoreline; at about 12 nm WNW of ZZZ; we were over the water; still on a heading to intercept final; when the following EICAS Advisory (cyan) message appeared: 'CRG FWD FIREX HI ARM'. Associated with this was the illumination (in red) of the FWD CARGO fire extinguisher pushbutton; which indicated that the high-rate cargo fire bottle had indeed armed.We were on the lookout for the EICAS Warning (red) message CRG FWD SMOKE; but this NEVER appeared. Because of the lack of any Warning (red) or Caution (yellow) EICAS message and because there was NO secondary abnormality or indication of ANY kind (no other system failure indication and neither the pilots nor the FAs smelled smoke); we did not press the illuminated FWD CARGO fire extinguisher button. We want to emphasize that if a SMOKE condition HAD been sensed- or if smoke or fire had been reasonably-suspected by the crew; we would have IMMEDIATELY pushed the illuminated FWD CARGO fire extinguisher button (to discharge the high-rate bottle immediately followed automatically by the low-rate bottle one minute later) per the Immediate Action Card (IAC); and then transitioned to the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) checklist. But since there was no Smoke/Fire Condition sensed or reasonably-suspected; we did not go this route.Instead; the PF took the radios and instructed the PM to look in the QRH for anything related to the 'CRG FWD FIREX HI ARM' advisory (cyan) EICAS message; but there was zero guidance. There were also no cargo fire detection system failure messages on EICAS. The PM then called the FAs to inquire as to whether or not they smelled any odors or observed smoke of any kind. Neither the pilots; FAs; nor passengers; sensed nor observed any visible smoke or discernible abnormal odors (NOTE: only FAs were asked about odors; NOT the passengers; but we assume the passengers would have told the FAs if they had sensed something). Indeed; the Advisory (cyan) EICAS message disappeared about 30-40 seconds after it appeared; along with the FWD CARGO fire extinguisher push button ceasing to illuminate. This indicated to us that we had potentially made the right call and a SMOKE/FIRE Condition in the FWD CARGO BAY had indeed NOT BEEN DETECTED.The PM and PF discussed their options; and decided the safest option was to continue with the visual approach without pressing the illuminated FWD CARGO fire extinguisher button; BUT also BE READY TO PRESS that button; Declare Emergency; call for Fire Trucks; and continue for immediate landing IF either the Warning (red) EICAS message or ANY secondary indication were to appear. The existing clearance for visual approach was already the most expeditious landing clearance possible; and would get us on the ground the fastest if anything was to go wrong.After landing; as an additional measure of caution; we told Station to alert Ramp Agents to use extreme caution when opening the FWD Cargo Door; just in case there was somehow smoke; odors; or Halon in that bay. After Block-In and during the regular post-flight walk-around inspection; neither the CA nor any Rampers observed ANY signs of fire; smoke; nor odors in; nor discharged Halon extinguisher into; the Fwd Cargo Bay. After the flight; we debriefed with both Rampers and Flight Crew; called Maintenance Control and also warned the next flight crew (who was swapping into the aircraft) about what we had observed. We planned and briefed a visual approach to XXL. About 20-25 miles from ZZZ; we were cleared by ATC for the visual approach to XXL. We immediately turned direct for the visual approach.After landing; as an additional measure of caution; we told Station to alert Ramp Agents to use extreme caution when opening the FWD Cargo Door; just in case there wassomehow smoke; odors; or Halon in that bay. After Block-In and during the regular post-flight walk-around inspection; neither the CA nor any Rampers observed ANY signs of fire; smoke; nor odors in; nor discharged Halon extinguisher into; the Fwd Cargo Bay. After the flight; we debriefed with both Rampers and Flight Crew; called Maintenance Control and also warned the next flight crew (who was swapping into the aircraft) about what we had observed.This was a tough judgement call.An argument could be made to press the illuminated FWD Cargo fire extinguisher push button; immediately; as soon as it illuminates; even WITHOUT ANY 'CRG FWD SMOKE' EICAS Warning (red) message; as the arming of the fire bottle may be the sole (or advance) indication of a SMOKE or Fire condition.However; the cargo fire protection system is designed so that if all sensors are operational; several sensors must independently sense smoke before the fire detection system determines that a SMOKE Condition exists (resulting in 'CRG FWD SMOKE' EICAS Warning [red] message). Indeed; the QRH has a checklist for EICAS-annunciated 'CRG FWD SMOKE' Warning [red] message; not for Advisory (cyan) or Caution (yellow) messages related to Cargo Smoke.In addition; blowing the fire extinguisher bottles unnecessarily comes with its own issues (albeit with less serious consequences); such as ruining loss of luggage; death of any live animals in FWD Cargo Bay; and small safety hazard to ground crew opening the FWD Cargo door (due to lingering extinguishing material in the bay); following an in-flight discharge of fire extinguisher(s) into that bay. After a call to Maintenance Control; they suspected some sort of fault in the system; but that is unconfirmed.We believe we made the right judgement call; and the entire fellow flight crew- both the FO and FAs- are to be commended for assisting the CA in making the best decisions for safety of flight and ground crew.

C172 Flight Instructor reported expediting a previous landing and braking hard to make a taxiway contributed to a later occurrence of a nose wheel failure and a temporary runway closure at the airport.

While on an approximate 3-mile final to Runway XX at ZZZ in a Cessna Skyhawk 172S with a pre-solo student pilot; ZZZ Tower cleared a regional jet for takeoff. Departing aircraft was either a Regional Jet CRJ700 or an Embraer 175 E-175. The Tower Controller gave myself and my student the option to either 'extend upwind and expect landing clearance in 3 minutes;' or 'make a full stop taxi-back landing.' I made a transmission stating; 'Full stop taxi-back; Aircraft X.' Then we were cleared for a full stop taxi-back Runway XX. I advised my student we will come in on final approach slightly high and land long; desired touchdown point being the 1;000 ft. white blocks rather than the numbers 'XX.' After our higher-than normal approach to avoid wake turbulence from [the] departing jet and longer-than-normal touchdown point; I had to brake aggressively to make the right turn onto Taxiway XX. My student and I got off the runway; completed the items on the 'after landing' checklist; and then contacted Ground on [frequency]. I felt an abnormal shimmy coming from the nose wheel after letting the airplane slow to a stop on Taxiway XX; holding short of Taxiway XY. We then received our clearance to taxi via Taxiway XY to Runway XX. While holding short Runway XX on Taxiway XY; my student completed the 'pre-takeoff' checklist items and made his radio transmission for 'right closed traffic.' Tower told us to line-up-and-wait Runway XX and he also advised us of traffic coming in on final. I cannot remember if they were 5 miles out or 3 miles. During our takeoff roll I felt a slight shimmy coming from the nose wheel again; same sensation as when we first slowed to a stop while exiting on Taxiway XX. I also noticed our pitch attitude during the takeoff roll was slightly lower than normal. We continued with the takeoff because traffic was close behind us for Runway XX. I did not want to abort the takeoff and make the traffic behind me have to go around; so I decided to have my student continue with the takeoff. After reaching our right downwind leg; we advised Tower we would be making a full stop landing. I advised my student we would be making a soft-field landing; to keep as much weight off the nose wheel for as long as possible; because I suspected an issue with the nosewheel. The soft-field landing was successful; and the nose wheel did not make contact with the ground till rounding the turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. Once back pressure was released and the nose wheel made contact with the ground; the issue became apparent. The nose-wheel tire was completely deflated. Tower then asked if I could make it to the other side of the hold-short lines and I replied that I could and that I would bring the aircraft to a stop on the 'Compass Rose.' Tower then temporarily suspended operations on Runway XX so personnel could make a FOD inspection. Then two firetrucks and two county airport vehicles crossed Runway XX on Taxiway XZ to assist my student and I on the Compass Rose. We then pushed the aircraft to its parking space. A county airport worker called for clearance to cross Taxiway XA before we continued back to our parking space.My personal assessment of the factors leading to the deflated nose wheel tire and the temporary closure of Runway XX. An issue with the ATIS recording at the beginning of the flight was the first abnormality in a series of abnormalities on this flight. During this flight leading up to the events described previously; my student and I were advised to extend upwind and fly runway heading; make right traffic; make a 360; extend our upwind; and finally come in to land. A desire to come in and land after being delayed for so long caused me to make the decision to make the full-stop taxi-back under time-sensitive circumstances; rather than taking Tower's other option presented to me; which was to extend upwind and expect a landing clearance in another 3 minutes.After the full-stop taxi-back and after we were told toline-up-and-wait and that traffic was on final for Runway XX behind us; I decided to commit to the takeoff rather than to abort to prevent the traffic behind me from having to go around; despite my feeling that something was wrong with the nose wheel.Pressure from Tower and the busy environment of the ZZZ airport that day; along with the added pressures and obligations of instructing a pre-solo private pilot student led me to make two errors. Failing to ask to taxi back to our parking space during the initial shimmy experienced on Taxiway XX. Failing to abort the takeoff out of fear of causing an inconvenience to another pilot.Although my student was doing most of the manipulations of the flight controls and making most of the radio calls; I was responsible for the hard-braking to make Taxiway XX; and I was on the controls during the soft-field landing and during the left turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. I was also the pilot-in-command; therefore the responsibilities of this flight were mine; and I should have aborted the takeoff when I suspected an issue with the nose wheel.Traffic pattern was busy; my student and I were only able to make 2 landings with a Hobbs recording of 0.9 hours for the pattern-flight. No one was injured during this flight. Winds were variable during this mishap and weather was not a factor. I am not sick; I am not on any medications; I am not stressed; I have complied with Federal Aviation Regulation (FAR) 91.17; I got well-rested sleep the night before and was not fatigued during the flight; I am emotionally healthy and stable. The aircraft was thoroughly preflighted. All preflight checklists were adhered to and completed; FAR 91.9(a) adhered to.

Flight Crew reported multiple bird strikes and rejected the take off causing 2 main wheel fuse plugs to melt and deflate the tires; requiring a tow back to the ramp.

On takeoff roll ZZZ-ZZZ1 at (XA05L); we went through a large flock of birds. I observed numerous birds illuminated by the landing lights passing by both sides of the aircraft. We simultaneously heard several thumps as birds impacted the aircraft nose area. Considering the quantity of birds and impacts; I expeditiously decided to reject the takeoff in the interest of safety; concerned about the possibility of bird ingestion by the engines. Windshield wipers were on high in moderate rain with somewhat reduced visibility. Estimated speed at the time of the event was between 105-120 knots. We applied the rejected takeoff procedure; stopping with approximately 2;500 feet remaining; notified ATC; and initiated the rejected takeoff QRH checklist. Initially we expected more moderate brake temperatures; and did a 180 turn at tower's direction; expecting that we would later be able to taxi clear. We stopped; completed the Recommended Brake Cooling Schedule charts in the QRH Performance Inflight section; and monitored the Brake Temperature Monitoring System (BTMS) display. As the temperatures increased and we saw brake temp values increasing above 4-5; a decision was made to remain in place and request fire trucks; which were dispatched to our location; arriving after several minutes. In hindsight; remaining stopped straight ahead may have been the best option; however the turn did enable the fire trucks to approach us from the front; which aided in coordination; and possibly safety. The BTMS indications peaked at 7 on most brakes; 8 on two; and one eventually reached 9. The fire trucks monitored us for a time; seeing no indication of fire or smoke; but eventually informed us that we had 2 flat tires; one on each truck. At this point I shut down both engines and we ran the after landing checklist. We informed [the company] and the duty officer what had occurred; as well as coordinating through tower control; who was helpful at relaying information. The fire trucks continued to monitor us as the brakes cooled to the normal range and we coordinated with maintenance to be towed back to parking. Once the brakes had cooled; and the tug crew was on scene; the fire trucks were released; and maintenance towed us slowly to parking IAW their procedures. Maintenance inspections later found bloodstains on the leading edge slats #2 and #9. I wish to point out that the First officer performed in an exemplary fashion; providing extremely helpful and timely inputs and suggestions; his excellent CRM skills undoubtedly contributed to the safe outcome for this event. Thank you for your time. Multiple Bird Strikes on Takeoff Roll; leading to a rejected takeoff.Bird control at ZZZ; bird strike events are frequent

At (XA05 L) we were cleared for takeoff from runway XX. It was a rainy night after a typhoon had passed through; and although the wind was calm; we needed our wipers on for the rain. We were accelerating normally; I called 80 knots and the captain acknowledged. A few seconds later when my eyes were scanning the engine instruments I heard several thumps against the fuselage and heard the captain say 'Birds.' He later told me he said this when he saw many medium-sized white streaks pass through our lights. I saw the captain pull the thrust levers to idle and say 'Reject.' I believe we were about 110 knots (V1 of 143 knots was well above our speed on the speed scale) but I did not notice the exact speed. After a normal RTO procedure; the captain called and I completed the QRH procedure for Rejected Takeoff. Tower instructed us to make a 180 degree turn on the runway; and after the turn we noticed that the BTMS was climbing more than expected.I calculated for a 120 knots reject at our takeoff weight (345;000 lbs) we should see a BTMS Indication of 5. When the BTMS indication on several brakes increased above 5; I called Tower and requested the fire services to come check for fire and smoke from the brakes. After the fire services arrived and told us (via Tower because fire services did not have an aviation frequencies radio) there was no smoke or fire; we saw one wheel (#2) indicate BTMS 9; and two wheels (#3 and #4) indicate BTMS 8; so asked fire services if any tires were flat. They told us that one wheel on the left side was flat; and at that point the captain decided to start the APU and shut off the engines as it was clear that we would not be taxiing back. I tried calling Company ramp/maintenance on the frequency on the chart but we got no answer; so we asked Tower to relay information to our maintenance and request assistance. Fire services then relayed to us that a tire on the right side was also flat. Maintenance arrived around time XA50 and plugged in to the intercom to let us know they would inspect and decide on a course of action. At XB25 with BTMS in the range of 1-2; they started slowly towing us back to the ramp. We exited the runway at around XC05 and set the parking brake on the ramp at XC25 Z.Multiple Bird strikes on takeoff roll causing a rejected takeoffAirport authority should be better at controlling the birds at ZZZ airport

Air Carrier Captain reported a passenger and flight attendants felt ill during flight which was complicated by communications issues with Medlink. Passenger and flight attendants were treated by medical personnel on arrival at destination.

Roughly 2:30 into our flight I/We were informed by the #1 (flight attendant) [name 1] that our 3 other FA's(Flight Attendant) 'were not feeling to well' I asked some basic questions and asked to be updated as more info became available. Minutes later a rest room break and crew meals were coordinated and Name 1 came in the cockpit. During her time in the cockpit she once again told me that over all the other 3 FA's where 'not feeling well' I suggested hydration; inquired about ingestion of food and suggested portable O2. We talked about the possibility of contact with MedLink and even initiated several attempts on both of our iPads and quickly found out that both phone apps were not working. As she left the cockpit I once again asked to kept informed. I then proceeded to transfer radios and the aircraft to FO (First Officer) while I pursued alternate communication methods (VHF Press To Talk) Once communication was established with [company] I passed on the information of 'not feeling to well' gave [employee info] and requested to have medical personal to meet us upon our arrival into ZZZ (ETA at this time 70 minutes) I asked to be patched to MedLink to obtain some guidance. On my conversation with the medlink rep I gave the broad explanation that I had been told (This due to the lack of the [medical form]; I had requested from Name 1 at her earliest availability; in her absolute defense I understood she was alone handling the initial situation; not to mention later with the Pax occurrence) Simultaneously we had coordinated with ATC Direct routing and had gotten a Direct destination. VHF Press To Talk Communication issues arose and several calls were dropped/disconnected. I then was informed that a female pregnant passenger 'was having trouble breathing and did not feel well' At this juncture I verified all systems related to atmosphere conditions in the aircraft and requested even further decent from altitude to alleviate cabin altitude environment in the cabin.After several inquiries to Name 1 and Name 2 of possible scenarios including unfamiliar smells; I informed them that all relatable cabin atmospheric condition indications were normal and that we had the lowered the cabin Alt by 2;500 feet to alleviate the possible situations (to which I was told they 'felt better'). I continued my efforts to communicate with MedLink and once again requested [medical] sheets. (ETA at this point is apron 50 minutes) Considering the information that was passed along and the proximity to ZZZ and com issues I asked Name 1 to prioritize the [medical] Sheets because I would not have enough time (Proximity and Com. Issues ) to address all 4 situations! I was informed that Name 2 was feeling better and was actually present in the last several Inter-phone communications. At approximately ETA 35 minutes I was handed 3 [medical] forms to proceed communications with MED Link. The com issues continued (comm bleed communications etc etc) on top of the high load working environment; as ATC was starting to bring down the aircraft from Altitude. I started to feel out of the green and decided that due to the proximity of our destination; the expeditious handling (ATC) and the last information relayed to us with adjectives that signaled to stability and no apparent incapacitation; to desist with MedLink and concentrate on the arrival. (Also a Medical professional on board had addressed the patients and used the medical kit on Name 1 initiative.An emergency was not declared and landed uneventfully. We made a PA prior to reaching the gate asking the Pax to remain seated so Med personnel could come on board an attend the patients. On arrival at the gate and after shut down checklist items I proceeded to the galley to access the situation. There were several law enforcement officers meeting us initially and talking to the FA's (all 4) [name 1] then told me they had been authorized to deplane so a deplaning process commenced only to be halted 30 second laterby an apparent intervention of a Med Professional who had just arrived. The Main cabin door of the aircraft on both ends was very crowded with no regards to social distancing; I was overhearing and watching as the medical Professional was interviewing all 4 flight attendants. After the health state questions were answered and 'stability' was diagnosed; the Medical professional rushed off; (I assumed and concurred) advised Name 1 that a medical intervention or continuance would be better suited after deplaning. The female Pax patient was also at the cabin door; I had a brief conversation with her as to how she was feeling; to which she answered 'Much better now thank you.' I proceeded back to the cockpit to establish external electrical power and write in the logbook the need to re service all 3 O2 bottles that were used during the flight. By this time in the deplaning process a Maintenance employee had come on board; I told him that I was writing up the O2 bottles (he knew they were used in the flight) I stood in the cockpit door as the deplaning continued and also had a brief exchange of words with Name 3 and Name 1 in regards to their condition and coordinated follow up actions with Medical personnel. Which both acknowledged. I then expressed my concerns and hope you feel better sentiments. I would like to point out that at NO POINT in this entire situation and after queries on my behalf; was Crew incapacitation informed to me or First Officer. The use of FUMES AND ODORS IN THE CABIN was also at NO POINT reported/mentioned; nor we as the front end crew perceive such . In any of those situations I would have not hesitated to [request priority handling] and divert to nearest suitable airfield do to the obvious reasons. In two occasions in the many cabin inter phone communications I inquired about 'crew incapacitation' and my intentions if that were the case. As the other two crew members in the flight neither First Officer or myself had any symptoms of any kind from the start to the end of the flight. First Officer and myself crosschecked our physiological conditions and deemed we did not require any medical assistance of any kind and proceeded to conclude our duties.[A contributing cause] Air Phone App not working. Broad Communication. This situation had very Broad Human Physiological State communications breakdown due to the inability (at no ones fault) to have Professional medical evaluations in-place. And all seemed to line up to make things worse and get the entire team out of the green in several different moments and several times. I am not satisfied with the lack of SOPS that we all succumbed to once the aircraft was met at the gate by a Overwhelming amount of personnel. As I watched the medical professional interview the 'Patients' In this case 3 out of 4 FA'S (not the Passenger) considering my/our stable health state I knew I had no place to interfere or nothing to contribute. The well being of the 'Patients' was my main concern and I judged the Medical Professionals to be their best alternative at that moment. The lack of functionality of the Phone App was impacting unwarranted and complicated this situation immensely.

Flight Crew reported minor engine rumbles on takeoff and continuing the flight. After arrival at destination airport; it was discovered that the #2 engine had FOD damage. Reporters surmised it was probably caused by a technician leaving their Company iPad in the engine inlet.

At XA:10 we arrived at the aircraft in ZZZ for Flight X parked at gate X. In the logbook of Aircraft X was an open write up for Air Pack 2 REG fault. I spoke with the gate agent about it and then called dispatch. Dispatch conferenced me in with maintenance. It was known about the open write up since the night before. Maintenance advised me maintenance was on the way. We completed all the preflight duties and walk around items at about XA:35. Maintenance had come out to ascertain the problem at about XA:50; 10 minutes prior to our scheduled push time. Maintenance informed me that we would be delayed about one hour at the gate for a solution. Eventually maintenance informed me the pack would be selected off and the valve had to be visually scanned closed. To do that he would have to open a panel. Upon completion of the procedure by maintenance; I walked outside to see all the panels were closed on the right side of the aircraft. They were. Once back on the flight deck I received the signed off logbook with the deferred MEL item and proceeded with our checklists. As we were being pushed back; the maintenance member drove up to the guide man. We were asked to look on the flight deck and 1st class galley for an iPad. We found none and relayed the message back. We continued our start of both engines normally with no issues. We taxied out via Taxiway 1 to Taxiway 2 and took off from ZZZ on runway XX at about XC:48 local. After takeoff rotation there was just a slight rumble that sounded like an out of round tire usually does as the gear is raised. It abated quickly and no engine anomalies noted. Upon cruise to ZZZ1 we received an ACARS message from dispatch at XI:03; regarding FOD on the runway after our takeoff. Dispatch noted the possibility it was the maintenance member's iPad he was looking for. I told dispatch all engine parameters are normal and we proceeded to ZZZ1 with a normal landing on runway XXR. After the shutdown; I met the ZZZ1 Maintenance manager outside by the number 2 engine. It had signs of ingesting FOD. It is apparent that contract maintenance at ZZZ left the iPad inside the nacelle after our initial preflight and caused damage to the engine.Maintenance having laid an item in an engine nacelle and leaving it there after our preflight was complete.Not laying any tool or item in the nacelle of an engine.
